Title: AZR-004: Azure VM Disk Full — Diagnosing and Resolving Low or Exhausted Disk Space
Content:
# Azure VM Disk Full — Diagnosing and Resolving Low or Exhausted Disk Space

**Category:** Azure > Compute
**Article Code:** AZR-004
**Tier:** 2
**Audience:** Administrators / Technicians
**Estimated Resolution Time:** 20–45 minutes

## Symptoms / When to Use

Use this article when an Azure Virtual Machine reports low or full disk space. Typical signals:

- Applications or services fail to start, or the VM becomes unresponsive.
- Windows event logs show "There is not enough space on the disk."
- Linux commands report "No space left on device" (`ENOSPC`).
- Azure Monitor "OS Disk / Data Disk % Free Space" alerts fire.
- Users cannot save files; logs stop being written; SQL/IIS/app pools crash.

## Background

Azure VMs use managed disks with a **fixed provisioned size**. The OS disk and each data disk are separate volumes with independent capacity. Running out of space happens for a few recurring reasons: unbounded log growth, Windows Update/component store bloat, temp files, database/transaction-log growth, or a volume that was simply provisioned too small for its workload. Because managed disks do not auto-expand, resolution is either **reclaiming space** inside the guest OS or **growing the disk** at the Azure platform level and then extending the partition inside the OS.

## Resolution

### Step 1: Identify which disk is full

**Windows (in the VM):**
```powershell
Get-Volume | Sort-Object SizeRemaining | Format-Table DriveLetter, FileSystemLabel, `
  @{N='Size(GB)';E={[math]::Round($_.Size/1GB,1)}}, `
  @{N='Free(GB)';E={[math]::Round($_.SizeRemaining/1GB,1)}}
```

**Linux (in the VM):**
```bash
df -h            # human-readable free space per filesystem
sudo du -xh / --max-depth=1 2>/dev/null | sort -rh | head -20   # biggest top-level dirs
```

### Step 2: Reclaim space inside the guest OS (do this first)

Reclaiming is faster and cheaper than resizing. Common wins:

**Windows:**
```powershell
# Clear Windows Update / component store bloat
Dism.exe /online /Cleanup-Image /StartComponentCleanup
# Purge temp files
Remove-Item "$env:TEMP\*","C:\Windows\Temp\*" -Recurse -Force -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue
# Find the largest files on C:
Get-ChildItem C:\ -Recurse -File -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue |
  Sort-Object Length -Descending | Select-Object FullName,
  @{N='GB';E={[math]::Round($_.Length/1GB,2)}} -First 20
```
Also check IIS logs (`C:\inetpub\logs`), SQL backups/`.ldf` files, and `C:\Windows\Minidump`.

**Linux:**
```bash
sudo journalctl --vacuum-size=200M        # trim systemd journal
sudo apt-get clean || sudo yum clean all  # package cache
# Find files >500MB
sudo find / -xdev -type f -size +500M -exec ls -lh {} \; 2>/dev/null
```

### Step 3: If reclaiming isn't enough, grow the managed disk

Expanding a disk requires the VM to be **deallocated** (stopped) for OS disks; data disks on many VM sizes support online resize, but stopping is the safe default. **You cannot shrink a managed disk** — only grow.

```bash
# Azure CLI — resize the OS or data disk (VM should be stopped/deallocated)
az vm deallocate --resource-group <rg> --name <vm>
az disk update --resource-group <rg> --name <disk-name> --size-gb 256
az vm start --resource-group <rg> --name <vm>
```

### Step 4: Extend the partition inside the OS

Growing the Azure disk does **not** grow the partition — the OS still sees the old size until you extend it.

**Windows:**
```powershell
$drive = "C"
$size = (Get-PartitionSupportedSize -DriveLetter $drive)
Resize-Partition -DriveLetter $drive -Size $size.SizeMax
```

**Linux (example for /dev/sda1):**
```bash
sudo growpart /dev/sda 1
sudo resize2fs /dev/sda1     # ext4;  use xfs_growfs /mountpoint for XFS
```

### Step 5: Verify

Re-run `Get-Volume` / `df -h` and confirm free space. Restart any services that failed, and clear the Azure Monitor alert once metrics recover.

## Troubleshooting

- **Resize-Partition shows no extra space:** confirm the disk resize completed in Azure and that Windows sees the new size in Disk Management (rescan disks).
- **XFS vs ext4:** use `xfs_growfs` for XFS root volumes; `resize2fs` only works on ext2/3/4.
- **Temp disk confusion:** the ephemeral temp disk (`D:` on Windows, `/mnt` on Linux) is **not** persistent — never store data there expecting it to survive deallocation.
- **Data disk online resize fails:** some VM sizes require a stop/deallocate; deallocate and retry.

## Prevention

- Set Azure Monitor alerts on **% Free Space** at 20% and 10% thresholds.
- Redirect application/IIS/SQL logs to a dedicated, right-sized data disk with log rotation.
- Enable log rotation (`logrotate` on Linux; scheduled cleanup on Windows).
- Right-size disks at deployment and review growth quarterly.
- Schedule `StartComponentCleanup` and temp cleanup as a recurring task.

**Tags:** azure, virtual machine, disk full, managed disk, resize, storage, powershell

Title: AZR-006: Azure AD (Entra) Connect Health Sync Errors
Content:
# Azure AD (Entra) Connect Health Sync Errors

**Category:** Azure > Identity
**Article Code:** AZR-006
**Tier:** 3
**Audience:** Administrators / Technicians
**Estimated Resolution Time:** 30 minutes – 4 hours (longer where data cleanup or agent re-registration is required)

Microsoft Entra Connect Health surfaces synchronization problems from the on-premises Microsoft Entra Connect (formerly Azure AD Connect) server into the Microsoft Entra admin center. This article covers the two failure classes technicians most often confuse: **object-level sync errors** (duplicate attributes, data validation, data mismatch) reported under **Sync errors**, and **Connect Health infrastructure alerts** (agent not reporting, sync service down, export blocked). Both show up in the same portal blade, but they have different root causes and different fixes.

## Symptoms / When to Use

- Connect Health raises an alert such as **Export to Microsoft Entra ID failed**, **Import from Microsoft Entra ID failed**, **Password Hash Synchronization stopped working**, or **Microsoft Entra Connect Sync Service isn't running**.
- The **Sync errors** blade lists object errors: `AttributeValueMustBeUnique`, `QuarantinedAttributeValueMustBeUnique`, `InvalidSoftMatch`, `ObjectTypeMismatch`, or `IdentityDataValidationFailed`.
- A **Health service data isn't up to date** alert fires — the portal shows stale data because the agent has not uploaded in the last two hours.
- End users report a new hire's account, mailbox, or license is missing, or that changes made in on-premises AD are not appearing in Microsoft 365.
- A banner reads **Alert evaluation is limited. Update your settings to enable all alerts.**
- The **Export to Microsoft Entra ID was stopped. Accidental delete threshold was reached** alert appears after a bulk change or OU move.
- Email digests of sync errors arrive daily at the tenant's technical contact address.

## Background

Microsoft Entra Connect runs a scheduler (default cycle: 30 minutes) that performs import, sync, and export steps between on-premises Active Directory and Microsoft Entra ID. Separately, the **Microsoft Entra Connect Health agent** installed on the same server uploads operational data, error events, and performance metrics to the cloud Health service roughly every few minutes. The portal you look at is a view of that uploaded data — so a stale portal can mean the *agent* is broken even when *sync* is healthy, and vice versa.

Object-level errors originate in the export step: Microsoft Entra ID rejects an object because it violates a uniqueness or format constraint. The most common is duplicate `proxyAddresses` or `userPrincipalName` values across two objects with different `sourceAnchor` (immutableId) values. Microsoft's duplicate attribute resiliency feature quarantines the conflicting value rather than blocking the whole object, which is why you see the `Quarantined...` variants. These errors are **data problems** — restarting services will not fix them; the source data must be corrected, almost always on-premises.

Infrastructure alerts originate from the agent or the sync engine itself: a stopped service, a blocked outbound endpoint, TLS inspection breaking the agent certificate, or an export halted by the accidental-deletion safeguard. A key gotcha: if Connect uses a **customized attribute filtering** configuration (not the default), the Health agent will not upload error events, alert evaluation is limited, and the **Sync errors** list under-reports. Enable full error upload in Health settings before trusting the portal.

## Resolution

Work top-down: confirm the agent is reporting, confirm the sync engine is running, then remediate individual object errors.

### Step 1: Confirm the Connect Health agent is reporting

On the Connect server, verify the two agent services are running.

```powershell
Get-Service "Microsoft Entra Connect Health Agent", "Microsoft Entra Connect Agent Updater" |
    Select-Object Name, Status, StartType
```

Test outbound connectivity from the agent to the Health service. The `-Role` value for a sync server is `Sync`:

```powershell
Test-AzureADConnectHealthConnectivity -Role Sync
```

If the test fails, the agent cannot reach one or more required endpoints. Confirm outbound access (TCP 443, and TCP 5671 for older agents) to at least:

- `*.aadconnecthealth.azure.com`
- `*.adhybridhealth.azure.com`
- `*.blob.core.windows.net`
- `*.servicebus.windows.net`
- `https://management.azure.com`
- `https://login.microsoftonline.com` and `https://login.windows.net`

Do not apply TLS inspection/termination to these URLs — it replaces the agent certificate and breaks registration and uploads.

### Step 2: Enable full error upload (clear the limited-evaluation banner)

If the portal shows the **Alert evaluation is limited** banner, the Health service is not receiving all error events (typically because attribute filtering is customized).

1. Go to the [Microsoft Entra admin center](https://entra.microsoft.com).
2. Search for and open **Microsoft Entra Connect Health**.
3. Select **Microsoft Entra Connect (sync)**, then your sync service, then **Settings**.
4. Set the option to allow the agent to upload all error logs to **ON**, and **Save**.

Allow up to two hours for the portal to reflect the full error set.

### Step 3: Verify the sync scheduler and service state

Load the ADSync module (required if you are on a domain controller or hardened host), then read the scheduler configuration:

```powershell
Import-Module ADSync
Get-ADSyncScheduler
```

Check these fields:

- **SyncCycleEnabled** — should be `True`. If `False`, no import/sync/export runs.
- **MaintenanceEnabled** — should be `True` (rotates keys/certs, purges logs).
- **NextSyncCycleStartTimeInUTC** — confirms the schedule is advancing.

If the scheduler is disabled and the server is not intentionally in staging mode, re-enable it:

```powershell
Set-ADSyncScheduler -SyncCycleEnabled $true
```

If the **Microsoft Entra Connect Sync Service isn't running** alert is present, start the sync service via the Services console (**Services.msc** → **Microsoft Entra ID Sync** → **Start**) or restart it after a Password Hash Sync heartbeat alert.

### Step 4: Force a sync cycle to refresh errors

The **Sync errors** report reflects the latest sync attempt and refreshes about every 30 minutes. To re-evaluate immediately after a change, trigger a delta cycle:

```powershell
Start-ADSyncSyncCycle -PolicyType Delta
```

Use a full (initial) cycle only when you changed sync rules or filtering, because it reprocesses every object and is time-consuming:

```powershell
Start-ADSyncSyncCycle -PolicyType Initial
```

To avoid a full cycle across all connectors, mark only the affected connector for a full import or full sync, then run a delta cycle. Get the connector name first:

```powershell
Get-ADSyncConnector | Select-Object Name, Identifier
Set-ADSyncSchedulerConnectorOverride -ConnectorName "contoso.com" -FullImportRequired $true
Start-ADSyncSyncCycle -PolicyType Delta
```

If a cycle is already running and blocking a config change, stop it (non-destructive; pending changes process on the next run):

```powershell
Stop-ADSyncSyncCycle
```

### Step 5: Remediate duplicate attribute errors

For `AttributeValueMustBeUnique` and `QuarantinedAttributeValueMustBeUnique`, two objects share a value on a uniqueness-constrained attribute (`mail`, `proxyAddresses`, `signInName`, `userPrincipalName`, `onPremisesSecurityIdentifier`, `sipProxyAddress`).

First try the built-in diagnostic, which can auto-fix orphaned-object cases from the cloud side (requires Azure RBAC **Contributor** at minimum on the Health resource):

1. In the admin center, open **Microsoft Entra Connect Health** → **Microsoft Entra Connect (sync)** → **Sync errors**.
2. Locate the error and check the **Diagnose status** column (`Not Started`, `Manual Fix Required`, `Pending Sync`).
3. Select **Diagnose**, answer the identification questions, and if an **Apply Fix** button appears, apply it. This is only offered for the *orphaned object* scenario — it updates the `Source Anchor` on the existing cloud object and deletes the conflicting one. It never edits other attributes.

For the common scenario (two genuinely different users), fix the data at the source:

1. Identify the two objects and the duplicated value. The Connect Health sync error report names both.
2. Decide which object legitimately keeps the value.
3. Remove or correct the duplicated value on the *other* object, in the directory that sources it (usually on-premises AD via **Active Directory Users and Computers** → **Attribute Editor**, or PowerShell such as `Set-ADUser`).
4. Let the next sync cycle (Step 4) clear the error.

If Apply Fix reports **User with conflicting attribute is soft deleted**, hard-delete the conflicting cloud object first:

```powershell
# Remove the object from the Microsoft Entra recycle bin (permanent)
Remove-MgDirectoryDeletedItem -DirectoryObjectId "<objectId>"
```

Then retry the fix on the next cycle.

### Step 6: Clear the accidental-deletion export block

If **Export to Microsoft Entra ID was stopped. Accidental delete threshold was reached** fired, more objects were staged for deletion than the configured threshold (default 500), and *no* deletions were exported.

1. Review the pending deletes in **Synchronization Service Manager** → **Operations**, or:

```powershell
Get-ADSyncExportDeletionThreshold
```

2. If the deletions are legitimate (for example, a planned OU decommission), allow this export to proceed once:

```powershell
Enable-ADSyncExportDeletionThreshold -DeletionThreshold 800
Start-ADSyncSyncCycle -PolicyType Delta
```

3. If the deletions are **not** expected, do not raise the threshold — investigate what removed the objects from sync scope (a filtering change, an OU move, or an accidental bulk delete in AD) and restore scope before running export.

## Troubleshooting

**Portal shows old data / "Health service data isn't up to date."** The agent has not uploaded complete data in two hours. Re-run `Test-AzureADConnectHealthConnectivity -Role Sync`. If connectivity is fine but data is still stale, re-register the agent. On current builds use:

```powershell
Register-MicrosoftEntraConnectHealthAgent
```

On older agent builds the sync-specific cmdlet is still valid:

```powershell
Register-AzureADConnectHealthSyncAgent -AttributeFiltering:$false -StagingMode:$false
```

Registration requires a Global Administrator or Hybrid Identity Administrator (or a delegated identity via Azure RBAC) **without** MFA enforced on that sign-in, since registration is non-interactive-capable. Wait about two hours after re-registration before judging the result.

**`The sync command or cmdlet isn't available`.** The ADSync module is not loaded — common on domain controllers or hardened servers. Run `Import-Module ADSync`, or point to the full path:

```powershell
Import-Module "C:\Program Files\Microsoft Azure AD Sync\Bin\ADSync\ADSync.psd1"
```

**Errors persist after fixing the data.** Confirm you edited the *source* directory, not the cloud object, for synced users — cloud edits are overwritten on the next cycle. Then force a delta cycle. If the object attribute you changed is not currently imported, the connector needs a full import: use `Set-ADSyncSchedulerConnectorOverride -ConnectorName "<name>" -FullImportRequired $true` before the cycle.

**`InvalidSoftMatch`.** A soft match failed because the incoming object carries an `immutableId`/`sourceAnchor` that differs from an existing cloud object matched on `proxyAddresses`/`userPrincipalName`. With duplicate attribute resiliency enabled tenant-wide, you typically will not see this on new-object provisioning. When it does occur, resolve the duplicate source values, or clear the conflicting `immutableId` on the intended object.

**`IdentityDataValidationFailed`.** The `userPrincipalName` contains unsupported characters or an invalid format. Correct the UPN in the source directory to a valid RFC-compliant format with a routable, verified domain suffix.

**High CPU / High Memory alerts on the Connect server.** These are performance alerts, not sync errors. Identify the offending process and confirm it is expected before restarting:

```powershell
Get-Process | Sort-Object -Descending CPU | Select-Object -First 10
```

Sustained pressure means the server is undersized for object count — re-evaluate sizing.

**Password Hash Sync heartbeat skipped / stopped.** Restart the **Microsoft Entra ID Sync** service (Services.msc). If it recurs, check that PHS is still enabled in the Connect wizard and that outbound auth endpoints are reachable.

## Prevention

- **Keep attribute filtering at default where possible**, and if you must customize it, enable full error-log upload in Health settings so alert evaluation stays complete.
- **Enforce a single authoritative source for `proxyAddresses` and UPN.** Provision new accounts from a template and validate `mail`/UPN uniqueness at the HR/IdM layer before they reach AD to prevent duplicate-attribute errors at the source.
- **Enable Connect Health email notifications** so the daily error digest reaches the service desk queue, not an individual mailbox. Configure this under **Sync errors** → **Notification Settings**, and include a shared distribution list.
- **Allowlist the required Health endpoints explicitly** and exclude them from TLS inspection. Prefer the latest agent so only TCP 443 is required.
- **Keep the agent on auto-upgrade** (default) and monitor the **Microsoft Entra Connect Agent Updater** service.
- **Right-size the accidental-deletion threshold** for your environment and treat any threshold-reached alert as an incident, not a nuisance — never blindly raise it.
- **Use staging mode** for a warm-standby Connect server so you can fail over without re-solving sync errors during an outage.
- **Run `Get-ADSyncScheduler` as a periodic health check** to confirm `SyncCycleEnabled` and `MaintenanceEnabled` remain `True` after upgrades and reboots.

---

Sources verified against Microsoft Learn:
- https://learn.microsoft.com/entra/identity/hybrid/connect/how-to-connect-health-diagnose-sync-errors
- https://learn.microsoft.com/entra/identity/hybrid/connect/how-to-connect-sync-feature-scheduler
- https://learn.microsoft.com/entra/identity/hybrid/connect/how-to-connect-health-agent-install

Title: AZR-007: Azure Backup Retention Policy Configuration and Failures
Content:
# Azure Backup Retention Policy Configuration and Failures

**Category:** Azure > Backup
**Article Code:** AZR-007
**Tier:** 2
**Audience:** Administrators / Technicians
**Estimated Resolution Time:** 30–90 minutes (longer if a policy-update job fails on individual items and requires a fix pass)

## Symptoms / When to Use

- Recovery points are aging out sooner than expected, or the vault is retaining more restore points than the policy defines.
- A retention change made in the portal or via script did not apply to existing recovery points.
- `Set-AzRecoveryServicesBackupProtectionPolicy` or `az backup policy set` returns an error, or the policy-update job completes with some items in a failed/inconsistent state.
- A policy modification is blocked with an authorization error on a vault protected by Multi-user authorization (MUA) / Resource Guard.
- Client asks to extend retention for compliance (LTR — weekly/monthly/yearly) or reduce it to cut storage cost.
- Backup items where the source VM/share was deleted keep incurring cost because the last recovery point is retained.

## Background

An Azure Backup policy in a Recovery Services vault has two components: a **schedule** (when backups run — daily or weekly) and a **retention** definition (how long each recovery point is kept). Retention is defined independently for **daily**, **weekly**, **monthly**, and **yearly** recovery points. Monthly and yearly retention is called **Long-Term Retention (LTR)**.

Two behaviors drive most tickets:

1. **Policy changes apply retroactively.** When you change retention duration, the new duration is applied to existing recovery points as well as future ones. Reducing retention marks older points for pruning in the next cleanup (garbage-collection) job; increasing it extends existing points. Changing daily→weekly cleans up existing daily points; weekly→daily retains existing weekly points for their remaining days. (Note: for LTR-only workloads such as Azure SQL Database LTR, changes apply to *future* backups only — a different model.)
2. **Pruning is asynchronous.** Expired points are removed by a periodic cleanup job, not instantly, so a storage/count drop lags the policy change. Additionally, if the source data no longer exists, up to the two most recent recovery points can be retained beyond policy expiry by garbage-collection cycles, and the latest point is kept until you stop protection and delete data.

Policy edits go through the **Az.RecoveryServices** PowerShell module or the **az backup** CLI. On MUA-protected vaults, reducing retention is a protected operation and requires a Resource Guard authorization token.

## Resolution

### Step 1: Confirm the current policy and its assigned items

PowerShell — set the vault context first, then read the policy:

```powershell
Connect-AzAccount
$vault = Get-AzRecoveryServicesVault -ResourceGroupName "rg-backup" -Name "rsv-prod01"
Set-AzRecoveryServicesVaultContext -Vault $vault

$pol = Get-AzRecoveryServicesBackupProtectionPolicy -Name "DefaultPolicy" -VaultId $vault.ID
$pol.RetentionPolicy
```

CLI equivalent (export to JSON so you can edit it):

```bash
az backup policy show \
  --resource-group rg-backup \
  --vault-name rsv-prod01 \
  --name DefaultPolicy \
  --output json > policy.json
```

### Step 2: Modify retention with PowerShell (VM example)

Fetch base objects, adjust the retention properties, then apply. This example keeps 30 daily, 12 weekly (Sunday), and 60 monthly points, and disables yearly:

```powershell
$schPol = Get-AzRecoveryServicesBackupSchedulePolicyObject -WorkloadType "AzureVM"
$retPol = Get-AzRecoveryServicesBackupRetentionPolicyObject -WorkloadType "AzureVM"

# Daily
$retPol.IsDailyScheduleEnabled = $true
$retPol.DailySchedule.DurationCountInDays = 30

# Weekly
$retPol.IsWeeklyScheduleEnabled = $true
$retPol.WeeklySchedule.DaysOfTheWeek.Clear()
$retPol.WeeklySchedule.DaysOfTheWeek.Add("Sunday")
$retPol.WeeklySchedule.DurationCountInWeeks = 12

# Monthly
$retPol.IsMonthlyScheduleEnabled = $true
$retPol.MonthlySchedule.DurationCountInMonths = 60

# Yearly off
$retPol.IsYearlyScheduleEnabled = $false

Set-AzRecoveryServicesBackupProtectionPolicy `
  -Policy $pol `
  -RetentionPolicy $retPol `
  -SchedulePolicy $schPol `
  -VaultId $vault.ID
```

For **Azure Files**, get the retention object with the workload and tier, e.g. `Get-AzRecoveryServicesBackupRetentionPolicyObject -WorkloadType AzureFiles -BackupTier VaultStandard`.

### Step 3: Modify retention with the Azure CLI (JSON edit)

Edit the exported `policy.json`. Retention counts live under `retentionPolicy` in blocks keyed by `retentionDuration`:

```json
"retentionDuration": {
  "count": 60,
  "durationType": "Weeks"
}
```

`durationType` accepts `Days`, `Weeks`, `Months`, or `Years`. Save, then apply:

```bash
az backup policy set \
  --resource-group rg-backup \
  --vault-name rsv-prod01 \
  --name DefaultPolicy \
  --policy @policy.json
```

If you need a clean template to start from, generate one with `az backup policy get-default-for-vm`.

### Step 4: Confirm the change and let cleanup run

Re-read the policy (Step 1) to confirm the new counts. The policy-update job appears under **Backup Jobs**; existing recovery points are re-marked immediately, but expired points are physically removed by the next cleanup cycle — allow several hours before judging storage/count.

```powershell
Get-AzRecoveryServicesBackupJob -VaultId $vault.ID -Operation ConfigureBackup |
  Select-Object WorkloadName, Status, StartTime, EndTime
```

## Troubleshooting

**Policy update fails on some items ("inconsistent items").** When a policy protects many items and a subset fails to update, re-run the apply with the fix flag so Azure Backup retries only the failed items:

```powershell
Set-AzRecoveryServicesBackupProtectionPolicy -Policy $pol -VaultId $vault.ID -FixForInconsistentItems
```

```bash
az backup policy set \
  --resource-group rg-backup --vault-name rsv-prod01 \
  --name DefaultPolicy --policy @policy.json \
  --fix-for-inconsistent-items true
```

**Authorization error on an MUA / Resource Guard–protected vault.** Reducing retention is a critical operation. Obtain a Resource Guard token (from the tenant that owns the guard) and pass it. On the CLI, supply `--tenant-id` when the Resource Guard lives in a different tenant; in PowerShell, pass `-Token` (or `-SecureToken`) to `Set-AzRecoveryServicesBackupProtectionPolicy`. Confirm the requesting identity has the required Reader/approver role on the Resource Guard.

**Retention reduced but storage/count did not drop.** This is expected latency — pruning happens in the async cleanup job. Also verify no **on-demand** recovery points are inflating the count: on-demand backups carry their own retention and are *not* governed by policy retention. Reserved-instance blob storage and incremental-chain merging also mean storage reduction is gradual, not 1:1 with expired points.

**Backup item keeps costing money after the source is gone.** If a VM or share was deleted without stopping protection, scheduled jobs fail (e.g. `UserErrorVmNotFoundV2`), data is retained per policy, and the most recent recovery point is kept indefinitely. To stop charges, stop protection and delete backup data on that item (soft delete then holds it 14 additional days before permanent removal).

**Version errors from the cmdlets.** `Set-AzRecoveryServicesBackupProtectionPolicy` and the Azure Files retention objects require current Az.RecoveryServices. Update with `Update-Module Az.RecoveryServices` (minimum 2.6.0 for Azure Files scenarios) and reconnect.

**Portal path if scripting is blocked:** Recovery Services vault > **Backup policies** > select the policy > adjust the Retention range grid (daily/weekly/monthly/yearly) > **Update**. Track the resulting **Configure backup** job under **Backup jobs**.

## Prevention

- **Model retention before applying.** Because changes are retroactive, a reduction permanently prunes existing points at the next cleanup. Document the client's RPO/RTO and compliance retention, and get sign-off before reducing.
- **Group items with identical schedule + retention under one policy;** split large fleets (e.g. 100 VMs per policy, staggered start times) to distribute backup load rather than overloading a single policy.
- **Use LTR (monthly/yearly) for compliance,** short daily/weekly for operational recovery — don't inflate daily retention to satisfy audit needs.
- **Enable soft delete and MUA/Resource Guard** on production vaults so retention reductions and deletes require a second approval and a 14-day recovery window.
- **Audit orphaned backup items** periodically for sources whose primary data no longer exists, and clean up restore-point collections left behind by resource-group locks.
- **Version-control policy JSON** exported via `az backup policy show` so retention definitions are reproducible and diffable across tenants.
- **Validate after every change** by re-reading the policy and watching the update job to completion; never assume the count/storage impact is immediate.

**Tags:** azure-backup, recovery-services-vault, retention-policy, long-term-retention, powershell, az-cli, resource-guard, mua, garbage-collection, backup-policy

Title: AZR-010: Azure Load Balancer Backend Health Probe Failures
Content:
# Azure Load Balancer Backend Health Probe Failures

**Category:** Azure > Networking
**Article Code:** AZR-010
**Tier:** 2
**Audience:** Administrators / Technicians
**Estimated Resolution Time:** 20–60 minutes (longer if an application-side fix is required)

Azure Load Balancer health probes continuously test each backend instance. When a probe fails the configured number of times, the platform removes that instance from rotation, so traffic stops flowing to it. This article covers diagnosing and resolving probe failures on Standard (and Basic) Azure Load Balancer for both TCP and HTTP/HTTPS probes.

## Symptoms / When to Use

- Azure portal shows backend pool instances with a health status of **Down** or **Degraded** on the load balancing rule's health status view.
- The **Health Probe Status** metric reads 0% (or below 100%) for one or more backend instances.
- Clients report intermittent timeouts, uneven traffic distribution, or `connection refused` against the frontend IP.
- Load balancer health event log shows a **NoHealthyBackends** or **DataPathAvailabilityCritical** event.
- Portal reason codes such as `Down_Probe_TcpProbeTimeout`, `Down_Probe_HttpStatusCodeError`, `Down_Probe_HttpEndpointUnreachable`, or `Down_Probe_HttpNoResponse`.
- A newly deployed VM or scale set instance never enters rotation.

## Background

The Azure Load Balancer health probe originates from the fixed platform IP address **168.63.129.16**, not from the frontend or client IP. Every backend instance must accept traffic from this source on the probe port, or the probe fails.

A probe evaluates one endpoint (port + protocol, plus a path for HTTP/HTTPS) and marks an instance **Down** after `numberOfProbes` consecutive failures at the configured `intervalInSeconds`. For HTTP/HTTPS probes, only an HTTP **200** response counts as healthy; any other status code, a reset, or no response marks the instance down. TCP probes require a completed three-way handshake.

The five most common root causes are:

1. The backend application is not listening on the probe port (crashed, stopped, or bound to `127.0.0.1` instead of `0.0.0.0`).
2. An NSG or host firewall blocks the probe source IP `168.63.129.16` on the probe port.
3. Ghosted / stale NIC references remain in the backend pool.
4. Probe port, protocol, or HTTP path does not match what the application actually serves.
5. The application responds more slowly than the probe timeout allows (cold start or heavy load).

Set these environment variables to shorten the commands below:

```bash
RG="myResourceGroup"
LB="myLoadBalancer"
PROBE="myHealthProbe"
```

## Resolution

### Step 1: Confirm probe status and read the reason code

In the portal: **Load Balancers** > your LB > **Settings** > **Load balancing rules** > **View details** under **Health status**. Note the per-instance reason code — it points directly at the failure class (TCP timeout vs. HTTP status error vs. endpoint unreachable).

Then dump the current probe definition so you know exactly what is being tested:

```bash
az network lb probe show \
  --resource-group "$RG" \
  --lb-name "$LB" \
  --name "$PROBE" \
  --output table
```

Record the `protocol`, `port`, `requestPath`, `intervalInSeconds`, and `numberOfProbes`. Everything downstream is compared against these values.

PowerShell equivalent:

```powershell
$slb = Get-AzLoadBalancer -Name "myLoadBalancer" -ResourceGroupName "myResourceGroup"
Get-AzLoadBalancerProbeConfig -Name "myHealthProbe" -LoadBalancer $slb
```

### Step 2: Verify the backend is listening on the probe port

Sign in to a backend VM and confirm a process is bound to the probe port on all interfaces, not just loopback.

Windows:

```cmd
netstat -ano | findstr :80
```

Linux:

```bash
sudo ss -tlnp | grep ':80'
```

If the port is missing, the service is down or misbound. A `127.0.0.1:80` binding will fail the probe — the application must listen on `0.0.0.0` (all interfaces). Start or restart the service and re-check:

```bash
sudo systemctl restart nginx
sudo systemctl status nginx
```

### Step 3: Test the probe endpoint the way Azure does

TCP probe — verify the handshake completes from another VM in the same VNet:

```bash
nc -vz 10.0.0.4 80
```

HTTP/HTTPS probe — the path must return HTTP **200**:

```bash
curl -sS -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code}\n" http://10.0.0.4:80/health
```

Any non-200 result (301, 302, 401, 403, 404, 500) fails the probe. Point the probe at a lightweight endpoint that returns 200 and does not depend on slow downstream services.

### Step 4: Allow the probe source IP in NSGs

The probe traffic carries source IP `168.63.129.16` and is represented by the **AzureLoadBalancer** service tag. Ensure no rule with higher priority than the default `AllowAzureLoadBalancerInBound` blocks it. Inspect the effective rules on the NIC or subnet NSG:

```bash
az network nsg rule list \
  --resource-group "$RG" \
  --nsg-name "myBackendNsg" \
  --output table
```

If a deny rule shadows the probe, add a high-priority allow rule:

```bash
az network nsg rule create \
  --resource-group "$RG" \
  --nsg-name "myBackendNsg" \
  --name "Allow-AzureLoadBalancer-Probe" \
  --priority 100 \
  --direction Inbound \
  --access Allow \
  --protocol "*" \
  --source-address-prefixes AzureLoadBalancer \
  --destination-port-ranges 80 \
  --destination-address-prefixes "*"
```

Also confirm the in-guest firewall permits the probe. Windows example:

```powershell
New-NetFirewallRule -DisplayName "Allow LB Probe" -Direction Inbound `
  -Protocol TCP -LocalPort 80 -RemoteAddress 168.63.129.16 -Action Allow
```

Linux (firewalld):

```bash
sudo firewall-cmd --permanent --add-rich-rule='rule family="ipv4" source address="168.63.129.16" port port="80" protocol="tcp" accept'
sudo firewall-cmd --reload
```

### Step 5: Remove ghosted NICs from the backend pool

A backend pool that references deleted NICs or NICs in a failed provisioning state produces phantom "down" members. List the pool and inspect its members:

```bash
az network lb address-pool show \
  --resource-group "$RG" \
  --lb-name "$LB" \
  --name "myBackendPool" \
  --output json
```

Review `backendIPConfigurations` / `loadBalancerBackendAddresses`. Remove any entry whose NIC no longer exists or is not in a `Succeeded` provisioning state, then re-add valid NICs.

### Step 6: Correct a port, protocol, or path mismatch

If Step 1 and Step 3 show the probe pointing at the wrong port or path, update it. The probe and the application must agree.

```bash
az network lb probe update \
  --resource-group "$RG" \
  --lb-name "$LB" \
  --name "$PROBE" \
  --protocol Http \
  --port 8080 \
  --path /healthz
```

PowerShell — modify the probe in memory and commit with `Set-AzLoadBalancer`:

```powershell
$slb = Get-AzLoadBalancer -Name "myLoadBalancer" -ResourceGroupName "myResourceGroup"
$slb | Set-AzLoadBalancerProbeConfig -Name "myHealthProbe" `
  -Protocol Http -Port 8080 -RequestPath "/healthz" `
  -IntervalInSeconds 15 -ProbeCount 2
$slb | Set-AzLoadBalancer
```

Note: for `Set-AzLoadBalancerProbeConfig`, the `Name`, `Port`, `IntervalInSeconds`, and `ProbeCount` parameters are mandatory even if you are only changing one value — supply the current values for the fields you are not modifying, or they will be reset.

### Step 7: Verify recovery

Wait two to three probe intervals (30–45 seconds at a 15-second interval), then re-check Step 1. Instances should transition from **Down** to healthy as consecutive probes succeed. Confirm the **Health Probe Status** metric returns to 100%.

## Troubleshooting

**Probe still failing after config looks correct.** Re-read the portal reason code. `Down_Probe_TcpProbeTimeout` means no TCP response at all — suspect a blocked port, host firewall, or a dead application. `Down_Probe_HttpStatusCodeError` means the TCP handshake succeeded but the app returned a non-200 code — fix the endpoint, not the network. `Down_Probe_HttpEndpointUnreachable` means the handshake completed but the HTTP session was rejected — an NSG on the port or no healthy listener.

**Slow application / cold start.** If the app is healthy but takes longer than the probe window to answer, tighten timing tolerances instead of the app. Reasonable starting values for slow backends: `intervalInSeconds` 15–30, `numberOfProbes` 2–4.

```bash
az network lb probe update \
  --resource-group "$RG" \
  --lb-name "$LB" \
  --name "$PROBE" \
  --interval 30 \
  --number-of-probes 3
```

The interval should be at least twice the worst-case measured response time. Probe tuning is a workaround — if the app consistently takes more than 30 seconds to answer, investigate the application separately.

**High CPU on the backend.** Check the instance's **Percentage CPU** metric. A pegged VM cannot answer probes in time and flaps between healthy and down.

**HTTPS probe against an HTTP-only listener (or vice versa).** A protocol mismatch fails silently. Ensure the probe protocol matches the listener; for HTTPS probes the backend must present a valid TLS endpoint on the probe port.

**All instances down at once.** This usually points at a shared cause: a subnet NSG change, a bad application deployment, or a wrong probe path pushed to every node. Check recent change history before touching individual VMs.

**`--threshold` behavior.** In Azure CLI, `--number-of-probes` and `--threshold` are aliases for the consecutive-failure count. The separate `--probe-threshold` parameter (consecutive successes/failures to flip health state) is in preview — leave it at the default of 1 for production unless you have a specific reason to change it.

**Basic vs. Standard SKU.** Basic Load Balancer requires the probe traffic path but does not support the newer `NoHealthyBackendsBehavior` option. Standard SKU also defaults to a "deny all" security posture, so an explicit NSG allowing the probe and client traffic is mandatory.

## Prevention

- Expose a dedicated, lightweight health endpoint (for example `/healthz`) that returns 200 quickly and does not chain to slow dependencies.
- Bind services to `0.0.0.0`, not `127.0.0.1`, and configure them to auto-start after reboot.
- Standardize NSGs with an explicit high-priority `AzureLoadBalancer` service-tag allow rule on every backend subnet.
- Keep probe timing realistic for the workload — avoid `intervalInSeconds` of 5 with `numberOfProbes` of 1, which can flap a healthy backend on a single slow response.
- Create an Azure Monitor alert on **Health Probe Status** and **DataPathAvailability** so degradation is caught before customers notice.
- Audit backend pools periodically for stale NIC references after VM or scale set churn.
- Document each probe's port, protocol, and path alongside the application it fronts so mismatches are caught in change review.

Title: AZR-011: Azure Firewall and NSG Rules Blocking Traffic
Content:
# Azure Firewall and NSG Rules Blocking Traffic

**Category:** Azure > Networking
**Article Code:** AZR-011
**Tier:** 2
**Audience:** Administrators / Technicians
**Estimated Resolution Time:** 30-90 minutes

## Symptoms / When to Use

- A VM, app, or service is unreachable and connections time out (no RST) or are actively refused.
- RDP (TCP 3389) or SSH (TCP 22) to an Azure VM fails, but the VM is running and the guest OS firewall is open.
- Outbound calls from a VM to the internet or a SaaS endpoint hang or return nothing, and traffic is routed through an Azure Firewall.
- A change to an NSG, Azure Firewall policy, or User-Defined Route (UDR) immediately preceded the outage.
- Application logs show connection timeouts to a private endpoint, storage account, or database behind a firewalled subnet.
- Traffic works from one subnet or source IP but not another that "should" be equivalent.

## Background

Azure applies traffic filtering at two independent layers, and either can silently drop a packet.

**Network Security Groups (NSGs)** are stateful, 5-tuple (source/destination IP, port, protocol) filters attached to a **subnet**, a **NIC**, or both. When both are present, inbound traffic is evaluated against the subnet NSG first, then the NIC NSG; outbound is the reverse. Rules are processed by priority (100-4096, lower number wins) and the first match terminates evaluation. Every NSG carries default rules, including `DenyAllInbound` (priority 65500) and `AllowVnetInBound`/`DenyVnetInBound` behaviors driven by service tags such as `VirtualNetwork`. A common failure is a low-priority custom `Deny` (or a `DenyVnetInBound` override) shadowing a higher-numbered `Allow`.

**Azure Firewall** is a stateful, managed network appliance placed in a dedicated subnet (`AzureFirewallSubnet`). Traffic reaches it only when a UDR forces the subnet's next hop to the firewall's private IP. Azure Firewall **denies all traffic by default** until you add explicit allow rules. Rules live in a **Firewall Policy** as rule collection groups containing DNAT, network, and application rule collections, processed DNAT -> Network -> Application, in priority order. Threat intelligence and IDPS (in deny mode) can drop traffic before or after rule evaluation. Because the firewall is stateful, it permits return traffic for established flows, so an explicit deny in the reverse direction only blocks *new* connections.

Because these layers stack, "blocked traffic" is a diagnosis problem first: identify *which* layer and *which* rule is responsible before changing anything.

## Resolution

### Step 1: Confirm which layer is dropping the packet with IP flow verify

Network Watcher's IP flow verify tells you Allow/Deny and names the responsible NSG rule for a specific 5-tuple. Run it before touching config.

```azurecli
az network watcher test-ip-flow \
  --resource-group myResourceGroup \
  --vm myVM \
  --direction Inbound \
  --protocol TCP \
  --local 10.0.0.4:3389 \
  --remote 203.0.113.50:60000
```

PowerShell equivalent:

```powershell
$networkWatcher = Get-AzNetworkWatcher -ResourceGroupName "NetworkWatcherRG" -Name "NetworkWatcher_eastus"
Test-AzNetworkWatcherIPFlow `
  -NetworkWatcher $networkWatcher `
  -TargetVirtualMachineId $vm.Id `
  -Direction Inbound `
  -Protocol TCP `
  -LocalIPAddress 10.0.0.4 `
  -LocalPort 3389 `
  -RemoteIPAddress 203.0.113.50 `
  -RemotePort 60000
```

The result returns `Access allowed` or `Access denied` plus the rule name. IP flow verify only evaluates NSGs. If it returns **Allowed** but traffic still fails, the block is at the Azure Firewall, a UDR, or the guest OS, not the NSG.

### Step 2: View the effective security rules on the NIC

Effective rules show the merged result of subnet-level and NIC-level NSGs, including inherited defaults, so you can see which rule actually wins.

```azurecli
az network nic list-effective-nsg \
  --resource-group myResourceGroup \
  --name myVM-nic \
  --output table
```

```powershell
Get-AzEffectiveNetworkSecurityGroup `
  -NetworkInterfaceName "myVM-nic" `
  -ResourceGroupName "myResourceGroup"
```

Look for the lowest-priority rule matching your port and source. If a `Deny` sits at a lower priority number than your `Allow`, the `Deny` wins.

### Step 3: Run NSG diagnostics for a full rule trace (optional, deeper)

When multiple NSGs and Virtual Network Manager admin rules are in play, `run-configuration-diagnostic` shows every rule assessed along the path and which one made the decision.

```azurecli
az network watcher run-configuration-diagnostic \
  --resource myVM \
  --resource-group myResourceGroup \
  --resource-type virtualMachines \
  --direction Inbound \
  --protocol TCP \
  --source 203.0.113.50 \
  --destination 10.0.0.4 \
  --port 3389
```

### Step 4: Fix the NSG rule

If an NSG is the culprit, add or correct an allow rule with a priority *lower* than the blocking deny. Match the port to the service (RDP 3389, SSH 22, HTTP 80, HTTPS 443).

```azurecli
az network nsg rule create \
  --resource-group myResourceGroup \
  --nsg-name myVM-nsg \
  --name Allow-RDP-Admin \
  --priority 300 \
  --direction Inbound \
  --access Allow \
  --protocol Tcp \
  --source-address-prefixes 203.0.113.50/32 \
  --source-port-ranges '*' \
  --destination-address-prefixes '*' \
  --destination-port-ranges 3389
```

Scope the source to a specific IP or range rather than `*`. After the change, re-run Step 1 to confirm the tuple now returns `Access allowed`.

### Step 5: If the NSG is clean, inspect Azure Firewall

If IP flow verify says Allowed but traffic still fails and the subnet has a UDR pointing to a firewall, confirm the route, then check firewall logs.

Confirm the effective route so you know traffic is actually going to the firewall:

```azurecli
az network nic show-effective-route-table \
  --resource-group myResourceGroup \
  --name myVM-nic \
  --output table
```

Query the firewall's structured logs in the Log Analytics workspace. Denied flows appear in `AZFWNetworkRule` and `AZFWApplicationRule` with a matched rule (or the implicit deny). Run this in the workspace **Logs** blade or via CLI:

```kusto
AZFWNetworkRule
| where Action == "Deny"
| project TimeGenerated, SourceIp, DestinationIp, DestinationPort, Protocol, Action, Policy, RuleCollection, Rule
| order by TimeGenerated desc
| take 50
```

For HTTP/HTTPS traffic filtered by FQDN, query `AZFWApplicationRule` instead. Note that `AZFWNetworkRule` entries have no FQDN field, so filter network rules by IP and port. If the firewall uses legacy diagnostics, query the `AzureDiagnostics` table filtered on `Category == "AzureFirewallNetworkRule"`.

### Step 6: Add the missing Azure Firewall rule

Azure Firewall denies by default, so a missing allow rule is the usual cause. Add a network rule (IP/port) to the policy's rule collection group:

```azurecli
az network firewall policy rule-collection-group collection add-filter-collection \
  --resource-group myResourceGroup \
  --policy-name myFirewallPolicy \
  --rule-collection-group-name DefaultNetworkRuleCollectionGroup \
  --name Allow-App-Outbound \
  --collection-priority 300 \
  --action Allow \
  --rule-name allow-https \
  --rule-type NetworkRule \
  --source-addresses 10.0.1.0/24 \
  --destination-addresses 203.0.113.0/24 \
  --destination-ports 443 \
  --ip-protocols TCP
```

For outbound web traffic filtered by hostname, create an **application rule** instead (`--rule-type ApplicationRule` with `--target-fqdns` and `--protocols Https=443`). After the change, retest the flow and confirm an `Allow` entry now appears in the logs.

## Troubleshooting

- **IP flow verify says Allowed but the connection still fails.** The NSG is not the problem. Check, in order: the Azure Firewall (Step 5), the UDR next hop, the guest OS firewall (Windows Defender Firewall / `iptables`/`firewalld`), and any Azure Load Balancer health probe or backend pool config.
- **Works from within the VNet but not from on-premises or a peered VNet.** A `DenyVnetInBound`-style rule or a service-tag mismatch is likely. The `VirtualNetwork` service tag includes peered VNets, VPN/ExpressRoute address spaces, and UDR prefixes, so a broad `Deny` on that tag blocks more than the local subnet.
- **Asymmetric routing.** If a UDR sends outbound traffic through the firewall but return traffic bypasses it, the stateful firewall drops the mismatched flow. Ensure both directions traverse the same appliance.
- **Traffic intermittently dropped with no matching deny rule.** Check IDPS. In *Alert and Deny* mode the IDPS engine drops sessions silently after rule evaluation on a signature match, and threat-intelligence filtering blocks before any rule runs. Look for `AZFWThreatIntel` and `AZFWIdpsSignature` log entries.
- **Rule change not taking effect.** NSG changes apply within seconds, but confirm you edited the NSG actually bound to the NIC/subnet (Step 2 shows the effective set). For Azure Firewall, verify you edited the policy attached to *that* firewall, not a parent or draft policy.
- **Port opens but app still unreachable.** Confirm the destination port ranges and protocol match exactly (TCP vs UDP), and that DNAT rules on the firewall translate the public IP/port to the correct backend.

## Prevention

- Document a rule-priority convention (e.g., allows in the 100-499 band, denies 500-899) and space priorities in increments of 100 to leave room for insertions.
- Keep an explicit, high-priority allow for management access (RDP/SSH) scoped to jump hosts or Azure Bastion subnets, not `Any`.
- Prefer Azure Bastion or Just-In-Time VM access over broad inbound RDP/SSH rules from the internet.
- Enable NSG/Virtual Network flow logs and Azure Firewall structured logs to a Log Analytics workspace before an incident, so you have data when one occurs. Note NSG flow logs retire on 30 September 2027, migrate to VNet flow logs.
- Use service tags and IP Groups instead of hardcoded address lists so rules stay maintainable as the environment grows.
- Test firewall and NSG changes in a non-production subscription and validate with IP flow verify before applying to production tenants.
- Review effective security rules and effective routes after every network change as a standard checklist item.

**Tags:** azure-firewall, nsg, network-security-group, network-watcher, ip-flow-verify, effective-security-rules, udr, firewall-policy, connectivity-troubleshooting, blocked-traffic

Title: AZR-012: Azure Policy Assignment Not Enforcing or Showing Non-Compliant
Content:
# Azure Policy Assignment Not Enforcing or Showing Non-Compliant

**Category:** Azure > Governance
**Article Code:** AZR-012
**Tier:** 3
**Audience:** Administrators / Technicians
**Estimated Resolution Time:** 30 minutes – 4 hours (evaluation cycles are asynchronous and can add significant wait time)

An Azure Policy assignment that appears configured but does not deny, audit, or remediate resources — or that reports a compliance state you did not expect — is almost always a symptom of evaluation timing, scope, mode, or effect configuration rather than a platform fault. This article walks through the verification path for both problems: assignments that fail to *enforce* and assignments that report *unexpected compliance*.

## Symptoms / When to Use

Use this article when one or more of the following is true:

- A `deny` policy is not blocking non-compliant resource creation, and there is no entry in the Azure Activity log for the blocked action.
- An `audit` or `auditIfNotExists` policy shows resources as **Compliant** that you expect to be non-compliant (or the reverse).
- The compliance dashboard shows **Not started** or stale results hours after assigning the policy.
- A policy or initiative reports `0/0` resources — no resources evaluated at all.
- A `deployIfNotExists` or `modify` policy evaluates resources as non-compliant but never remediates them.
- Remediation tasks fail with authorization / role errors.
- Compliance state is **Error** or **Conflicting**.
- A newly created resource that should have triggered the policy was created successfully with no effect applied.

## Background

Azure Policy is an **asynchronous, evaluation-driven** governance engine. A policy definition (JSON business rule) is assigned to a scope — management group, subscription, resource group, or individual resource — and Azure evaluates in-scope resources against it. Understanding *when* and *why* evaluation happens is essential, because most "not working" reports are actually timing or configuration issues.

Evaluation is triggered by these events:

1. A policy or initiative is newly assigned to a scope. It takes about **five minutes** for the assignment to propagate, after which the evaluation cycle begins.
2. An existing assignment is updated (same timing as a new assignment).
3. A resource is created or updated in scope via ARM/REST/SDK. Effect events (`deny`, `audit`, `append`, `deploy`) apply at request time; the individual resource's compliance record surfaces in the portal roughly **15 minutes** later.
4. A subscription is created or moved within a management group hierarchy with a targeting assignment — around **30 minutes**.
5. A policy exemption is created, updated, or deleted.
6. The **standard compliance cycle**, which runs automatically once every **24 hours**.
7. An on-demand scan triggered manually.

Key configuration facts that govern behavior:

- **enforcementMode**: When set to `Disabled` (also called "Don't enforce" / DoNotEnforce in the portal), the policy effect is *not applied* and no Activity log entry is written — but compliance is still assessed. This is the single most common cause of "deny isn't denying."
- **Definition mode**: `all` evaluates all resource types including resource groups and subscriptions; `indexed` evaluates only resources that support tags and location. A tag or location policy left in the wrong mode can silently skip resources.
- **Effect timing**: `deny` and `deployIfNotExists` act on *new/updated* resources at request time; *existing* resources are only reported as non-compliant, never auto-blocked retroactively. `deployIfNotExists` and `modify` require a **remediation task** and a **managed identity** with the correct RBAC roles to actually change existing resources.
- **Applicability, exclusions, and exemptions**: A resource that is out of scope, in an excluded sub-scope, or covered by an exemption will not be evaluated or acted upon.

## Resolution

Work these steps in order. Steps 1–4 cover enforcement failures; steps 5–7 cover unexpected compliance and remediation.

### Step 1: Confirm enforcement mode is Enabled

A disabled enforcement mode is the top cause of an effect that never fires. Check the assignment.

Azure PowerShell (`Az.Resources`):

```powershell
Get-AzPolicyAssignment -Name '<assignmentName>' -Scope '/subscriptions/<subscriptionId>' |
  Select-Object Name, EnforcementMode, Scope, DisplayName
```

Azure CLI:

```azurecli
az policy assignment show --name "<assignmentName>" \
  --scope "/subscriptions/<subscriptionId>" \
  --query "{name:name, enforcementMode:enforcementMode, scope:scope}"
```

If `EnforcementMode` returns `Disabled` (CLI shows `DoNotEnforce`), re-enable it:

```azurecli
az policy assignment update --name "<assignmentName>" \
  --scope "/subscriptions/<subscriptionId>" \
  --enforcement-mode Default
```

In the portal: **Policy > Assignments >** select the assignment **> Edit assignment > Policy enforcement** must be set to **Enabled**.

### Step 2: Verify scope, exclusions, and exemptions

Confirm the resource you expect to be governed is actually inside the assignment scope and not excluded or exempted.

```azurecli
# Confirm the assignment scope and any excluded sub-scopes
az policy assignment show --name "<assignmentName>" \
  --scope "/subscriptions/<subscriptionId>" \
  --query "{scope:scope, notScopes:notScopes}"

# List exemptions that may be suppressing evaluation for this assignment
az policy exemption list --scope "/subscriptions/<subscriptionId>" \
  --query "[].{name:name, policyAssignmentId:policyAssignmentId, category:exemptionCategory}" -o table
```

Compare the resource ID against the scope. A resource governed by an assignment at resource-group scope will not be evaluated by an assignment scoped to a *different* resource group. If the resource appears under `notScopes` or an exemption, that explains the missing effect.

### Step 3: Check the definition mode

If the policy inspects tags or location but resources are being skipped, the definition mode may be wrong.

```azurecli
# Get the definition ID referenced by the assignment
az policy assignment show --name "<assignmentName>" \
  --scope "/subscriptions/<subscriptionId>" --query "policyDefinitionId"

# Inspect the definition mode
az policy definition show --name "<definitionName>" --query "{displayName:displayName, mode:mode}"
```

Expected values:

- `mode` should be `all` for policies that target any resource type (including resource groups/subscriptions).
- `mode` should be `indexed` for policies that check **tags or location**, so Azure evaluates only resources that support those properties.

Mode is set on the *definition*, not the assignment. For a custom definition, correct it in the definition JSON and re-create/update it. Built-in definitions cannot be edited — duplicate the built-in, fix the mode, and reassign.

### Step 4: Force an on-demand evaluation scan

If configuration is correct but compliance is **Not started** or stale, do not wait for the 24-hour cycle — trigger a scan. Scans are asynchronous and evaluate every in-scope resource against every assigned policy, so they can run for a long time.

Azure PowerShell (`Az.PolicyInsights` module). Scan the current subscription, a resource group, or run as a background job:

```powershell
# Entire current subscription
Start-AzPolicyComplianceScan

# A single resource group
Start-AzPolicyComplianceScan -ResourceGroupName '<resourceGroupName>'

# Run in the background and wait on the job
$job = Start-AzPolicyComplianceScan -AsJob
$job | Wait-Job
```

Azure CLI (`az policy state trigger-scan`). Defaults to the current subscription; scope to a resource group with `-g`:

```azurecli
# Current subscription
az policy state trigger-scan

# A single resource group, returning immediately
az policy state trigger-scan --resource-group "<resourceGroupName>" --no-wait
```

After the scan completes, re-read the compliance state (see Step 5).

### Step 5: Read the actual compliance state and reason

Pull the current per-resource state to see what Azure actually evaluated. This distinguishes "not evaluated" from "evaluated and genuinely compliant."

```powershell
# Latest states for a specific assignment
Get-AzPolicyState -PolicyAssignmentName '<assignmentName>' |
  Select-Object ResourceId, ComplianceState, PolicyDefinitionAction, Timestamp
```

Azure CLI:

```azurecli
az policy state list \
  --filter "PolicyAssignmentName eq '<assignmentName>'" \
  --query "[].{resource:resourceId, state:complianceState, effect:policyDefinitionAction}" -o table
```

If a resource is non-compliant but you expected compliant (or vice versa), determine *why* in the portal: **Policy > Compliance >** select the assignment **>** select the non-compliant resource **>** the **Compliance details** show the evaluated property, the **current value**, and the **target value**. If the target value is wrong, the definition logic is at fault; if the current value is wrong, validate the resource payload at `resources.azure.com`.

A `0/0` result means no applicable resources were found in scope — recheck the definition's resource-type logic and the assignment scope from Steps 2–3.

### Step 6: Remediate deployIfNotExists / modify policies

`deployIfNotExists` and `modify` effects only *report* existing resources as non-compliant. To change them you must run a remediation task, and the assignment's managed identity must hold the roles listed in the definition's `roleDefinitionIds`.

First confirm the assignment has a managed identity. If it was created via SDK/CLI without the portal, the identity may exist but lack role assignments — the portal grants roles automatically, but SDK/CLI assignments require manual grants.

```azurecli
# Confirm the assignment has a managed identity
az policy assignment show --name "<assignmentName>" \
  --scope "/subscriptions/<subscriptionId>" --query "identity"

# Find the roles the definition needs
az policy definition show --name "<definitionName>" \
  --query "policyRule.then.details.roleDefinitionIds"
```

Grant each required role to the assignment's identity principal ID (using `az role assignment create --assignee <principalId> --role "<roleName>" --scope <scope>`), then start the remediation task:

```azurepowershell
Start-AzPolicyRemediation -Name 'remediation-<date>' `
  -PolicyAssignmentId '/subscriptions/<subscriptionId>/providers/Microsoft.Authorization/policyAssignments/<assignmentName>'
```

Azure CLI equivalent:

```azurecli
az policy remediation create --name "remediation-<date>" \
  --policy-assignment "/subscriptions/<subscriptionId>/providers/Microsoft.Authorization/policyAssignments/<assignmentName>"
```

For an initiative (policy set), add `-PolicyDefinitionReferenceId` (PowerShell) / `--definition-reference-id` (CLI) to target the specific `deployIfNotExists`/`modify` policy within the set. Track progress with `Get-AzPolicyRemediation` or in **Policy > Remediation > Remediation tasks**.

### Step 7: Re-verify after the wait window

Because evaluation is asynchronous, re-run Step 5 after the appropriate window (about 5 minutes for a new/updated assignment to apply, up to 15–30 minutes for individual resource compliance to surface). Confirm the effect now appears: for `deny`, attempt to create a non-compliant test resource and confirm it is blocked and logged in the Activity log; for `audit`/remediation, confirm the compliance state updated.

## Troubleshooting

If the main path does not resolve the issue, check these variations:

- **Deny still not blocking after enforcement is Enabled.** Confirm you are testing a *create or update* operation, not an existing resource. `deny` never retroactively deletes or blocks resources that already exist — those only show as non-compliant. Also confirm your test resource genuinely matches the policy condition (a mismatched alias or value silently passes).
- **No Activity log entry at all.** This is the signature of `enforcementMode = Disabled`. If enforcement is Enabled and there is still no log entry, the resource is out of scope, excluded, or exempt (Step 2), or the definition mode excludes the resource type (Step 3).
- **Compliance state stuck on "Not started."** A new or updated assignment takes ~5 minutes to apply and then begins evaluation; new resources under an existing assignment take ~15 minutes. Force a scan (Step 4). Note that some resource providers — for example Azure Virtual Network Manager — do not support on-demand scans or the daily cycle; consult the specific provider's documentation.
- **State is "Error."** An Error state indicates a template or evaluation error (common with `deployIfNotExists`/`modify` definitions). Open the resource's **Compliance details > Related events** in the portal to read the error, and check the remediation task's deployment for the failing ARM template.
- **State is "Conflicting."** Two or more assignments apply conflicting effects to the same resource (for example, one `deny` and one `append` on the same property). Review overlapping assignments at parent scopes (management group vs. subscription) and reconcile.
- **Remediation task fails with authorization errors.** The managed identity is missing a role. A newly created identity must finish replicating through Microsoft Entra ID before role grants take effect — wait a few minutes and retry. Verify every ID in `roleDefinitionIds` is granted at a scope that covers the target resources. Changing a definition does **not** update the assignment's identity or its role grants automatically.
- **Wrong or nonexistent alias.** If a custom definition never matches resources, an incorrect alias may be in use. Validate aliases with the Azure Policy extension for Visual Studio Code, which also supports on-demand single-resource evaluation for fast iteration.
- **Initiative (policy set) reports compliant but a member policy should fail.** Compliance rolls up across the set. Drill into the individual policy within the initiative in **Compliance details** rather than reading only the top-level state.
- **Assignment created via IaC/SDK behaves differently from portal.** Portal assignment wizards auto-grant managed-identity roles and default enforcement to Enabled. SDK/CLI/Bicep/Terraform assignments require you to set `enforcementMode` and grant identity roles explicitly. Re-check both.

## Prevention

- **Standardize on `all` mode** for custom definitions unless the policy specifically checks tags or location, in which case use `indexed` deliberately and document why.
- **Test with `enforcementMode = DoNotEnforce` first** on new `deny` or `deployIfNotExists` policies to observe compliance impact, then flip to Enabled once the blast radius is understood. Never leave production enforcement disabled by accident — audit it periodically.
- **Assign at the highest sensible scope** (management group) and use exclusions/exemptions sparingly and with expiry dates, so governance is predictable and you avoid `0/0` scope gaps.
- **Automate identity role grants** in your IaC pipeline for every `deployIfNotExists`/`modify` assignment so remediation never fails on missing RBAC. Keep granted roles to the least privilege required by `roleDefinitionIds`.
- **Do not rely on the 24-hour cycle for validation.** Build an on-demand `az policy state trigger-scan` or `Start-AzPolicyComplianceScan` step into deployment pipelines, and gate releases with the Azure Policy Compliance Scan GitHub Action where appropriate.
- **Duplicate, don't fight, built-ins.** When a built-in definition's mode or logic doesn't fit, duplicate it into a custom definition rather than assuming the platform is broken.
- **Monitor compliance drift** with scheduled compliance queries or Azure Monitor, and alert on transitions to **Error** or **Conflicting** so misconfigurations surface before an audit does.
