Title: EID-006: Troubleshooting Microsoft Entra Connect Hybrid Identity Sync Problems
Content:
# Troubleshooting Microsoft Entra Connect Hybrid Identity Sync Problems

**Category:** Entra ID > Hybrid Identity
**Article Code:** EID-006
**Tier:** 3
**Audience:** Administrators / Technicians
**Estimated Resolution Time:** 30 minutes – 3 hours (longer for orphaned-object or bulk-deletion recovery)

Microsoft Entra Connect Sync (formerly Azure AD Connect) replicates on-premises Active Directory objects to Microsoft Entra ID on a scheduled cycle. When the cycle stalls, an object fails to export, or attribute values collide in the cloud, changes made on-premises stop appearing in Microsoft 365. This article covers diagnosis and remediation for the sync engine, the scheduler, connector-level errors, and the most common object-level export failures.

## Symptoms / When to Use

- A new or modified on-premises user, group, or contact does not appear in Microsoft Entra ID / Microsoft 365 after 30+ minutes.
- The Microsoft Entra admin center reports "Last sync" was more than 3 hours ago, or you receive an email that sync has not registered in over 24 hours.
- The Synchronization Service Manager **Operations** tab shows a run profile ending in `stopped-server-down`, `stopped-extension-dll-exception`, or `stopped-deletion-threshold-exceeded`.
- Export to Microsoft Entra ID fails with `AttributeValueMustBeUnique`, `QuarantinedAttributeValueMustBeUnique`, `InvalidSoftMatch`, or `IdentityDataValidationFailed`.
- The **Microsoft Azure AD Sync** (ADSync) Windows service is stopped or will not start.
- Password Hash Synchronization has stopped; on-premises password changes are not reflected in the cloud.
- A user disappears from Microsoft Entra ID, or a batch of objects is unexpectedly pending deletion.

## Background

Microsoft Entra Connect Sync runs a built-in scheduler (default every 30 minutes) that executes a sequence of connector run profiles: import from each source, synchronization through the metaverse, then export to each target. A **delta** cycle processes only changes; an **initial/full** cycle reimports and reprocesses every object and every sync rule.

Data flows through three stages: the Active Directory Connector Space (ADCS), the Metaverse (MV), and the Microsoft Entra Connector Space (AADCS), before export to the tenant. A failure at any stage stops the object from reaching the cloud. The ADSync service runs under a dedicated service account (virtual service account by default, or a domain/gMSA/local account); if that account's credentials expire, the service stops and no sync occurs.

Cloud-side write operations enforce uniqueness on `userPrincipalName`, `mail`, `proxyAddresses`, and `signInName`. When Entra Connect tries to write a duplicate, or when a soft-match collides with an object owned by a different `sourceAnchor` (immutableId), the export for that object is rejected and quarantined while the rest of the batch continues. These object-level errors surface in the Synchronization Service Manager and, for build 2.5.79.0 or later, in the Microsoft Entra Connect Health **Object Level Synchronization Error Report**.

All ADSync cmdlets require the module to be loaded. On a domain controller or a hardened server, the cmdlets may not autoload; import the module first.

```powershell
Import-Module ADSync
```

## Resolution

Work these steps in order. Steps 1–3 diagnose and restart the pipeline; Steps 4–6 address the most common object-level failures.

### Step 1: Confirm the scheduler is enabled and running

Check the current scheduler configuration. Note `SyncCycleEnabled` (must be `True`), `NextSyncCyclePolicyType`, `NextSyncCycleStartTimeInUTC`, and `CurrentlyEffectiveSyncCycleInterval`.

```powershell
Get-ADSyncScheduler
```

If `SyncCycleEnabled` is `False`, the built-in scheduler is turned off (commonly left off after a maintenance change or a paused install wizard). Re-enable it:

```powershell
Set-ADSyncScheduler -SyncCycleEnabled $true
```

Check whether the engine is currently busy. An empty result means idle; a connector name means a cycle is in progress.

```powershell
Get-ADSyncConnectorRunStatus
```

### Step 2: Trigger a manual sync cycle

Force a delta cycle to push pending changes immediately rather than waiting for the next scheduled run:

```powershell
Start-ADSyncSyncCycle -PolicyType Delta
```

Use a full (initial) cycle only when you have changed sync rules, OU/domain filtering, or attribute flows. A full cycle reimports and reprocesses every object and can take a long time on large directories.

```powershell
Start-ADSyncSyncCycle -PolicyType Initial
```

If you get an error that a cycle is already running and you need to make configuration changes, stop the current cycle first. Stopping is not harmful; pending changes are picked up on the next run.

```powershell
Stop-ADSyncSyncCycle
```

### Step 3: Review connector run results in the Synchronization Service Manager

1. Open **Synchronization Service** from the Start menu (`C:\Program Files\Microsoft Azure AD Sync\UIShell\miisclient.exe`).
2. On the **Operations** tab, inspect the most recent run profiles. A green result is `success`. Investigate any of the following:
   - `stopped-server-down` – the sync engine could not reach a source or target. Check the ADSync service, network connectivity, and firewall/proxy to the required Microsoft Entra endpoints.
   - `stopped-extension-dll-exception` – a rules-extension or connector fault. Review the **Application** and **System** Event Viewer logs for ADSync events.
   - `stopped-deletion-threshold-exceeded` – the accidental-delete guard blocked the export (see Step 6).
   - `completed-export-errors` – the cycle finished but some objects failed to export (see Steps 4–5).
3. Select a run with errors, then select an object to view the per-object error text. Column settings let you add `onPremisesDistinguishedName` and other identifying attributes.

### Step 4: Resolve duplicate-attribute export errors

`AttributeValueMustBeUnique` and `QuarantinedAttributeValueMustBeUnique` mean two objects present the same `userPrincipalName`, `proxyAddresses`, `mail`, or `sipProxyAddress` value to the tenant.

1. Identify the conflicting value and both objects. The Connect Health **Object Level Synchronization Error Report** shows the two objects side by side and can be exported to CSV.
2. Determine which object should keep the value.
3. Remove or correct the duplicate value **in the source directory** (on-premises AD) for the object that should not hold it. Fixing it at the source is required — editing the cloud object alone will be overwritten on the next sync.
4. Force a delta cycle so the corrected value flows and the quarantine clears:

```powershell
Start-ADSyncSyncCycle -PolicyType Delta
```

For duplicate `userPrincipalName` and `proxyAddresses` conflicts on user objects, the Microsoft Entra admin center provides a cloud-side **Diagnose** flow (Connect Health) that can remap a `sourceAnchor` in orphaned-object cases. This requires at least **Contributor** RBAC and only updates the source anchor — it does not change other attributes.

### Step 5: Resolve soft-match and data-validation errors

- **InvalidSoftMatch** – Entra ID tried to match a newly synced object to an existing cloud object by `proxyAddresses`/`userPrincipalName`, but the existing object already carries a different `immutableId`. Remove the duplicate value from the object that should not own it (at the source), then run a delta cycle. If the objects are genuinely the same identity that lost its anchor, use the Connect Health orphaned-object diagnosis.
- **IdentityDataValidationFailed** – the `userPrincipalName` contains unsupported characters or an invalid format. Note that invisible/whitespace characters in UPN or proxyAddresses are silently discarded by ProxyCalc and can cause the cloud UPN to fall back to `mailNickname@tenant.onmicrosoft.com`. Export the source value with LDIFDE/PowerShell and paste it into a PowerShell window — invisible characters render as `?`. Correct the source value, then run a delta cycle.

### Step 6: Handle a blocked export from the accidental-delete threshold

A `stopped-deletion-threshold-exceeded` run means more objects were staged for deletion than the configured threshold, so **no** deletions (and no other exports in that step) were applied.

1. In the Synchronization Service Manager, go to **Connectors**, select the **Windows Azure Active Directory** connector, then **Search Connector Space** under Actions.
2. Set **Scope** to **Pending Export** and enable the **Delete** checkbox, then **Search** to list every object about to be deleted. Add `onPremisesDistinguishedName` via **Column Settings** to identify them.
3. If the deletions are unexpected (typically caused by an OU rename or a filtering change that dropped objects out of scope), fix the scope — re-select the OU in the Entra Connect wizard or correct the sync rule — then run a full cycle so the objects return to scope:

```powershell
Start-ADSyncSyncCycle -PolicyType Initial
```

4. If all pending deletions are intended, allow that single export to proceed above the threshold, then let normal cycling resume. Manage the threshold with the accidental-deletes feature rather than disabling it permanently.

## Troubleshooting

**The ADSync cmdlets are not recognized.** Run `Import-Module ADSync`. This is common on domain controllers or servers with elevated PowerShell restriction levels.

**The `Microsoft Azure AD Sync` service is stopped or will not start.** The service account credentials are the usual cause. In `Services.msc`, open **Microsoft Azure AD Sync**, and on the **Log On** tab confirm the account. In Active Directory Users and Computers, verify the account is not disabled, its password is not expired, and **User must change password at next logon** is not set — set **Password never expires** for a dedicated service account. If the password changed, update it on the service's **Log On** tab and restart the service. Do not reconfigure the service to log on as Local System.

**MIISClient shows `Stopped-Server-Down` or `Stopped-Extension-DLL-Exception`.** Confirm the ADSync service is running, the sync service account is healthy, and the server has outbound connectivity to the required Microsoft Entra endpoints. Review Application/System event logs for the specific ADSync error.

**A rule, filter, or attribute change did not take effect.** Rule changes require a full **sync** step; new imported attributes and filtering changes require a full **import** on the affected connector. Instead of a tenant-wide full cycle, scope the full step to one connector:

```powershell
Set-ADSyncSchedulerConnectorOverride -ConnectorName "contoso.com" -FullImportRequired $true
Set-ADSyncSchedulerConnectorOverride -ConnectorName "contoso.com" -FullSyncRequired $true
Start-ADSyncSyncCycle -PolicyType Delta
```

Confirm the pending overrides:

```powershell
Get-ADSyncSchedulerConnectorOverride -ConnectorName "contoso.com"
```

**You need to run a single connector step manually.** Use the connector and run-profile names exactly as shown in the Synchronization Service Manager. This cmdlet is synchronous and returns only when the step completes:

```powershell
Invoke-ADSyncRunProfile -ConnectorName "contoso.com" -RunProfileName "Delta Import"
```

**Password Hash Synchronization stopped.** In `Services.msc`, restart the **Microsoft Azure AD Sync** service, ensuring no sync operation is in progress. Confirm password sync is enabled for the tenant and check Event Viewer for source-side events (e.g., Event ID 611, 6900). If credentials were recently updated through the wizard, rerun the Entra Connect configuration wizard.

**Two Entra Connect servers appear to conflict.** Only one server should be active; all others must be in **staging mode**. A staging server imports and synchronizes but does not export. Verify staging status in the Entra Connect wizard (**Configure staging mode**). Two active servers exporting to the same tenant produce authentication and export conflicts.

**A configuration change requires suppressing sync temporarily.** Disable the scheduler, confirm no operation is in progress on the **Operations** tab, make the change, then re-enable:

```powershell
Set-ADSyncScheduler -SyncCycleEnabled $false
# make your changes, verify no in-progress operations
Set-ADSyncScheduler -SyncCycleEnabled $true
```

Never leave the install wizard open — it suspends the scheduler for the duration.

## Prevention

- **Keep Entra Connect current.** Legacy builds are being blocked; Microsoft is auto-upgrading to a minimum secure build, and unpatched servers will have all synchronization services fail. Confirm auto-upgrade is enabled or manually update to a supported version. Object-level error reporting requires build 2.5.79.0 or later.
- **Protect the service account.** Set **Password never expires** on any custom ADSync service account, or use a group Managed Service Account (gMSA) so credential rotation is automatic.
- **Deploy Microsoft Entra Connect Health for sync.** It surfaces the Object Level Synchronization Error Report, connectivity/authentication alerts, and the accidental-delete alert, all refreshed roughly every 30 minutes.
- **Keep the accidental-delete threshold enabled.** It prevents an OU rename or filtering mistake from cascading into mass deletions in Microsoft Entra ID. Review pending deletes before overriding.
- **Enable the Active Directory Recycle Bin.** It allows fast recovery of a deleted source object without a reinstall, and the Entra Connect wizard warns if it is missing.
- **Maintain attribute hygiene at the source.** Enforce unique `userPrincipalName` and `proxyAddresses`, and screen for invisible/whitespace characters to avoid duplicate-attribute and validation errors before they quarantine objects.
- **Run a staging server.** A second Entra Connect server in staging mode provides a warm standby and lets you preview export changes before promoting it.
- **Standardize maintenance.** Always disable the scheduler before rules changes and re-enable it afterward, and never make configuration edits while a sync cycle is running.

Title: EML-058: Outlook Desktop Crashes or Will Not Start
Content:
# Outlook Desktop Crashes or Will Not Start

**Category:** Email > Outlook
**Article Code:** EML-058
**Tier:** 1
**Audience:** Technicians
**Estimated Resolution Time:** 15–40 minutes

Quick-fix path for a Windows Outlook desktop client that crashes on launch, closes during use, or refuses to open. Covers both **classic Outlook** (`outlook.exe`) and **new Outlook** (`olk.exe`).

## Symptoms / When to Use

- Outlook closes immediately after the splash screen or hangs at "Processing."
- Outlook prompts to start in Safe Mode after a prior crash, then crashes again.
- Application crashes when opening an email, calendar, or attachment.
- New Outlook shows "Something went wrong" or fails 30–60 seconds after launch.
- Event Viewer logs Application Error / Event ID 1000 referencing `outlook.exe`, `olmapi32.dll`, or an add-in DLL.

## Background

Classic Outlook crashes are most often caused by a faulty **COM add-in**, a corrupted **profile**, or a damaged data file (`.ost`/`.pst`). Safe Mode loads Outlook without add-ins to isolate the cause. New Outlook (`olk.exe`) uses a different architecture with web add-ins and a single profile, so its recovery path centers on **Safe/Recovery mode** and clearing local cached state rather than rebuilding profiles.

## Resolution

### Step 1: Confirm which client is affected

Classic Outlook is `outlook.exe`; new Outlook is `olk.exe`. If both are installed, test each. New Outlook has no Safe Mode profile prompt — use the switches in Step 5 instead.

### Step 2: Start classic Outlook in Safe Mode and disable add-ins

Close Outlook, press **Win + R**, and run:

```cmd
outlook.exe /safe
```

If Outlook opens cleanly in Safe Mode, a COM add-in is the cause. Go to **File > Options > Add-ins**, set **Manage: COM Add-ins**, click **Go**, and clear all checkboxes. Restart Outlook normally, then re-enable add-ins one at a time to find the culprit.

### Step 3: Run an Online Repair of Office

If Safe Mode also crashes, repair the Office installation. Open **Control Panel > Programs and Features**, right-click the Microsoft 365 / Office entry, select **Change**, choose **Online Repair**, and click **Repair**. This requires internet access and reinstalls damaged binaries.

### Step 4: Repair the Outlook data file (classic)

A corrupt `.ost`/`.pst` can crash Outlook on load. Close Outlook and run the Inbox Repair tool (`SCANPST.EXE`), typically located at:

```cmd
"C:\Program Files\Microsoft Office\root\Office16\SCANPST.EXE"
```

Browse to the data file (default: `%LocalAppData%\Microsoft\Outlook`), then **Start**. Run it repeatedly until it reports zero errors. For an Exchange/M365 `.ost`, you can instead close Outlook, rename `Outlook.ost` to `Outlook.old`, and let Outlook rebuild the cache on next launch.

### Step 5: Reset new Outlook (olk.exe)

For new Outlook, start Safe Mode or Recovery mode via **Win + R**:

```cmd
olk.exe --safe
```

```cmd
olk.exe --recovery
```

If it still fails, clear the local cached state (you will re-enter the account password afterward):

```cmd
olk.exe --clearLocalState
```

### Step 6: Rebuild the Outlook profile (classic)

If crashes persist, create a fresh profile. Open **Control Panel > Mail (Microsoft Outlook)** > **Show Profiles** > **Add**, create a new profile, add the account, then set **Always use this profile**. Launch Outlook against the new profile.

## Troubleshooting

- **Still crashing after profile rebuild:** Run the **Microsoft Support and Recovery Assistant (SaRA)**, select **Outlook**, and let the Advanced Diagnostics / Connectivity scenario run. SaRA does not work against new Outlook.
- **New Outlook won't launch or loops on startup:** Close all Office apps and delete `%LocalAppData%\Microsoft\Olk` and `%LocalAppData%\Microsoft\OneAuth`. These folders are recreated on next launch (cached mail re-syncs).
- **Crash only when opening/composing mail:** Suspect a hardware-graphics conflict. In **File > Options > Advanced > Display**, enable **Disable hardware graphics acceleration**, and clear the **Roaming Signatures** / try disabling the offending add-in.
- **Crash tied to a recent Windows/Office update:** Check **Settings > Windows Update > Update history > Uninstall updates** for a recently installed KB, and confirm Office is on the current channel build.
- **Repeated "start in Safe Mode" prompt with no crash cause:** This can be a known service incident. Verify tenant Service Health / Message Center before deep troubleshooting.
- **AppData redirected to a network share:** Roamed AppData causes instability. Confirm `%LocalAppData%` resolves locally.

## Prevention

- Keep Office/Microsoft 365 Apps on a supported update channel and apply updates promptly.
- Vet and minimize COM add-ins; remove abandoned or third-party add-ins from managed devices.
- For large mailboxes, cap the cached-mode sync window (**Account Settings > Change > Mail to keep offline**) to reduce `.ost` size and corruption risk.
- Ensure roaming profiles do not redirect `%LocalAppData%`; keep OST/PST files on local storage, not network shares.
- Standardize the client (classic vs. new Outlook) across the fleet so troubleshooting stays consistent.

Title: EML-061: Microsoft 365 Distribution List Delivery Issues
Content:
# Microsoft 365 Distribution List Delivery Issues

**Category:** Email > Distribution Lists
**Article Code:** EML-061
**Tier:** 2
**Audience:** Administrators / Technicians
**Estimated Resolution Time:** 20-60 minutes

## Symptoms / When to Use

Use this article when messages sent to a Microsoft 365 distribution list (distribution group, mail-enabled security group, or dynamic distribution group) do not reach some or all members.

- External senders receive an NDR such as `550 5.7.1 RESOLVER.RST.AuthRequired; authentication required` or `550 5.7.12` when emailing the list.
- Senders emailing a Microsoft 365 Group receive `550 5.7.193 UnifiedGroupAgent; Delivery failed because the sender isn't a group member or external senders aren't permitted to send to this group.`
- Internal senders can email the list but external partners cannot.
- Messages sit in a "Pending" state or silently disappear (moderation awaiting approval).
- Only specific members fail to receive mail while the rest of the list is fine.
- The sender is rejected because they are not on the list's allowed-senders list.
- Mail to the list bounces for exceeding the maximum message size.

## Background

A distribution list is not a mailbox. When mail arrives for the group, the categorizer performs **recipient resolution** and expands the group into its individual members, then applies each restriction before fanning the message out. A delivery failure is almost always one of these gates rejecting the message rather than a routing fault:

- **Sender authentication** — By default, `RequireSenderAuthenticationEnabled` is `$True` on newly created distribution groups. This blocks all unauthenticated (external) senders. This is the single most common cause of external-sender NDRs.
- **Delivery management / allowed senders** — `AcceptMessagesOnlyFromSendersOrMembers` and `RejectMessagesFromSendersOrMembers` restrict who may post. If an accept-list is populated, everyone not on it is rejected.
- **Moderation** — If `ModerationEnabled` is `$True`, every message waits for a moderator to approve it. If no moderator is set, approval requests route to the group owners. Unapproved or unattended messages never arrive.
- **Membership / expansion** — A member whose mailbox has its own delivery restrictions, or a nested group with its own gates, can fail while the rest of the list succeeds.
- **Message size** — `MaxReceiveSize` on the group caps inbound message size.

Note that mail contacts are always treated as external (unauthenticated) senders, even when added to an internal-only allowed list. Standard distribution groups and Microsoft 365 Groups use **different cmdlets** (`Set-DistributionGroup` vs. `Set-UnifiedGroup`); applying the wrong one is a frequent misstep.

All PowerShell below assumes you are connected to Exchange Online with an account holding the **Exchange Administrator** or **Organization Management** role.

```powershell
Connect-ExchangeOnline
```

## Resolution

### Step 1: Confirm the group type and inspect its settings

Identify the recipient type before choosing cmdlets. A standard distribution list returns `MailUniversalDistributionGroup` or `MailUniversalSecurityGroup`; a Microsoft 365 Group returns `GroupMailbox`.

```powershell
Get-Recipient -Identity "sales@contoso.com" | Format-List Name,RecipientTypeDetails,PrimarySmtpAddress
```

For a standard distribution list, dump the delivery-relevant properties:

```powershell
Get-DistributionGroup -Identity "sales@contoso.com" | Format-List Name,PrimarySmtpAddress,RequireSenderAuthenticationEnabled,ModerationEnabled,ModeratedBy,AcceptMessagesOnlyFromSendersOrMembers,RejectMessagesFromSendersOrMembers,MaxReceiveSize
```

### Step 2: Run a message trace to confirm the failure point

Trace the specific message to see exactly where it stopped. `Get-MessageTraceV2` is the current cmdlet (it supersedes the retired `Get-MessageTrace`). Keep the date window tight for performance.

```powershell
Get-MessageTraceV2 -RecipientAddress "sales@contoso.com" -StartDate "2026-07-04T00:00:00Z" -EndDate "2026-07-05T00:00:00Z" | Format-Table Received,SenderAddress,RecipientAddress,Status,Subject
```

To pull the full event pipeline for one message, pipe into `Get-MessageTraceDetailV2`:

```powershell
Get-MessageTraceV2 -MessageTraceId <NetworkMessageId> -SenderAddress "partner@fabrikam.com" -StartDate "2026-07-04" -EndDate "2026-07-05" | Get-MessageTraceDetailV2
```

A `Failed` status with a `RESOLVER.RST.AuthRequired` reason confirms Step 3. A `Pending` status pointing at moderation confirms Step 5.

### Step 3: Allow external senders (fix the authentication NDR)

If external senders must be able to email the list, disable the authentication requirement. For a **standard distribution list**:

```powershell
Set-DistributionGroup -Identity "sales@contoso.com" -RequireSenderAuthenticationEnabled $false
```

For a **Microsoft 365 Group** (the `550 5.7.193` NDR), use the Unified Group cmdlet instead:

```powershell
Set-UnifiedGroup -Identity "sales@contoso.com" -RequireSenderAuthenticationEnabled $false
```

Portal equivalent (modern EAC): **Recipients > Groups >** select the group **> Settings > Edit delivery management >** choose **Allow messages from people inside and outside my organization > Save**. Exchange Online can take up to one hour to apply the change.

### Step 4: Correct the allowed-senders restriction

If only certain senders are permitted, verify the accept/reject lists. An empty `AcceptMessagesOnlyFromSendersOrMembers` value means "accept from anyone" (subject to Step 3). To clear a restrictive accept-list entirely:

```powershell
Set-DistributionGroup -Identity "sales@contoso.com" -AcceptMessagesOnlyFromSendersOrMembers $null
```

To add a specific sender without wiping existing entries:

```powershell
Set-DistributionGroup -Identity "sales@contoso.com" -AcceptMessagesOnlyFromSendersOrMembers @{Add="partner@fabrikam.com"}
```

To remove a sender that is being blocked by the reject-list:

```powershell
Set-DistributionGroup -Identity "sales@contoso.com" -RejectMessagesFromSendersOrMembers @{Remove="blocked@contoso.com"}
```

### Step 5: Resolve moderation-related delays

If messages are held for approval, either assign a working moderator or let known senders bypass moderation. This example enables moderation, sets a moderator, lets the HR group post directly, and notifies only internal senders on rejection:

```powershell
Set-DistributionGroup -Identity "sales@contoso.com" -ModerationEnabled $true -ModeratedBy "amy@contoso.com" -BypassModerationFromSendersOrMembers "HR@contoso.com" -SendModerationNotifications Internal
```

To turn moderation off completely:

```powershell
Set-DistributionGroup -Identity "sales@contoso.com" -ModerationEnabled $false
```

If the list nests other moderated groups, enable automatic approval of members after the parent message is approved:

```powershell
Set-DistributionGroup -Identity "sales@contoso.com" -BypassNestedModerationEnabled $true
```

### Step 6: Verify membership and raise the size limit if needed

Confirm the intended recipients are actually members:

```powershell
Get-DistributionGroupMember -Identity "sales@contoso.com" | Format-Table Name,PrimarySmtpAddress,RecipientType
```

Add a missing member:

```powershell
Add-DistributionGroupMember -Identity "sales@contoso.com" -Member "newuser@contoso.com"
```

If large messages bounce, raise the inbound cap:

```powershell
Set-DistributionGroup -Identity "sales@contoso.com" -MaxReceiveSize 25MB
```

### Step 7: Confirm the fix

Send a test message from the affected sender (external partner, if that was the failure) and re-run the trace from Step 2. A `Delivered` status against each member confirms resolution. Allow up to one hour for delivery-management changes to fully propagate before declaring failure.

## Troubleshooting

- **Change applied but still failing.** Delivery-management and authentication changes can take up to an hour to replicate across Exchange Online. Re-test after that window before escalating.
- **Wrong cmdlet, no effect.** `Set-DistributionGroup` silently does nothing useful against a Microsoft 365 Group. Re-check the type from Step 1 and use `Set-UnifiedGroup` for `GroupMailbox` recipients.
- **Only one member fails.** The problem is that member, not the list. Check the individual mailbox for its own delivery restrictions: `Get-Mailbox <member> | Format-List RequireSenderAuthenticationEnabled,AcceptMessagesOnlyFromSendersOrMembers,MaxReceiveSize`.
- **Nested group fails.** A member that is itself a distribution list has its own `RequireSenderAuthenticationEnabled` and accept/reject gates. Repeat Steps 3-4 against the nested group.
- **Mail contact rejected despite being on the allowed list.** Mail contacts are always unauthenticated. If the group is set to "only senders inside my organization," contacts are rejected even when explicitly added. Switch the group to allow inside-and-outside senders (Step 3).
- **Dynamic distribution group.** Membership is query-based and cannot be edited with `Add-DistributionGroupMember`. Verify the recipient filter with `Get-DynamicDistributionGroup <name> | Format-List RecipientFilter` and adjust delivery settings with `Set-DynamicDistributionGroup`.
- **Message trace returns nothing.** Data can take 5-10 minutes to appear. For messages older than about 10 days, run a historical trace (results arrive as a downloadable CSV within a few hours).

## Prevention

- Decide the external-sender posture when the list is created. If a list must receive partner or vendor mail, set `RequireSenderAuthenticationEnabled $false` at creation and document it.
- Keep accept/reject lists minimal and shallow. Deeply nested groups inside `AcceptMessagesOnlyFromSendersOrMembers` slow expansion and are easy to break.
- When moderation is required, always assign at least one active moderator and configure a bypass group for automated/service senders so operational mail is not delayed.
- Maintain accurate group ownership so approval requests and join/leave requests reach a real person.
- Standardize `MaxReceiveSize` across lists to match your organization-wide transport limits so behavior is predictable.
- Audit list settings periodically, exporting `RequireSenderAuthenticationEnabled`, `ModerationEnabled`, and restriction properties, so configuration drift is caught before users report failures.

**Tags:** distribution list, distribution group, exchange online, delivery restrictions, RequireSenderAuthenticationEnabled, moderation, message trace, NDR, external senders, microsoft 365 groups

Title: EML-062: Shared Mailbox Access and Send-As Problems
Content:
# Shared Mailbox Access and Send-As Problems

**Category:** Email > Shared Mailboxes
**Article Code:** EML-062
**Tier:** 2
**Audience:** Administrators / Technicians
**Estimated Resolution Time:** 15–45 minutes (plus up to 60 minutes for permission propagation)

## Symptoms / When to Use

Use this article when a user reports any of the following against an Exchange Online shared mailbox:

- The shared mailbox does not appear automatically in Outlook after being granted access.
- The user can open the mailbox but sending fails with **"You do not have permission to send the message on behalf of the specified user"** or a bounce with `550 5.7.520` / access-denied wording.
- Mail sent from the shared mailbox lands in the *sender's* Sent Items or shows the sender's own address instead of the shared address.
- The mailbox was removed but still appears (or a removed user still sees cached items).
- Access or Send-As was granted "minutes ago" but is not yet working.
- Access was granted to a security group, but automapping and encrypted-message access do not work for members.

## Background

Two distinct permissions control shared mailbox use, and they are managed by two different cmdlets:

- **Full Access** (`Add-MailboxPermission`) lets a delegate open the mailbox and read, create, and delete items. It does **not** grant the ability to send.
- **Send As** (`Add-RecipientPermission`) lets a delegate send mail that appears to come *from* the shared mailbox address. **Send on Behalf** (`Set-Mailbox -GrantSendOnBehalfTo`) is the alternative, and it stamps "on behalf of" in the header.

Both Full Access and a send permission are required for normal operation. Granting only Full Access is the single most common cause of "I can read but can't send."

**Automapping** is what makes a shared mailbox appear in Outlook automatically. When Full Access is granted directly to an individual user, Exchange writes the `msExchDelegateListLink` / `msExchDelegateListBL` attributes, and Autodiscover adds the mailbox to that user's profile on next Outlook restart. Automapping **only works for permissions granted directly to a user** — it does **not** expand security group membership. This is by design and explains most "mailbox doesn't show up" tickets where a group was used.

Permission changes are not instant. Directory replication and Autodiscover caching mean a new grant can take **up to 60 minutes** (occasionally longer) to take full effect in the Outlook desktop client.

## Resolution

Work top to bottom. Steps 1–4 fix the majority of cases.

### Step 1: Connect to Exchange Online PowerShell

```powershell
Install-Module -Name ExchangeOnlineManagement -Scope CurrentUser
Import-Module ExchangeOnlineManagement
Connect-ExchangeOnline -UserPrincipalName admin@yourtenant.onmicrosoft.com
```

### Step 2: Confirm current permissions before changing anything

Check who actually holds each permission so you do not double-grant or miss a group.

```powershell
# Full Access holders
Get-MailboxPermission -Identity "Sales Department" |
  Where-Object { $_.AccessRights -like "Full*" -and $_.IsInherited -eq $false } |
  Format-Table User, AccessRights, IsInherited -Auto

# Send As holders
Get-RecipientPermission -Identity "Sales Department" |
  Format-Table Trustee, AccessRights, AccessControlType -Auto

# Send on Behalf holders
Get-Mailbox -Identity "Sales Department" | Select-Object -ExpandProperty GrantSendOnBehalfTo
```

### Step 3: Grant Full Access

Grant directly to the user when you want the mailbox to automap into Outlook. `-InheritanceType All` is the standard value.

```powershell
Add-MailboxPermission -Identity "Sales Department" -User john.smith@contoso.com `
  -AccessRights FullAccess -InheritanceType All
```

To grant Full Access **without** automapping (large mailbox, or the user will add it as a separate account):

```powershell
Add-MailboxPermission -Identity "Sales Department" -User john.smith@contoso.com `
  -AccessRights FullAccess -InheritanceType All -AutoMapping $false
```

### Step 4: Grant the send permission

For **Send As** (recommended for shared mailboxes — mail appears to come straight from the shared address):

```powershell
Add-RecipientPermission -Identity "Sales Department" -Trustee john.smith@contoso.com `
  -AccessRights SendAs -Confirm:$false
```

For **Send on Behalf** instead (header shows "John Smith on behalf of Sales Department"). Note this **overwrites** the list, so use `@{Add=...}` to append:

```powershell
Set-Mailbox -Identity "Sales Department" `
  -GrantSendOnBehalfTo @{Add="john.smith@contoso.com"}
```

### Step 5: Verify the grants took

```powershell
Get-MailboxPermission -Identity "Sales Department" -User john.smith@contoso.com
Get-RecipientPermission -Identity "Sales Department" -Trustee john.smith@contoso.com
```

### Step 6: Have the user restart Outlook and wait

Automapped mailboxes appear only after Outlook is fully closed and reopened. If it does not show within an hour, proceed to Troubleshooting. In Outlook on the web, the user can also add it manually: right-click their mailbox name in the folder list > **Add shared folder or mailbox** > enter the address.

## Troubleshooting

**Send As still fails after the grant.** Send permissions can take up to an hour to replicate. Confirm with `Get-RecipientPermission`. If the user is choosing **From > Other Email Address** and typing the display name, have them type the exact **primary SMTP address** instead — an ambiguous or stale nickname-cache entry frequently triggers the "on behalf of" denial. Clear the Outlook nickname cache if a wrong address keeps resolving.

**Mail sends but from the wrong address / lands in the user's Sent Items.** This is Send on Behalf behaving as designed, or the user selected their own account in the **From** field. Confirm Send As is actually assigned (Step 2). For Sent Items routing so copies land in the shared mailbox, enable message-copy behavior:

```powershell
Set-Mailbox -Identity "Sales Department" `
  -MessageCopyForSentAsEnabled $true -MessageCopyForSendOnBehalfEnabled $true
```

**Mailbox does not automap.** The most likely cause is that Full Access was granted to a **security group** — automapping never expands group membership. Either grant Full Access directly to each user, or accept that group members must add the mailbox manually. Also confirm the earlier grant did not include `-AutoMapping $false`.

**Automapping is stuck — mailbox still shows after permission was removed, or you need to toggle it.** There is no switch to flip automapping on an existing grant. You must remove and re-add the permission:

```powershell
Remove-MailboxPermission -Identity "Sales Department" -User john.smith@contoso.com `
  -AccessRights FullAccess -InheritanceType All -Confirm:$false

Add-MailboxPermission -Identity "Sales Department" -User john.smith@contoso.com `
  -AccessRights FullAccess -InheritanceType All -AutoMapping $false
```

After removal, the mailbox clears from the Outlook profile on the next restart. If cached items linger, remove and recreate the Outlook profile.

**User can read but cannot open encrypted/protected messages in the shared mailbox.** Outlook requires Full Access granted **directly** (not via group) with automapping enabled to open encrypted mail. Grant Full Access directly to the user, or have them use **Open another mailbox** in Outlook on the web.

**Private items are not visible.** Items marked *Private* are hidden by design even with Full Access. Grant delegate rights on the folder:

```powershell
Add-MailboxFolderPermission -Identity "Sales Department:\Inbox" -User john.smith@contoso.com `
  -AccessRights Editor -SharingPermissionFlags Delegate,CanViewPrivateItems
```

**EAC portal path (when PowerShell is unavailable).** Exchange admin center (`admin.exchange.microsoft.com`) > **Recipients** > **Mailboxes** > select the shared mailbox > **Delegation** > edit **Read and manage (Full Access)**, **Send as**, or **Send on behalf**. Portal changes are subject to the same propagation delay.

**Access denied running the cmdlets.** The admin needs a role such as **Recipient Management** or **Organization Management**. A global admin without an Exchange role assignment cannot run these cmdlets until the role is assigned.

## Prevention

- **Always grant both permissions together** — Full Access plus Send As (or Send on Behalf). Track it as one change so "can't send" tickets don't recur.
- **Decide automapping policy up front.** For small mailboxes, grant Full Access directly so it automaps. For large or many-delegate mailboxes, use `-AutoMapping $false` to avoid Outlook performance problems from loading every mailbox at startup.
- **Prefer direct user grants over security groups** when automapping, encrypted-mail access, or per-user auditing matter. Use groups only when you accept the automapping and encryption limitations in exchange for easier membership management.
- **Set expectations on timing.** Tell users a new grant can take up to an hour and requires an Outlook restart, so they don't reopen a ticket at the 5-minute mark.
- **Standardize with `MessageCopyForSentAsEnabled`** on shared mailboxes so sent mail is retained in the shared Sent Items for the whole team.
- **Document delegations.** Keep a periodic export of `Get-MailboxPermission` / `Get-RecipientPermission` output per shared mailbox so access can be reviewed and cleaned up during offboarding.

**Tags:** shared mailbox, send as, full access, automapping, exchange online, add-mailboxpermission, add-recipientpermission, send on behalf, powershell, outlook, delegation

Title: EML-063: Outlook Calendar Sharing and Permission Issues
Content:
# Outlook Calendar Sharing and Permission Issues

**Category:** Email > Calendar
**Article Code:** EML-063
**Tier:** 1
**Audience:** Administrators / Technicians
**Estimated Resolution Time:** 10–25 minutes

## Symptoms / When to Use

- A user shared their calendar but the recipient sees "Free/Busy" only, or nothing at all.
- A delegate cannot open, edit, or receive meeting invites for a manager's calendar.
- The recipient gets *"Cannot display the folder. You do not have permission"* when opening a shared calendar.
- Calendar sharing invitations fail or the "Add" button is greyed out in Outlook/OWA.
- Permissions set in the Outlook client don't take effect, or revert after sync.
- Private items are visible to a delegate who should not see them (or vice versa).

## Background

Outlook calendar access is controlled by **folder-level permissions** on the `:\Calendar` folder of the mailbox, not by mailbox-level delegation. Each grant maps a user to an **access right** (role) such as `Reviewer`, `Editor`, or `Owner`, optionally with **sharing/delegate flags** (delegate status, private-item visibility).

Client-side changes can silently fail due to cached permissions, throttling, or a localized folder name (non-English mailboxes name the folder e.g. `:\Kalender`). Setting permissions server-side with Exchange Online PowerShell is authoritative and bypasses client sync problems. External sharing and publishing are a separate mechanism handled by `Set-MailboxCalendarFolder` and org-level sharing policies.

## Resolution

### Step 1: Connect to Exchange Online PowerShell

```powershell
Install-Module -Name ExchangeOnlineManagement -Scope CurrentUser
Connect-ExchangeOnline -UserPrincipalName admin@contoso.com
```

### Step 2: Inspect current calendar permissions

Confirm the folder name and existing grants before changing anything.

```powershell
Get-MailboxFolderPermission -Identity "ayla@contoso.com:\Calendar"
```

If the mailbox is localized and `:\Calendar` errors, find the real folder name:

```powershell
Get-MailboxFolderStatistics -Identity ayla@contoso.com -FolderScope Calendar |
    Format-Table Name, FolderPath
```

### Step 3: Grant or modify permissions

Add a new grant (fails if the user already has one):

```powershell
Add-MailboxFolderPermission -Identity "ayla@contoso.com:\Calendar" `
    -User laura@contoso.com -AccessRights Reviewer
```

Modify an existing grant with `Set-MailboxFolderPermission`:

```powershell
Set-MailboxFolderPermission -Identity "ayla@contoso.com:\Calendar" `
    -User laura@contoso.com -AccessRights Editor
```

Common `-AccessRights` roles: `AvailabilityOnly`, `LimitedDetails`, `Reviewer` (read), `Author`, `Editor` (read/write), `Owner`.

### Step 4: Configure delegate access (optional)

To make the user a true delegate who receives meeting invites and can view private items:

```powershell
Add-MailboxFolderPermission -Identity "ayla@contoso.com:\Calendar" `
    -User laura@contoso.com -AccessRights Editor `
    -SharingPermissionFlags Delegate,CanViewPrivateItems
```

Use `-SharingPermissionFlags Delegate` alone to grant delegate status without private-item access.

### Step 5: Verify

```powershell
Get-MailboxFolderPermission -Identity "ayla@contoso.com:\Calendar" -User laura@contoso.com
```

Have the recipient remove and re-add the shared calendar in Outlook (**Add Calendar > From Address Book**) to force a fresh sync.

## Troubleshooting

- **Grant already exists:** `Add-MailboxFolderPermission` throws if a grant exists. Use `Set-MailboxFolderPermission` instead, or `Remove-MailboxFolderPermission` then re-add.
- **Removing access:**
  ```powershell
  Remove-MailboxFolderPermission -Identity "ayla@contoso.com:\Calendar" -User laura@contoso.com
  ```
- **Default vs. named user:** The special principals `Default` and `Anonymous` set the baseline for everyone. If `Default` is `AvailabilityOnly`, non-delegated users see free/busy only — raise it or grant the user explicitly.
- **Delegate flag lost:** Running `Set-MailboxFolderPermission` with `-SendNotificationToUser` but no `-SharingPermissionFlags` resets flags to `None`, stripping delegate status. Always re-specify `-SharingPermissionFlags` when modifying a delegate.
- **Changes don't appear client-side:** Sync lag or cached credentials — wait, restart Outlook, or re-add the calendar. Server-side `Get-MailboxFolderPermission` output is the source of truth.
- **External/cross-tenant sharing fails:** This is governed by the org sharing policy (`Get-SharingPolicy`) and individual sharing rules (`Set-MailboxCalendarFolder`), not folder permissions. Confirm the tenant sharing policy allows the target domain.

## Prevention

- Standardize on server-side (PowerShell) permission changes for shared/resource mailboxes to avoid client sync issues.
- Grant the least-privilege role that meets the need (`Reviewer` for visibility, `Editor` for scheduling).
- Document delegate assignments; re-apply `-SharingPermissionFlags` on every modify to avoid accidental flag resets.
- Leave `Default` at `AvailabilityOnly` unless the org policy requires broader visibility, and grant named users explicitly.
- Review calendar permissions on manager/executive mailboxes periodically as part of offboarding and role changes.

**Tags:** outlook, calendar, sharing, permissions, delegate, exchange-online, powershell, mailboxfolderpermission, free-busy, microsoft-365

Title: EML-064: Exchange Online Retention Policies Not Applying
Content:
# Exchange Online Retention Policies Not Applying

**Category:** Email > Compliance
**Article Code:** EML-064
**Tier:** 3
**Audience:** Administrators / Technicians
**Estimated Resolution Time:** 30-90 minutes hands-on, plus up to 7 days of monitoring for the Managed Folder Assistant (MFA) to complete a full processing cycle on large mailboxes.

MRM (Messaging Records Management) retention policies in Exchange Online rely on retention tags, a retention policy that links those tags, and the Managed Folder Assistant that stamps and actions items. When items that should have been moved to archive or deleted remain in place, the failure is almost always in one of those three layers or in a hold that blocks processing. This article covers the diagnostic path for admins, plus the end-user-facing symptoms that generate the ticket.

> Note: This article covers classic **MRM retention tags and policies** (the `*-RetentionPolicy` / `*-RetentionPolicyTag` cmdlets), which remain the recommended mechanism for moving items to archive mailboxes. Microsoft Purview retention policies and retention labels are a separate system managed in the Microsoft Purview portal; if the "policy" in the ticket is a Purview retention/label policy, this MRM path does not apply.

## Symptoms / When to Use

- Email older than the configured retention age is **not** being moved to the archive mailbox, or is not being deleted.
- A newly created or newly assigned retention policy has had no visible effect after several days.
- Users report the "archive" or "expiration" countdown never triggers, or Outlook shows a retention period of **Never** on items that should expire.
- The Recoverable Items folder or the primary mailbox is filling up and nothing is being cleared.
- Archive mailbox is provisioned but stays empty despite an archive (Move to Archive) tag being in the policy.
- Only some folders honor the policy (e.g., Inbox works, Junk Email does not), or only some users in the same policy are affected.
- Items expire much later than expected, or a subset of very large messages are skipped.

## Background

MRM applies retention through three objects:

1. **Retention tags** — the actual settings (age, action). Three types: **DPT** (Default Policy Tag, applies to the whole mailbox), **RPT** (Retention Policy Tag, applies to a specific default folder such as Inbox or Junk Email), and **Personal tags** (opt-in, applied by the user to folders or individual items).
2. **Retention policy** — a container that links a set of tags via `RetentionPolicyTagLinks`. One policy is assigned per mailbox.
3. **Managed Folder Assistant (MFA)** — a throttle-based mailbox assistant that inspects items, stamps them with the applicable tag, and takes the retention action once an item passes its retention age.

Key behaviors that explain most "not applying" tickets:

- MFA is **not on a fixed schedule**. It is guaranteed to process each mailbox at least once every **7 days**. It usually runs more often, but you cannot predict the next run, so a brand-new policy legitimately may not act for up to a week unless you force it.
- MFA **does not process mailboxes smaller than 10 MB.** Small test mailboxes will appear "broken" until they exceed that size or you run MFA manually.
- If the mailbox account is **disabled** and the mailbox is a regular (non-shared) user mailbox, MFA does not process it and items are not moved to archive.
- **Holds block deletion.** Retention hold (`RetentionHoldEnabled = $true`) suspends MRM entirely. Litigation Hold / In-Place Hold / Purview holds do not stop tagging, but items "deleted" by a delete tag are retained in Recoverable Items for the hold duration rather than being purged.
- **Longest-duration tag wins.** A disabled tag or a "Never" tag (never move to archive / never delete) takes precedence over shorter tags, so a single mis-set personal tag can silently override the whole policy.
- MFA **won't move items larger than** the mailbox's `MaxSendSize` / `MaxReceiveSize`, which is why isolated large messages get skipped.

## Resolution

Work top-down: confirm the policy and tags are correct, confirm the mailbox is assigned the policy and is processable, then force MFA and verify. All commands run in **Exchange Online PowerShell**.

### Step 1: Connect to Exchange Online PowerShell

Install/import the module and connect with an account holding the appropriate admin role.

```powershell
Install-Module -Name ExchangeOnlineManagement -Scope CurrentUser
Import-Module ExchangeOnlineManagement
Connect-ExchangeOnline -UserPrincipalName admin@contoso.com
```

### Step 2: Confirm the policy assignment and retention-affecting properties on the mailbox

Check which policy is applied and whether any hold or processing block is set.

```powershell
Get-Mailbox user@contoso.com | Format-List *Retention*,ElcProcessingDisabled,LitigationHoldEnabled,InPlaceHolds
```

Verify:

- `RetentionPolicy` is the policy you expect. If it is blank or wrong, the mailbox is not covered by your policy.
- `RetentionHoldEnabled` is `False`. If `True`, MRM is suspended for this mailbox.
- `ElcProcessingDisabled` is `False`. If `True`, MFA will not process the mailbox at all.

Clear a retention hold or processing block if present (confirm with the requester first — holds are often intentional):

```powershell
Set-Mailbox user@contoso.com -RetentionHoldEnabled $false
Set-Mailbox user@contoso.com -ElcProcessingDisabled $false
```

If the policy is missing or wrong, assign the correct one:

```powershell
Set-Mailbox user@contoso.com -RetentionPolicy "Corp-Retention"
```

### Step 3: Inspect the policy's linked tags

List the tags actually linked to the assigned policy. A common cause is a policy that contains only personal (opt-in) tags — nothing acts automatically until the user applies them.

```powershell
Get-RetentionPolicy -Identity "Corp-Retention" | Select-Object -ExpandProperty RetentionPolicyTagLinks
```

Review each relevant tag's configuration:

```powershell
Get-RetentionPolicyTag "DPT-Corp-Delete" | Format-List Name,Type,RetentionEnabled,AgeLimitForRetention,RetentionAction,MessageClass
```

Confirm on each tag:

- `RetentionEnabled` is `True`. A disabled tag causes MFA to **ignore** matching items entirely — they are never moved or deleted and the DPT does not apply to them.
- `RetentionAction` is the expected action (`MoveToArchive`, `DeleteAndAllowRecovery`, or `PermanentlyDelete`).
- `AgeLimitForRetention` matches the intended age (in days).
- `Type` matches the intended scope (`All` for a DPT, a folder name like `Inbox`/`JunkEmail` for an RPT, `Personal` for opt-in tags).

Enable a tag that was mistakenly disabled, or correct its age:

```powershell
Set-RetentionPolicyTag "DPT-Corp-Delete" -RetentionEnabled $true -AgeLimitForRetention 730
```

### Step 4: Check for personal / "Never" tags overriding the policy

List optional personal tags the user has opted into beyond the assigned policy — these frequently override folder-level behavior.

```powershell
Get-RetentionPolicyTag -Mailbox user@contoso.com -OptionalInMailbox
```

Pay special attention to any tag with a **Never move to archive** or **Never delete** action applied to a folder or item. Because the longest-duration tag wins, an explicit "Never" personal tag on a folder blocks the DPT for everything in that folder. If found, the user must remove it in Outlook / Outlook on the web (right-click the folder or item > Assign Policy > Use Parent Folder Policy / a normal tag). Admins cannot strip a user-applied personal tag from an item via PowerShell.

### Step 5: Force the Managed Folder Assistant

Rather than waiting up to 7 days, trigger MFA against the mailbox.

```powershell
Start-ManagedFolderAssistant -Identity user@contoso.com
```

If the policy was changed and items were previously stamped with old tags, force a full re-crawl so MFA re-evaluates every item and regenerates the mailbox's retention configuration (`IPM.Configuration.MRM` / `PR_ROAMING_XMLSTREAM`):

```powershell
Start-ManagedFolderAssistant -Identity user@contoso.com -FullCrawl
```

To apply a new policy across many mailboxes, pipe them in:

```powershell
$mbx = Get-Mailbox -ResultSize Unlimited -Filter {RecipientTypeDetails -eq "UserMailbox"}
$mbx.Identity | Start-ManagedFolderAssistant
```

### Step 6: Verify MFA actually processed the mailbox

Export the MRM diagnostic log and confirm a recent successful run and non-zero action counts.

```powershell
$logProps = Export-MailboxDiagnosticLogs user@contoso.com -ExtendedProperties
$xmlprops = [xml]($logProps.MailboxLog)
$xmlprops.Properties.MailboxTable.Property | Where-Object {$_.Name -like "ELC*"}
```

Interpret the output:

- `ElcLastSuccessTimestamp` should show a time **after** you triggered MFA in Step 5. If it is stale, MFA has not completed a clean run.
- `ElcLastRunTaggedWithArchiveItemCount` / `ElcLastRunTaggedWithExpiryItemCount` — items stamped for archive / deletion on the last run.
- `ElcLastRunArchivedFromRootItemCount` / `ElcLastRunDeletedFromDumpsterItemCount` — items actually moved / purged.

Also pull the human-readable error log:

```powershell
Export-MailboxDiagnosticLogs user@contoso.com -ComponentName MRM
```

Most recent errors appear at the top. `no logs were found` means MFA processed the mailbox with no errors (a good sign, not a failure). A `resource unhealthy` message means the mailbox is being throttled because of size/item count — processing continues, just slowly (see Troubleshooting).

## Troubleshooting

If items still are not moving or deleting after Steps 1-6, work through these variations.

**Mailbox under 10 MB.** MFA does not process mailboxes smaller than 10 MB. This is the usual reason a policy "does nothing" on a fresh test mailbox. Either add content to exceed 10 MB or accept that manual `Start-ManagedFolderAssistant` runs are required for tiny mailboxes.

**Disabled account.** If the associated user account is disabled and the mailbox is a regular user mailbox, MRM will not move items to archive. Convert to a shared mailbox if the account must stay disabled, or re-enable the account.

**Compare the item's real age against the tag age.** Retention age is computed from the item's received/created date, not from when the policy was applied. Pull folder statistics with oldest/newest items and compare against the tag age.

```powershell
Get-MailboxFolderStatistics -Identity user@contoso.com -IncludeOldestAndNewestItems |
    Export-Csv -NoTypeInformation -Path .\primaryfolderstats.csv

Get-MailboxFolderStatistics -Identity user@contoso.com -Archive -IncludeOldestAndNewestItems |
    Export-Csv -NoTypeInformation -Path .\archivefolderstats.csv
```

For most folders, compare `OldestItemReceivedDate` to the tag's `AgeLimitForRetention`. For the Recoverable Items folder, compare `OldestItemLastModifiedDate` to the mailbox's `RetainDeletedItemsFor`. The `DeletePolicy`, `ArchivePolicy`, `CompliancePolicy`, and `RetentionFlags` columns show which tag each folder actually inherited — use these to spot a folder that inherited an unexpected or explicit tag. Note that **Contacts** are never processed (no date stamp), and **Deleted Items**, recurring **Calendar**, and recurring **Tasks** items age differently.

**Large messages skipped.** MFA will not move an item larger than the mailbox's `MaxSendSize` / `MaxReceiveSize`. Check those limits if only a few oversized items linger.

**Recoverable Items folder full.** If Recoverable Items is at quota, MRM cannot move items into the archive. Enable the archive mailbox and auto-expanding archiving, and (for holds) ensure the archive is provisioned so the Recoverable Items subtree can be relieved.

**Recoverable Items not emptying on a mailbox with a hold.** In hybrid, a Purview hold GUID synced to `msExchUserHoldPolicies` that the on-premises org cannot resolve causes MFA to skip purging `DiscoveryHolds`, filling Recoverable Items. Lowering the `AgeLimitForRetention` on the Recoverable Items archive tag (e.g., to 1 day) and running MFA moves those items to the archive's Recoverable Items and frees space:

```powershell
Get-RetentionPolicyTag | Format-Table Name,Type,RetentionAction,AgeLimitForRetention
Set-RetentionPolicyTag "Recoverable Items 14 days move to archive" -AgeLimitForRetention 1
Start-ManagedFolderAssistant -Identity user@contoso.com
```

**Policy config missing / corrupt stamping.** If the diagnostic XML shows the expected tags are absent from the mailbox's retention configuration, the hidden `IPM.Configuration.MRM` message (`PR_ROAMING_XMLSTREAM`) may be out of date. Running `Start-ManagedFolderAssistant -FullCrawl` regenerates it. In stubborn cases, MFCMAPI can be used to inspect (and, as a last resort, delete) the `IPM.Configuration.MRM` message under Inbox associated contents so a subsequent full-crawl rebuilds it.

**Throttling on large mailboxes.** `resource unhealthy` in the MRM log means the mailbox is being processed slowly due to size. This is expected and self-resolves over multiple runs; do not treat a single run's low counts as failure — re-check `ElcLastSuccessTimestamp` over a few days.

**Portal-based validation.** For a quick automated check without PowerShell, in the **Microsoft 365 admin center** open the retention policy diagnostics flyout (search **Diag: Verify Retention Policy** / the "Run diagnostics on retention policy settings" self-help), enter the mailbox address, and run the tests. This validates the assigned policy, tags, and hold state. (Not available for Microsoft 365 Government, 21Vianet, or Germany.)

**Confirm the right system.** If nothing above matches, verify whether the retention is actually a **Microsoft Purview** retention policy/label rather than MRM. Purview policies are managed at the Microsoft Purview portal (`purview.microsoft.com`) and have their own distribution and processing behavior — the MRM cmdlets in this article will not diagnose them.

## Prevention

- **Always force and verify** after any policy change: `Start-ManagedFolderAssistant` then confirm `ElcLastSuccessTimestamp` advanced. Don't assume "applied" until MFA has run cleanly.
- **Include at least one non-personal tag** (a DPT and/or RPTs) in every policy meant to act automatically. Personal-only policies do nothing until users opt in.
- **Audit for disabled and "Never" tags** during change reviews — they silently override shorter tags and are the top cause of partial failures.
- **Set the archive DPT age lower than the delete DPT age** so items move to archive before a deletion tag would remove them.
- **Provision the archive and enable auto-expanding archiving** before placing high-volume mailboxes on hold to keep Recoverable Items from filling.
- **Document intentional holds** (`RetentionHoldEnabled`, `ElcProcessingDisabled`, Litigation/Purview holds) so a future technician doesn't misread them as a bug.
- **Test on a mailbox over 10 MB with a live user account** — small or disabled test mailboxes give misleading results.
- **Allow the full 7-day window** before escalating a policy as "not working" on mailboxes where you have not manually forced MFA.

Title: EML-065: Exchange Online Mailbox Quota Exceeded — Restoring Send/Receive
Content:
# Exchange Online Mailbox Quota Exceeded — Restoring Send/Receive

**Category:** Email > Storage
**Article Code:** EML-065
**Tier:** 2
**Audience:** Administrators / Technicians
**Estimated Resolution Time:** 15–40 minutes

## Symptoms / When to Use

Use this article when an Exchange Online user can no longer send or receive mail due to mailbox size limits:

- NDR to senders: "The recipient's mailbox is full and can't accept messages."
- User sees "Your mailbox is full" or cannot send new mail.
- Outlook prompts to free up space; items won't move to folders.
- Admin center shows the mailbox near or at its storage quota.

## Background

Every Exchange Online mailbox has three quota thresholds: **Issue Warning**, **Prohibit Send**, and **Prohibit Send/Receive**. Standard plans provide 50 GB or 100 GB of primary mailbox storage depending on license; archive mailboxes add more. When usage crosses Prohibit Send, the user cannot send; at Prohibit Send/Receive, inbound mail bounces. The mailbox size also includes **Recoverable Items** (the "dumpster"), which can silently consume several GB and is a common hidden cause of a mailbox that looks under quota but still blocks.

## Resolution

### Step 1: Confirm current usage and quota

Connect to Exchange Online PowerShell:
```powershell
Connect-ExchangeOnline -UserPrincipalName admin@yourtenant.com

Get-MailboxStatistics -Identity user@yourtenant.com |
  Select DisplayName, TotalItemSize, TotalDeletedItemSize, ItemCount

Get-Mailbox -Identity user@yourtenant.com |
  Select ProhibitSendQuota, ProhibitSendReceiveQuota, IssueWarningQuota, `
         ArchiveStatus, AutoExpandingArchiveEnabled
```

### Step 2: Enable the archive (fastest structural fix)

If the license includes archiving, enable it and let managed folder assistant move old mail out of the primary mailbox.
```powershell
Enable-Mailbox -Identity user@yourtenant.com -Archive
# Enable auto-expanding archive for large mailboxes
Enable-Mailbox -Identity user@yourtenant.com -AutoExpandingArchive
```
Apply a retention/archive policy so items older than N years auto-move to the archive:
```powershell
Set-Mailbox -Identity user@yourtenant.com -RetentionPolicy "Default MRM Policy"
Start-ManagedFolderAssistant -Identity user@yourtenant.com
```

### Step 3: Reclaim space from Recoverable Items ("dumpster")

Recoverable Items counts against quota. Check and, if the user has confirmed nothing is needed, purge:
```powershell
Get-MailboxFolderStatistics -Identity user@yourtenant.com -FolderScope RecoverableItems |
  Select Name, FolderAndSubfolderSize, ItemsInFolderAndSubfolders
```
Note: if the mailbox is on **Litigation Hold** or covered by a retention policy, Recoverable Items cannot be freed until the hold is released — this is by design for compliance.

### Step 4: Have the user reduce mailbox size

- Empty **Deleted Items** and **Junk**.
- Delete or archive large-attachment threads (Outlook → sort by Size).
- Move old mail to the online archive (In-Place Archive appears as a separate folder tree).

### Step 5: (If licensed) temporarily raise the quota

For plans that allow it, quotas are managed by license and generally fixed at 50/100 GB. If the user is on a lower plan, assign an appropriate license (e.g., a plan with 100 GB) as the durable fix rather than a manual override.

### Step 6: Verify

Re-run `Get-MailboxStatistics`. Confirm the user can send and receive a test message and that the warning clears (allow time for the store to catch up).

## Troubleshooting

- **Usage still high after archiving:** run `Start-ManagedFolderAssistant` and allow up to 24–72h; MFA processes on a schedule.
- **Cannot purge Recoverable Items:** check for `LitigationHoldEnabled $true` or retention holds with `Get-Mailbox | Select LitigationHoldEnabled, InPlaceHolds`.
- **Shared mailbox over 50 GB:** shared mailboxes require a license once they exceed 50 GB or need an archive.

## Prevention

- Deploy a tenant-wide **MRM retention policy** that archives mail older than 2 years.
- Enable **auto-expanding archive** for heavy users.
- Alert on mailboxes crossing 80% of quota via a scheduled Graph/PowerShell report.
- Educate users to store large files in OneDrive/SharePoint and share links, not attachments.

Title: EML-066: Outlook Delegate Access Configuration Issues
Content:
# Outlook Delegate Access Configuration Issues

**Category:** Email > Delegation
**Article Code:** EML-066
**Tier:** 2
**Audience:** Administrators / Technicians (with end-user verification steps)
**Estimated Resolution Time:** 20–45 minutes

Delegate access in Exchange Online spans three distinct permission layers: full mailbox access, Send As / Send on Behalf, and folder-level (calendar) delegation. Most "delegate isn't working" tickets come from mixing these layers or from client-side caching (auto-mapping, Autodiscover, hidden GAL entries). This article covers diagnosis and remediation from both the admin (PowerShell/EAC) and end-user angles.

## Symptoms / When to Use

- A delegate reports they cannot open a manager's or shared mailbox, or the mailbox stopped auto-appearing in Outlook.
- Delegate can open the mailbox but gets "You do not have permission to send on behalf of the specified user" when sending.
- Meeting requests are not routed to the delegate, or the delegate cannot accept invitations on behalf of the manager.
- Calendar shows as free/busy only when the delegate should have Editor rights, or private items are unexpectedly visible/hidden.
- A shared mailbox no longer auto-maps into a user's Outlook profile, or auto-maps for a user who no longer needs it.
- Send As / Send on Behalf silently fails only in Outlook desktop but works in Outlook on the web (OWA).
- Delegate access worked on-premises but broke after mailbox migration to Exchange Online.

## Background

Exchange Online exposes delegation through separate mechanisms, and each is stored and evaluated independently:

- **Full Access** (`Add-MailboxPermission`) lets a delegate open and read/manage the entire mailbox but does **not** grant the ability to send. By default it triggers **auto-mapping**, where Autodiscover automatically mounts the target mailbox in the delegate's Outlook profile. Auto-mapping works only for individual users, never for groups.
- **Send As** (`Add-RecipientPermission`) makes mail appear to come directly from the mailbox. **Send on Behalf** (`Set-Mailbox -GrantSendOnBehalfTo`) stamps "Delegate on behalf of Owner" in the From line. These are stored in different places and managed by different cmdlets.
- **Folder/calendar delegation** (`Add-MailboxFolderPermission` with `-SharingPermissionFlags Delegate`) is what Outlook's classic Delegates dialog writes. This is the only layer that controls meeting-request routing and private-item visibility.

Common failure modes: Full Access is confused with send rights; auto-mapping is cached in the client and lags behind directory changes; and `HiddenFromAddressListsEnabled = $true` on the target breaks Send As / Send on Behalf in Outlook desktop because those permissions require the mailbox to resolve in the Global Address List. All PowerShell steps below assume an Exchange Online PowerShell session.

## Resolution

### Step 1: Connect to Exchange Online PowerShell

Install the module once, then connect with an Exchange Administrator account.

```powershell
Install-Module -Name ExchangeOnlineManagement -Scope CurrentUser
Import-Module ExchangeOnlineManagement
Connect-ExchangeOnline -UserPrincipalName admin@contoso.com
```

### Step 2: Audit the current permission state

Identify which layer is actually misconfigured before changing anything. Run all three checks against the target mailbox.

```powershell
# Full Access delegates (ignore NT AUTHORITY\SELF and inherited entries)
Get-MailboxPermission -Identity manager@contoso.com |
  Where-Object { $_.User -notlike "NT AUTHORITY\SELF" -and $_.IsInherited -eq $false }

# Send As delegates
Get-RecipientPermission -Identity manager@contoso.com

# Send on Behalf delegates
Get-Mailbox -Identity manager@contoso.com | Format-List GrantSendOnBehalfTo

# Calendar folder delegates
Get-MailboxFolderPermission -Identity manager@contoso.com:\Calendar
```

Note the `AccessRights` and, for the calendar, the `SharingPermissionFlags` column (`None`, `Delegate`, or `Delegate,CanViewPrivateItems`).

### Step 3: Grant Full Access (open the mailbox)

For a delegate who needs to open the mailbox. `-InheritanceType All` is standard. Add `-AutoMapping $false` if you do **not** want the mailbox to auto-mount in the delegate's profile (recommended for large or shared mailboxes).

```powershell
Add-MailboxPermission -Identity manager@contoso.com -User delegate@contoso.com `
  -AccessRights FullAccess -InheritanceType All
```

To suppress auto-mapping:

```powershell
Add-MailboxPermission -Identity manager@contoso.com -User delegate@contoso.com `
  -AccessRights FullAccess -InheritanceType All -AutoMapping $false
```

### Step 4: Grant send rights (choose Send As or Send on Behalf)

Send As — mail appears to come directly from the manager:

```powershell
Add-RecipientPermission -Identity manager@contoso.com -Trustee delegate@contoso.com `
  -AccessRights SendAs -Confirm:$false
```

Send on Behalf — mail shows "delegate on behalf of manager". Use the `@{Add=...}` form to avoid overwriting existing delegates:

```powershell
Set-Mailbox -Identity manager@contoso.com -GrantSendOnBehalfTo @{Add="delegate@contoso.com"}
```

Do not grant both Send As and Send on Behalf to the same delegate on the same mailbox; Send As always wins and the mixed state causes confusion.

### Step 5: Configure calendar / folder delegation

This is what enables meeting-request routing and private-item control. `-SharingPermissionFlags Delegate` is what makes the user a true delegate rather than someone with plain folder rights.

```powershell
Add-MailboxFolderPermission -Identity manager@contoso.com:\Calendar `
  -User delegate@contoso.com -AccessRights Editor -SharingPermissionFlags Delegate
```

To also allow the delegate to see items marked Private:

```powershell
Add-MailboxFolderPermission -Identity manager@contoso.com:\Calendar `
  -User delegate@contoso.com -AccessRights Editor `
  -SharingPermissionFlags Delegate,CanViewPrivateItems
```

If a permission entry already exists for that user, `Add-MailboxFolderPermission` fails with "an existing permission entry was found." Use `Set-MailboxFolderPermission` instead to modify it:

```powershell
Set-MailboxFolderPermission -Identity manager@contoso.com:\Calendar `
  -User delegate@contoso.com -AccessRights Editor -SharingPermissionFlags Delegate
```

### Step 6: (Optional) Keep sent copies in the manager's mailbox

By default, messages a delegate sends land only in the delegate's Sent Items. To also copy them to the manager's mailbox:

```powershell
Set-Mailbox -Identity manager@contoso.com -MessageCopyForSendOnBehalfEnabled $true
Set-Mailbox -Identity manager@contoso.com -MessageCopyForSentAsEnabled $true
```

### Step 7: Verify

Re-run the Step 2 audit commands to confirm the entries. Then have the delegate restart Outlook and confirm they can open the mailbox and send. Directory changes can take up to a few hours to fully propagate.

## Troubleshooting

**Mailbox does not auto-map (or won't stop auto-mapping).** Auto-mapping is set at grant time and cached client-side. Changing it requires removing and re-adding the Full Access permission with the desired `-AutoMapping` value, then restarting Outlook:

```powershell
Remove-MailboxPermission -Identity manager@contoso.com -User delegate@contoso.com `
  -AccessRights FullAccess -Confirm:$false
Add-MailboxPermission -Identity manager@contoso.com -User delegate@contoso.com `
  -AccessRights FullAccess -InheritanceType All -AutoMapping $false
```

**Send As / Send on Behalf fails only in Outlook desktop.** Check whether the target is hidden from the address list. Send As and Send on Behalf require the mailbox to resolve in the GAL for the Outlook desktop client.

```powershell
Get-Mailbox -Identity manager@contoso.com | Format-List HiddenFromAddressListsEnabled
```

If `True` and the delegate must send, set it to `$false`, or have them use OWA where GAL resolution is not required.

**Delegate cannot accept meetings for a resource/room mailbox.** Full Access to a shared mailbox does not inherit calendar rights on a linked room. Grant explicit editor rights on the room calendar, and for resource booking set the delegate via `Set-CalendarProcessing`:

```powershell
Add-MailboxFolderPermission -Identity room@contoso.com:\Calendar `
  -User delegate@contoso.com -AccessRights Editor
Set-CalendarProcessing -Identity room@contoso.com -ResourceDelegates delegate@contoso.com
```

**Free/busy or delegate settings are corrupt (errors when opening Delegates dialog).** Reset the delegate collection on the manager's calendar, then re-add delegates. Export current permissions first so you can rebuild them:

```powershell
Get-MailboxFolderPermission -Identity manager@contoso.com:\Calendar
Remove-MailboxFolderPermission -Identity manager@contoso.com:\Calendar -ResetDelegateUserCollection
Add-MailboxFolderPermission -Identity manager@contoso.com:\Calendar `
  -User delegate@contoso.com -AccessRights Editor -SharingPermissionFlags Delegate
```

**"Existing permission entry was found."** The user already has a folder permission — use `Set-MailboxFolderPermission` (Step 5), not `Add-`.

**Broke after migration from on-premises.** Send on Behalf (`publicDelegates` / `GrantSendOnBehalfTo`) is not written back to on-premises AD by default in hybrid. Enable Exchange hybrid writeback in Microsoft Entra Connect, or reapply the permission directly in Exchange Online with `Set-Mailbox -GrantSendOnBehalfTo`.

**EAC/GUI alternative.** For single mailboxes, the same settings live in the Exchange admin center under **Recipients > Mailboxes > [mailbox] > Delegation**, and in the Microsoft 365 admin center under **Users > Active users > [user] > Mail > Mailbox delegation**. Note that Send on Behalf for shared mailboxes cannot be assigned from the classic EAC — use PowerShell or the Microsoft 365 admin center.

## Prevention

- **Match the permission to the need.** Full Access = open/read only; Send As / Send on Behalf = sending; folder delegation = calendar and meeting routing. Grant the minimum required.
- **Use `-AutoMapping $false`** for shared and high-volume mailboxes to avoid Outlook profile bloat and OST sync problems.
- **Prefer mail-enabled security groups** for Full Access on shared mailboxes so membership changes don't require re-running permission cmdlets. Groups do not auto-map.
- **Standardize on either Send As or Send on Behalf** per mailbox — never both for the same delegate.
- **Document delegate assignments** and audit periodically with the Step 2 commands; remove access promptly on role changes or offboarding.
- **Verify GAL visibility** before assigning send rights; avoid hiding mailboxes that delegates must send from.
