Title: EML-067: Outlook Meeting and Calendar Sync Problems
Content:
# Outlook Meeting and Calendar Sync Problems

**Category:** Email > Calendar
**Article Code:** EML-067
**Tier:** 1
**Audience:** Technicians (with Exchange admin escalation)
**Estimated Resolution Time:** 20-45 minutes

Quick fixes for classic Outlook (Windows) desktop calendars that fall out of sync with the Exchange Online mailbox. Most cases resolve at the client with a rebuilt offline cache or a cleared calendar view.

## Symptoms / When to Use

- Meetings appear in Outlook on the web (OWA) but are missing from the classic Outlook desktop client, or vice versa.
- Accepted meetings do not land on the calendar, or declined/canceled meetings still show.
- Duplicate calendar items or stale reminders that keep reappearing.
- Recurring meetings show wrong times or the wrong time zone for one attendee.
- Free/busy shows incorrect availability; delegates can't see calendar changes.
- Mobile (Exchange ActiveSync) calendar is out of sync with the mailbox.

## Background

Classic Outlook works from a cached local copy of the mailbox (the `.ost` file). Calendar sync issues usually come from a corrupted `.ost`, a damaged calendar view or navigation pane, corrupted individual calendar items (bad global object IDs, missing required properties), or a stale free/busy message. Because OWA reads the mailbox directly on the server, "OWA is correct but Outlook is wrong" almost always points at the local cache or view — not the server data. Server-side item corruption and delegate/free-busy problems are the exceptions and require Exchange Online PowerShell.

## Resolution

### Step 1: Confirm where the data is correct

Have the user check the same meeting in OWA (`https://outlook.office.com`). If the item is correct in OWA but wrong in the desktop client, treat it as a client-side cache/view problem (Steps 2-4). If it's wrong in OWA too, the item is corrupt server-side — go to Step 5.

### Step 2: Rebuild the offline cache (.ost)

Clearing offline items forces a fresh download from the server and fixes most single-calendar sync gaps. In classic Outlook, right-click the affected calendar and select **Properties** > **Clear Offline Items** > **OK**, then force a resync:

```text
Send / Receive tab  >  Update Folder
```

If the whole profile is out of sync, close Outlook and rename the `.ost` (Outlook rebuilds it on next launch):

```cmd
ren "%LOCALAPPDATA%\Microsoft\Outlook\*.ost" *.ost.old
```

### Step 3: Reset corrupted views and navigation pane

Corrupted calendar views cause missing or misrendered items. Close Outlook, then run each switch (Start > Run, or the search box):

```cmd
outlook.exe /cleanviews
outlook.exe /resetnavpane
```

Note: after `/resetnavpane` you must re-add any previously opened shared calendars.

### Step 4: Fix stuck reminders

If reminders can't be dismissed or keep reappearing, close Outlook and run:

```cmd
outlook.exe /cleanreminders
```

### Step 5: Repair a server-side corrupt item (admin)

If the item is wrong in OWA, pull the calendar diagnostic logs from Exchange Online PowerShell to identify the bad item. In cloud mailboxes use `Get-CalendarDiagnosticObjects` (the on-premises `Get-CalendarDiagnosticLog` does **not** work against Exchange Online):

```powershell
Connect-ExchangeOnline
Get-CalendarDiagnosticObjects -Identity "user@contoso.com" -Subject "Weekly Sync" |
    Export-Csv "C:\Temp\caldiag.csv" -NoTypeInformation
```

The `CleanGlobalObjectID` column identifies the meeting. Have the organizer cancel and re-create the offending meeting to regenerate clean properties; attendees should ask the organizer to do so.

## Troubleshooting

- **Meetings still missing after cache rebuild:** run the Outlook Calendar diagnostic (SaRA-based CalCheck) to scan for corrupt items. Download from `https://aka.ms/sara-calcheck`, run `SetupProd_CalCheck.exe`; the scan starts automatically. On the classic standalone tool the equivalent is `calcheck -f -r` (moves flagged items to a CalCheck folder and mails a report). CalCheck only works with Exchange accounts, not IMAP/POP.
- **Free/busy or delegate data wrong:** the `/cleanfreebusy` switch was removed in Outlook 2016+ — use `outlook.exe /cleanroamedprefs`, or reset delegates server-side:

  ```powershell
  Remove-MailboxFolderPermission -Identity "user@contoso.com:\Calendar" -ResetDelegateUserCollection
  Add-MailboxFolderPermission -Identity "user@contoso.com:\Calendar" -User "delegate@contoso.com" -SharingPermissionFlag Delegate
  ```

- **Mobile calendar out of sync:** the ActiveSync partnership is likely corrupt. Remove the device relationship from the phone and from the mailbox, restart the device, then re-add the account.
- **Wrong time zone for one attendee only:** the attendee's stored work-hours/time-zone item is corrupt — escalate for an MFCMAPI reset of the `IPM.FlexibleWorkingHours` items.

## Prevention

- Keep classic Outlook and Windows fully patched; many calendar sync bugs are fixed in Click-to-Run updates.
- Discourage third-party calendar/meeting add-ins, which frequently corrupt items on write.
- Have organizers manage recurring series from a single client, and keep recurring series under ~1,300 occurrences (Outlook's hard limit).
- Prefer OWA or new Outlook as the source of truth when reconciling discrepancies.

Title: EML-068: Automatic Replies (Out-of-Office) Not Working
Content:
# Automatic Replies (Out-of-Office) Not Working

**Category:** Email > Automatic Replies
**Article Code:** EML-068
**Tier:** 1
**Audience:** Administrators / Technicians
**Estimated Resolution Time:** 15–30 minutes

## Symptoms / When to Use
- A user enabled Automatic Replies in Outlook or Outlook on the web, but senders never receive them.
- Internal (same-tenant) replies work, but **external** senders get nothing.
- Replies stopped after a scheduled window, or fire outside the intended dates.
- A shared or resource mailbox does not send Automatic Replies.
- Message trace shows a `Drop` event or no reply message is generated at all.

## Background
Microsoft 365 sends one Automatic Reply (OOF) per sender per enabled period — not one per message. Two independent layers must agree for a reply to leave the tenant:

1. **Mailbox layer** — the per-mailbox `AutoReplyState`, message text, audience, and start/end times set by the user or an admin.
2. **Remote domain layer** — tenant-wide policy (`AllowedOOFType`, `AutoReplyEnabled`) that can silently suppress replies to external domains. Remote domain settings **override** the mailbox setting, so a mailbox can be correctly configured yet still send nothing externally.

External-reply failures are almost always the remote domain layer. Internal-only failures are usually the mailbox layer or a Scheduled window that has expired. Note that if an inbound message is classified as spam and routed to Junk, no OOF is generated by design.

## Resolution

### Step 1: Connect to Exchange Online PowerShell
```powershell
Connect-ExchangeOnline -UserPrincipalName admin@yourtenant.com
```

### Step 2: Verify the mailbox configuration
Confirm the state, audience, and schedule. `AutoReplyState` must be `Enabled` or `Scheduled`; if `Scheduled`, the current time must fall between `StartTime` and `EndTime`.
```powershell
Get-MailboxAutoReplyConfiguration -Identity user@yourtenant.com |
    Format-List AutoReplyState,ExternalAudience,StartTime,EndTime,InternalMessage,ExternalMessage
```
- `ExternalAudience: None` means external senders get **no** reply. Set to `Known` (contacts only) or `All`.
- If `AutoReplyState` is `Disabled`, the feature is off.

### Step 3: Set or correct the mailbox configuration
Enable replies with both audiences (admin action on behalf of the user):
```powershell
Set-MailboxAutoReplyConfiguration -Identity user@yourtenant.com `
    -AutoReplyState Enabled `
    -ExternalAudience All `
    -InternalMessage "I am out of office and will reply on my return." `
    -ExternalMessage "Thank you for your email. I am currently out of office."
```
For a scheduled window, use `-AutoReplyState Scheduled` with `-StartTime` and `-EndTime`:
```powershell
Set-MailboxAutoReplyConfiguration -Identity user@yourtenant.com `
    -AutoReplyState Scheduled `
    -StartTime "2026-07-10 08:00:00" -EndTime "2026-07-17 17:00:00"
```

### Step 4: Check the remote domain policy (external replies)
```powershell
Get-RemoteDomain | Format-Table -AutoSize Name,DomainName,AllowedOOFType,AutoReplyEnabled
```
`AllowedOOFType` valid values are `External`, `ExternalLegacy`, `InternalLegacy`, and `None`. If the matching domain (or the `Default` `*` domain) shows `None`, external OOF replies are blocked.

### Step 5: Fix the remote domain policy
Allow external Automatic Replies on the default remote domain:
```powershell
Set-RemoteDomain -Identity Default -AllowedOOFType External -AutoReplyEnabled $true
```
A more specific remote domain entry overrides `Default`. If a per-domain entry (e.g. `contoso.com`) exists, apply the change to that entry instead:
```powershell
Set-RemoteDomain -Identity Contoso -AllowedOOFType External -AutoReplyEnabled $true
```

### Step 6: Test
From an external mailbox, send a message to the user. Confirm a single reply is received. Re-testing from the same sender within the enabled period will **not** produce a second reply — use a different sender or disable and re-enable to reset.

## Troubleshooting
- **No reply at all, internal or external:** Confirm the mailbox has an Exchange Online license and the message was not delivered to Junk. Spam-filtered mail never triggers OOF.
- **Portal alternative:** Set replies via **EAC > Recipients > Mailboxes >** *mailbox* **> Others > Manage automatic replies**, or **Microsoft 365 admin center > Users > Active users >** *user* **> Mail > Automatic replies**. Remote domains live under **EAC > Mail flow > Remote domains**.
- **Reply sent only once:** Expected behavior. OOF fires once per sender per enabled session, not per message.
- **`Drop` event in message trace** (`RESOLVER.OOF.IntToExt` / `ExtToInt`): Normal. Exchange generates both internal and external replies and drops the one that does not apply to the recipient.
- **Hybrid tenants:** For on-premises mailboxes, internal OOF requires `AllowedOOFType InternalLegacy`. `External` alone sends external replies only.
- **Shared mailbox:** Set Automatic Replies with `Set-MailboxAutoReplyConfiguration` against the shared mailbox identity; users cannot always set these from Outlook.
- **Transport rule interference:** Check **Mail flow > Rules** for rules that redirect, block, or delete auto-generated mail.

## Prevention
- Standardize the `Default` remote domain on `AllowedOOFType External` and `AutoReplyEnabled $true` unless a security policy requires suppression.
- Document any per-domain remote domain overrides — they silently supersede the default.
- For planned leave, prefer `-AutoReplyState Scheduled` with explicit start/end times so replies self-disable.
- Include both `-InternalMessage` and `-ExternalMessage` so no audience is left blank.

Title: EML-069: Mail Forwarding Rules Not Working or Blocked
Content:
# Mail Forwarding Rules Not Working or Blocked

**Category:** Email > Mail Flow
**Article Code:** EML-069
**Tier:** 2
**Audience:** Administrators / Technicians (with end-user verification steps)
**Estimated Resolution Time:** 20–45 minutes

## Symptoms / When to Use

- A user reports that mail is no longer arriving at an external address they previously forwarded to.
- An Inbox rule that forwards or redirects messages silently does nothing, even though it appears enabled.
- Senders receive a non-delivery report (NDR) containing `5.7.520 Access denied, Your organization does not allow external forwarding`.
- Admin-configured mailbox (SMTP) forwarding to an internal recipient works, but forwarding to an external domain fails.
- Forwarding worked historically and stopped after a tenant security hardening change or Microsoft secure-by-default rollout.
- A "keep a copy" expectation is not met — mail is forwarded but not retained in the source mailbox (or vice versa).
- Out-of-office / automatic replies stop firing on a mailbox that also forwards mail.

## Background

Microsoft 365 supports several independent forwarding mechanisms, and each is governed by different controls. Diagnosing a broken rule means identifying which mechanism is in play and which control is blocking it.

**Forwarding mechanisms:**

1. **Mailbox forwarding (SMTP forwarding)** — admin-configured on the mailbox via `ForwardingAddress` (internal recipient object) or `ForwardingSmtpAddress` (any SMTP address). `DeliverToMailboxAndForward` controls whether a copy is retained.
2. **Inbox rules** — user-configured client-side rules that forward or redirect messages. Subject to a limit of 10 individual recipients per rule.
3. **Mail flow rules (transport rules)** — org-level rules that can redirect or block messages.

**Controls that block forwarding:**

- **Outbound spam filter policy.** The `AutoForwardingMode` setting controls automatic external forwarding tenant-wide. Its three values are `Automatic`, `On`, and `Off`. Critically, `Automatic` (System-controlled) — the default — now behaves the same as `Off` for all tenants due to Microsoft's secure-by-default changes. This is the single most common reason external forwarding silently breaks. Disabling automatic forwarding disables both Inbox-rule forwarding and mailbox forwarding to external addresses. Internal forwarding is unaffected.
- **Remote domains.** The `AutoForwardEnabled` property on a remote domain allows or blocks auto-forwarding to that domain. When any control blocks forwarding, the block wins.
- **DeliverToMailboxAndForward interaction with Inbox rules.** If mailbox forwarding is set and `DeliverToMailboxAndForward` is `$true`, Inbox rules that redirect messages will not run. This is by design.
- **Restricted entities.** A compromised or over-limit account placed on the Restricted entities list cannot send, which also stops its forwarding.

## Resolution

### Step 1: Connect to Exchange Online PowerShell

```powershell
Import-Module ExchangeOnlineManagement
Connect-ExchangeOnline -UserPrincipalName admin@contoso.com
```

### Step 2: Inspect mailbox-level forwarding

Check whether admin-configured forwarding is set and how copies are handled.

```powershell
Get-Mailbox -Identity user@contoso.com | Format-List ForwardingAddress,ForwardingSmtpAddress,DeliverToMailboxAndForward
```

- `ForwardingAddress` populated = forwarding to an internal recipient object.
- `ForwardingSmtpAddress` populated = forwarding to a raw SMTP address (often external).
- `DeliverToMailboxAndForward $true` = copy retained in mailbox; `$false` = delivered only to the forwarding target.

### Step 3: Set or correct mailbox forwarding

To forward to an internal recipient and keep a copy:

```powershell
Set-Mailbox -Identity user@contoso.com -DeliverToMailboxAndForward $true -ForwardingAddress coworker@contoso.com
```

To forward to an external SMTP address and keep a copy:

```powershell
Set-Mailbox -Identity user@contoso.com -DeliverToMailboxAndForward $true -ForwardingSmtpAddress "external@partner.com"
```

To remove forwarding entirely:

```powershell
Set-Mailbox -Identity user@contoso.com -ForwardingAddress $null -ForwardingSmtpAddress $null
```

### Step 4: Verify the outbound spam policy is not blocking external forwarding

This is the most common cause of blocked external forwarding.

```powershell
Get-HostedOutboundSpamFilterPolicy | Format-List Name,AutoForwardingMode
```

If `AutoForwardingMode` is `Automatic` or `Off`, external forwarding is blocked. To explicitly allow external forwarding for a targeted policy, set it to `On`:

```powershell
Set-HostedOutboundSpamFilterPolicy -Identity "Default" -AutoForwardingMode On
```

Best practice is **not** to enable this on the default policy for all users. Instead, create a scoped custom policy for only the users who require external forwarding:

```powershell
New-HostedOutboundSpamFilterPolicy -Name "Allow-Ext-Forwarding" -AutoForwardingMode On
New-HostedOutboundSpamFilterRule -Name "Allow-Ext-Forwarding" -HostedOutboundSpamFilterPolicy "Allow-Ext-Forwarding" -From user@contoso.com
```

Portal path: **Microsoft Defender portal** (security.microsoft.com) > **Email & collaboration** > **Policies & rules** > **Threat policies** > **Anti-spam** > select the outbound policy > **Edit protection settings** > **Automatic forwarding rules**.

### Step 5: Verify remote domain settings

Even with the spam policy set to `On`, a remote domain with auto-forward disabled blocks delivery to that domain.

```powershell
Get-RemoteDomain | Format-List Name,DomainName,AutoForwardEnabled
```

To allow auto-forwarding to a specific domain:

```powershell
Set-RemoteDomain -Identity "Contoso Partner" -AutoForwardEnabled $true
```

### Step 6: Confirm the change and test

Re-run the mailbox and policy checks, then send a test message from an external mailbox to the source mailbox and confirm delivery to the target. Allow a few minutes for policy propagation.

## Troubleshooting

**Inbox rule forwards nothing, but the rule looks enabled.**
Mailbox-level forwarding suppresses redirecting Inbox rules. Check for the combination and disable the mailbox forwarding if the Inbox rule should own the behavior:

```powershell
Get-Mailbox user@contoso.com | Format-List ForwardingAddress,ForwardingSmtpAddress,DeliverToMailboxAndForward
Set-Mailbox user@contoso.com -DeliverToMailboxAndForward $false
```

To enumerate a user's Inbox rules and see forwarding targets:

```powershell
Get-InboxRule -Mailbox user@contoso.com | Format-List Name,Enabled,ForwardTo,RedirectTo,ForwardAsAttachmentTo
```

**Rule targets more than 10 recipients.**
Inbox rule forward/redirect actions are limited to 10 individual recipients. Consolidate recipients into a distribution group or Microsoft 365 group and target the group instead of listing addresses individually.

**Sender receives NDR `5.7.520`.**
This confirms the outbound spam policy is blocking external forwarding. Resolve via Step 4. NDRs are generated for external senders on all forwarding methods; for internal senders, an NDR is generated only when the method is mailbox forwarding (not Inbox rules).

**Forwarding suddenly stopped with no config change.**
This is typically the secure-by-default shift of `Automatic - System-controlled` to behave as `Off`. Set a scoped policy to `On` per Step 4.

**Automatic replies (OOF) stopped working on a forwarding mailbox.**
When forwarding is configured, set `DeliverToMailboxAndForward $true` so the message still lands in the mailbox and the automatic reply can generate:

```powershell
Set-Mailbox -Identity user@contoso.com -DeliverToMailboxAndForward $true
```

**Account cannot send at all.**
Check whether the mailbox is on the Restricted entities list (security.microsoft.com/restrictedusers). A compromised or over-limit account is blocked from sending, which also halts forwarding. Investigate sign-in logs and unexpected Inbox/forwarding rules before releasing it.

**Hybrid / migrated mailbox lost its forwarding.**
Forwarding configuration (`DeliverToMailboxAndForward`, `ForwardingAddress`, `ForwardingSmtpAddress`) is not copied to Exchange Online during migration. Re-apply it post-migration per Step 3.

**Identify who is currently auto-forwarding externally.**
Use the **Auto forwarded messages report** in the Exchange admin center (**Reports** > **Mail flow**) to find cloud mailboxes forwarding to external recipients.

## Prevention

- Keep the **default** outbound spam policy at `Automatic` or `Off` and grant external forwarding only through **scoped custom policies** for the specific users who need it.
- Prefer admin-configured mailbox forwarding (`Set-Mailbox`) over user Inbox rules for business-required forwarding — it is auditable and survives client changes but is not copied during migrations, so document it.
- Set `DeliverToMailboxAndForward $true` whenever a copy must be retained for compliance or continuity, and to preserve automatic replies.
- Review the Auto forwarded messages report periodically; unexpected external forwarding is a leading indicator of account compromise.
- Enforce MFA to reduce the compromise-driven forwarding rules that trigger restrictions.
- When forwarding to a partner domain, confirm both the outbound spam policy (`AutoForwardingMode On`) and the remote domain (`AutoForwardEnabled $true`) permit it — the more restrictive control always wins.
- Document each forwarding exception (user, target, business justification, expiry) so exceptions can be reviewed and revoked.

**Tags:** email-forwarding, mailbox-forwarding, smtp-forwarding, inbox-rules, outbound-spam-policy, autoforwardingmode, remote-domain, exchange-online, 5.7.520, mail-flow, deliver-to-mailbox-and-forward

Title: EML-070: Outlook on the Web (OWA) Slow Performance
Content:
# Outlook on the Web (OWA) Slow Performance

**Category:** Email > OWA
**Article Code:** EML-070
**Tier:** 1
**Audience:** Technicians / Administrators
**Estimated Resolution Time:** 15–30 minutes

Quick-fix guide for a user reporting that Outlook on the web (outlook.office.com) is slow to load, lags when switching folders, or hangs on send/receive. Work top-down: browser first, then account/policy, then network.

## Symptoms / When to Use

- OWA takes 10+ seconds to load the mailbox or is slow switching between Mail, Calendar, and People.
- Messages are slow to open, the reading pane spins, or search stalls.
- OWA loads in the **light version** with a reduced feature set (a symptom of a rendering/browser fallback, not a network issue).
- Slowness is isolated to the browser — the Outlook desktop or mobile app for the same mailbox is responsive.
- One user or one device is affected while other users on the same tenant are fine.

## Background

OWA is a single-page web app that keeps multiple long-lived HTTPS connections open to `outlook.office365.com`. Performance degrades from three common sources: heavy or corrupt browser state (cache, cookies, extensions), account-side load (large connected accounts, misbehaving OWA add-ins), and network conditions such as proxy authentication or idle-connection resets that force the client to rebuild connections. Because the app is browser-hosted, most Tier-1 fixes are client-side and do not require tenant changes.

## Resolution

### Step 1: Confirm scope and service health

Rule out a tenant-wide incident before touching the client. In the Microsoft 365 admin center go to **Health > Service health** and check **Exchange Online** for active advisories. If a service incident is posted, follow the advisory instead of local troubleshooting.

### Step 2: Test in a private/incognito window

Have the user open a private window (extensions disabled, fresh cache) and sign in to `https://outlook.office.com`.

- If OWA is fast in private mode, the cause is browser cache or an extension — continue to Step 3.
- If it is still slow, skip to Step 5 (account/network).

### Step 3: Clear cache and disable extensions

In the affected browser, clear cached images/files and cookies for the last 24 hours, then disable extensions (ad blockers, privacy, and security add-ins are frequent culprits) and reload OWA. Confirm the browser is a current, supported version. On Windows, a full cache clear can also be triggered from Run:

```cmd
inetcpl.cpl
```

Use the **Delete** button under Browsing history for Edge/IE-based stacks. Re-enable extensions one at a time to identify the offender.

### Step 4: Exit the light version (if applicable)

If OWA is stuck in the light version on a supported browser, the user likely enabled the low-vision/light experience. In OWA select **Settings (gear) > General > Accessibility** (or in the light version, **Options > Outlook Web App version**) and clear **Use the light version of Outlook Web App / blind and low vision experience**, then **Save** and sign out and back in.

### Step 5: Reduce account-side load

Slowness that follows the user across devices points at the mailbox/account:

- Remove unused **connected accounts** in **Settings > Accounts**.
- Disable third-party **OWA add-ins** in **Settings > Mail > Customize actions / Add-ins** — a slow add-in stalls message rendering.

Admins can review and disable org-deployed add-ins for a mailbox from Exchange Online PowerShell. Connect first:

```powershell
Connect-ExchangeOnline -UserPrincipalName admin@contoso.com
```

```powershell
Get-App -Mailbox user@contoso.com | Format-Table DisplayName, Enabled
```

### Step 6: Check the OWA mailbox policy

If OWA behavior differs from expected across a group of users, inspect the applied policy for disabled features that force fallback rendering:

```powershell
Get-OwaMailboxPolicy | Format-Table Name, IsDefault
```

Do not change policy for a single-user performance complaint — policy edits are tenant/group scope and can take up to 60 minutes to apply.

## Troubleshooting

- **Fast in incognito, slow normally, cache clear did not help:** create a fresh browser profile or reset the browser. A corrupt profile behaves like a permanent cache problem.
- **Slow only when switching Calendar ↔ Mail, or intermittent hangs on load:** suspect the network path. Proxy authentication on every new TCP connection and firewall/proxy idle-timeouts (often 100–300s) that reset OWA's long-lived connections both produce exactly this pattern. Escalate to the network team with Microsoft 365 URLs and IP ranges allowlisted for direct egress.
- **All users on one site are slow:** measure latency to the service and rule out local WAN/DNS:

```cmd
ping outlook.office365.com
```

- **Desktop Outlook also slow for the same mailbox:** the issue is not OWA-specific — reclassify as a mailbox or network problem.

## Prevention

- Keep browsers on a supported, auto-updating version; avoid heavyweight privacy/security extensions on the OWA origin.
- Allowlist Microsoft 365 URLs and IPs for direct egress and exempt Exchange Online endpoints from proxy authentication and idle-session teardown.
- Limit connected accounts and vet OWA add-ins before org-wide deployment.
- Educate users that the light-version toggle reduces features and is not a fix for slowness.

**Tags:** OWA, Outlook on the web, Exchange Online, performance, slow, browser cache, add-ins, light version, mailbox policy, proxy

Title: EML-073: Outlook Add-ins Missing or Not Loading
Content:
# Outlook Add-ins Missing or Not Loading

**Category:** Email > Add-ins
**Article Code:** EML-073
**Tier:** 2
**Audience:** Administrators / Technicians
**Estimated Resolution Time:** 20–45 minutes (add 24–72 hours for centralized deployment propagation)

Outlook add-ins that vanish from the ribbon, fail to load, or never appear after deployment usually trace back to one of four layers: centralized deployment state, per-mailbox availability, Office resiliency (auto-disable), or client-side privacy/policy settings. This article covers diagnosis across all four, plus the admin and end-user angles.

## Symptoms / When to Use

- A deployed add-in does not appear on the Outlook ribbon or in **Home > Get Add-ins > Admin-managed** for one or more users.
- An add-in that previously worked has disappeared after an Office update or crash.
- Outlook shows a notification: *"Outlook detected an add-in problem"* or *"An add-in was disabled."*
- The add-in appears in **File > Options > Add-ins** but its check box is cleared or it is listed under **Disabled Application Add-ins**.
- Add-ins are missing only in new Outlook / Outlook on the web, or only in classic Outlook, but not both.
- Users report the **Get Add-ins** / Store button is greyed out or absent.
- A freshly deployed add-in is not visible even after restarting Outlook (within the propagation window).

## Background

Modern Outlook add-ins (web add-ins, manifest-based) are managed centrally through the **Integrated apps** portal in the Microsoft 365 admin center and delivered per user/group. Legacy **COM/VSTO add-ins** are installed on the local machine and controlled by registry `LoadBehavior` values and Office's resiliency subsystem.

Four independent gates must all pass for an add-in to load:

1. **Deployment / assignment** — the add-in must be deployed and assigned to the user or a group they belong to.
2. **Per-mailbox availability** — Exchange Online must have the app enabled for that mailbox.
3. **Resiliency** — Office (2013+) auto-disables add-ins that load slowly, crash, or slow shutdown. It logs Event ID 45 (load time) and Event ID 59 (disabled for performance) in the Application event log.
4. **Client policy / privacy** — turning off **Optional connected experiences** or blocking unmanaged add-ins via Group Policy suppresses add-ins.

Centralized deployment can take up to 24 hours to reach clients and 24–72 hours for the icon to appear on the ribbon. Rule out propagation delay before deeper troubleshooting.

## Resolution

### Step 1: Confirm deployment and assignment in Integrated apps

1. Sign in to the [Microsoft 365 admin center](https://admin.microsoft.com) as a Global or Exchange Administrator.
2. Go to **Settings > Integrated apps**.
3. Locate the add-in. Confirm its **Status** is **Enabled** (not **Not assigned** or **Removed**), and that the affected user is in the assignment scope (**Everyone**, or a specific user/group).
4. If it was deployed through the legacy path, select the **Add-ins** link near the top of the **Integrated apps** page and verify the same there.

Add-in states in the admin center: **Enabled** (assigned, usable), **Not assigned** (deployed but no users can see it), **Removed** (nobody can access it). If the user is not in scope, edit the deployment to add them or their group.

### Step 2: Verify per-mailbox availability with Exchange Online PowerShell

Connect to Exchange Online, then confirm the app is present and enabled for the organization.

```powershell
Connect-ExchangeOnline -UserPrincipalName admin@contoso.com
```

List organization apps with their state:

```powershell
Get-App -OrganizationApp | Format-List DisplayName,AppId,Enabled,DefaultStateForUser
```

To inspect what a specific mailbox can see:

```powershell
Get-App -Mailbox user@contoso.com | Format-List DisplayName,AppId,Enabled
```

`Enabled $false` means the add-in is disabled and hidden for the org. `DefaultStateForUser` controls the per-user default (`Enabled`, `Disabled`, or `AlwaysEnabled`).

### Step 3: Enable or re-assign the add-in

To make an organization add-in available and enabled by default (replace `<AppId>` with the real GUID):

```powershell
Set-App -Identity <AppId> -OrganizationApp -Enabled $true -DefaultStateForUser Enabled
```

To make it mandatory and prevent users turning it off:

```powershell
Set-App -Identity <AppId> -OrganizationApp -Enabled $true -DefaultStateForUser AlwaysEnabled
```

To enable a specific installed app for one user's mailbox:

```powershell
Enable-App -Identity <AppId> -Mailbox user@contoso.com
```

Verify the change:

```powershell
Get-App -OrganizationApp | Format-List DisplayName,AppId,Enabled,DefaultStateForUser
```

If the add-in is missing entirely (not just disabled) and you have its manifest, re-deploy through **Integrated apps > Upload custom apps** (App type: **Office Add-in**), or in PowerShell:

```powershell
New-App -OrganizationApp -Url "https://<host>/manifest.xml" -DefaultStateForUser Enabled
```

### Step 4: Re-enable a resiliency-disabled add-in (classic Outlook, per user)

If Outlook auto-disabled a slow or crashing COM add-in, have the user re-enable it:

1. In classic Outlook, go to **File**.
2. Select **Slow and Disabled COM Add-ins** (Outlook 2016 and later) or **Slow and Disabled Add-ins** (Outlook 2013).
3. Under the affected add-in, select **Always enable this add-in** (or **Enable this add-in**).
4. Close, then exit and restart Outlook.

To force this at scale via Group Policy / registry, add the add-in's ProgID to the exemption list so Office cannot auto-disable it. The `x.0` node is `16.0` for Microsoft 365 / Office 2016–2024, `15.0` for Office 2013:

```cmd
reg add "HKCU\Software\Microsoft\Office\16.0\Outlook\Resiliency\DoNotDisableAddinList" /v "Contoso.AddIn" /t REG_DWORD /d 1 /f
```

The DWORD value (1–A) records the original disable reason; `1` is sufficient to exempt the add-in.

### Step 5: Verify COM add-in LoadBehavior (classic Outlook)

For COM/VSTO add-ins that never appear, confirm the load setting. The ProgID is a subkey under the `Addins` key (HKLM applies machine-wide, HKCU per-user):

```cmd
reg query "HKLM\Software\Microsoft\Office\Outlook\Addins\Contoso.AddIn" /v LoadBehavior
```

Set it to load at startup:

```cmd
reg add "HKLM\Software\Microsoft\Office\Outlook\Addins\Contoso.AddIn" /v LoadBehavior /t REG_DWORD /d 3 /f
```

`LoadBehavior` values: **3** = connected, loads at startup; **9** = demand/on-startup load; **2** = not loaded (may never load); **0** = disabled. For 64-bit Windows with a 32-bit add-in, also check the `WOW6432Node` path.

## Troubleshooting

**Add-in appears in some clients but not others.** Add-in availability differs by client when **Optional connected experiences** is turned off. Admin-deployed (centrally deployed) add-ins remain usable in Outlook on the web and new Outlook; on classic Windows all add-ins stay visible but the Store is blocked; on Mac add-ins disappear from the ribbon entirely; on iOS/Android only admin-deployed add-ins show. Check **File > Account > Account Privacy > Manage Settings** on the client, or the tenant policy *Allow the use of additional optional connected experiences in Office*.

**"Get Add-ins" / Store button is missing.** This is expected when optional connected experiences are disabled — admin-deployed add-ins still work, but users cannot browse the store. If the store is required, enable optional connected experiences via Cloud Policy or Group Policy.

**Add-in silently blocked by policy.** If a Group Policy managed list is in effect, users cannot override it. Check `HKCU\Software\Microsoft\Office\16.0\Outlook\Resiliency\AddinList` — string values are ProgIDs with `0` = blocked, `1` = always enabled, `2` = user-configurable. Also check whether **Block all unmanaged add-ins** is enabled, which suppresses any add-in not on the managed list. ProgIDs and registry key names are case-sensitive.

**Deployed add-in still missing after 24 hours.** Confirm the user has an Exchange Online mailbox and a valid license, the mailbox is not on a legacy/blocked plan, and the user holds the **My Custom Apps** role if self-install is expected. Have the user fully quit and relaunch Outlook; web add-ins can take 24–72 hours to surface on the ribbon.

**Add-in loads but crashes or is repeatedly re-disabled.** Review Application event log for Event ID 59 and the disable reason. A crashing or unloadable add-in cannot be kept enabled by policy — the vendor must ship a fix. Confirm the add-in version is current and the manifest source URL is reachable from the client network.

**Manifest / unified-manifest mismatch.** Add-ins using the unified (JSON) Microsoft 365 manifest must be deployed via the Integrated apps portal, not the legacy Add-ins page, and require supported Office builds. Verify the client channel and build meet the add-in's minimum.

## Prevention

- Deploy through the **Integrated apps** portal (centralized deployment) rather than per-mailbox sideloading, so assignments survive reinstalls and follow group membership.
- Use a phased rollout: pilot to IT and a small group, validate, then expand to all users.
- Document each add-in's `AppId` / GUID and ProgID in your tenant runbook for fast lookups.
- Keep add-ins on their latest versions; slow or crashing add-ins get auto-disabled by resiliency.
- Standardize the **Optional connected experiences** privacy policy tenant-wide so add-in visibility is predictable across clients and platforms.
- For business-critical add-ins, set `DefaultStateForUser AlwaysEnabled` or add the ProgID to `DoNotDisableAddinList` / the managed `AddinList` so users and resiliency cannot silently disable them.
- Communicate the 24–72 hour propagation window to end users so new deployments are not reported as failures prematurely.

Title: INT-003: Intune Device Not Compliant — Diagnosing Compliance Policy Failures
Content:
# Intune Device Not Compliant — Diagnosing Compliance Policy Failures

**Category:** Intune > Compliance
**Article Code:** INT-003
**Tier:** 2
**Audience:** Administrators
**Estimated Resolution Time:** 20–45 minutes

## Symptoms / When to Use

Use this article when a device shows **Not compliant** in Intune / Entra and the user is blocked from resources:

- User is denied access to M365 apps by Conditional Access citing device compliance.
- Company Portal shows "Device not compliant" with one or more failed checks.
- Intune admin center → Devices shows Compliance = **Not compliant** or **In grace period**.
- Newly enrolled devices never reach Compliant status.

## Background

An Intune **compliance policy** defines rules a device must meet (encryption, OS version, password, Defender/health attestation, etc.). Compliance state feeds **Conditional Access**, which gates access to corporate resources. A device becomes non-compliant when it fails a rule, hasn't checked in recently, or has no policy assigned (the tenant's "mark devices with no compliance policy" setting then decides the default). Because compliance evaluation is periodic, state can lag reality — a fixed device may still show non-compliant until its next sync.

## Resolution

### Step 1: Find the specific failing rule

In Intune admin center → **Devices** → select the device → **Device compliance**. Each policy lists which setting failed (e.g., "Encryption of data storage: Not compliant"). This is the single most important step — fix the actual failing check, not a guess.

You can also pull it via Graph:
```powershell
Connect-MgGraph -Scopes "DeviceManagementManagedDevices.Read.All"
Get-MgDeviceManagementManagedDevice -Filter "deviceName eq 'LAPTOP-01'" |
  Select DeviceName, ComplianceState, OperatingSystem, OsVersion, LastSyncDateTime
```

### Step 2: Remediate common failures

- **Encryption (BitLocker/FileVault):** enable device encryption. Windows: confirm `Get-BitLockerVolume` shows the OS drive protected; if a policy requires it, ensure TPM is present/enabled.
- **OS version below minimum:** run Windows/macOS updates to meet the policy's minimum build.
- **Password/PIN:** set a compliant screen-lock passcode meeting length/complexity.
- **Defender / threat level:** resolve outstanding threats; ensure Defender is running and signatures current. For "Require the device to be at or under machine risk score," clear the risk in Defender for Endpoint.
- **No compliance policy assigned:** ensure the device's user/group is targeted by a policy.

### Step 3: Force a sync (don't wait for the schedule)

After remediation, push a check-in:
- **Company Portal** app → Settings → **Sync**, or
- Intune admin center → device → **Sync**, or on Windows: Settings → Accounts → Access work or school → Info → **Sync**.

Graph:
```powershell
$id = (Get-MgDeviceManagementManagedDevice -Filter "deviceName eq 'LAPTOP-01'").Id
Sync-MgDeviceManagementManagedDevice -ManagedDeviceId $id
```

### Step 4: Handle grace period and Conditional Access

- If the device is **In grace period**, the user may still have access until the deadline — remediate before it expires.
- Confirm the blocking **Conditional Access** policy requires "compliant device" and that the now-compliant state has propagated (can take 5–15 min after sync).

### Step 5: Verify

Re-check the device's Compliance state = **Compliant** and confirm the user can access the previously blocked resource.

## Troubleshooting

- **Compliant in Intune but still blocked:** the compliance signal hasn't reached Entra/CA yet; wait and re-sync, or have the user sign out and back in.
- **Stuck "In grace period" after fix:** force a sync; grace state clears on next successful evaluation.
- **Conflicting policies:** two compliance policies with different settings — the most restrictive wins; reconcile them.
- **Enrollment/attestation errors:** for Windows health attestation, ensure Secure Boot/TPM 2.0 and internet access to the attestation service.

## Prevention

- Set the tenant default to **mark devices with no compliance policy as Not compliant** only after policies are broadly assigned.
- Use a reasonable **grace period** (e.g., 1–3 days) so users self-remediate without an instant lockout.
- Stage policy changes to a pilot group before tenant-wide rollout.
- Monitor the compliance report weekly and alert on spikes in non-compliance.

Title: INT-004: Intune MDM Device Enrollment Failures
Content:
# Intune MDM Device Enrollment Failures

**Category:** Intune > Enrollment
**Article Code:** INT-004
**Tier:** 2
**Audience:** Administrators / Technicians
**Estimated Resolution Time:** 20–60 minutes (longer if a directory sync or licensing change is required)

## Symptoms / When to Use

Use this article when a device fails to enroll into Microsoft Intune MDM, or auto-enrollment silently never completes. Common signals:

- End user sees **"Company Portal Temporarily Unavailable"**, **"Something went wrong"**, or **"You have added the maximum number of devices allowed by your IT support."**
- Error codes surfaced during Windows enrollment: **0x80180014** (org doesn't support this Windows version), **0x8018002b** (auto MDM enroll failed), **80180026**, or **0x80180023**.
- **"Looks like your IT admin hasn't set an MDM authority"** or **"MDM authority not defined."**
- Windows hybrid-joined devices never appear in Intune despite Group Policy auto-enrollment being configured.
- In Task Scheduler under **Microsoft > Windows > EnterpriseMgmt**, the *Schedule created by enrollment client for automatically enrolling in MDM from Microsoft Entra ID* task reports a failed last run result.
- Event ID **76** ("Auto MDM Enroll: Failed") logged under **DeviceManagement-Enterprise-Diagnostics-Provider/Admin**.

## Background

During enrollment, Intune installs an MDM certificate on the device that the Intune service uses to push compliance and configuration policy. Enrollment can fail at several distinct layers, and correct triage depends on identifying the layer:

1. **Tenant configuration** — MDM authority not set, Windows (MDM) platform blocked by enrollment restrictions, or a broken MDM Terms of Use URL.
2. **Identity / scope** — the user is out of **MDM user scope**, the UPN uses a non-routable domain (e.g. `.local`), or the WIP/MAM user scope is winning over MDM on a BYOD device.
3. **Licensing** — the user lacks an Intune (or qualifying Microsoft 365) license.
4. **Device state** — the device isn't correctly Microsoft Entra joined / hybrid joined, the device cap is reached, or a stale device record blocks re-enrollment.

For Windows, auto-enrollment via Group Policy is valid **only** for Microsoft Entra hybrid joined devices — the device must be joined to both on-premises AD and Microsoft Entra ID. Work these layers top-down before touching the client.

## Resolution

### Step 1: Confirm licensing and MDM authority

Verify the user has a valid Intune license in the Microsoft 365 admin center, then confirm the MDM authority is set. In the Microsoft Intune admin center (**intune.microsoft.com**), go to **Tenant administration** and confirm the **MDM authority** is **Microsoft Intune**. If it reads "MDM authority not defined," set it before proceeding — no device can enroll until this is defined.

### Step 2: Verify enrollment restrictions allow the platform

A blocked platform produces error **0x80180014** ("Your organization does not support this version of Windows"). In the Intune admin center:

1. Go to **Devices > Enrollment restrictions** and open the relevant **Device platform restriction** (or the **Default**).
2. Open **Properties > Edit** next to **Platform settings**.
3. Set **Windows (MDM)** (or the target platform) to **Allow**, then **Review + Save**.

If the platform already shows **Allow** but enrollment still fails, toggle it to **Block**, save, then back to **Allow** and save again to reset the setting. Wait ~15 minutes before retrying.

### Step 3: Confirm the user is in MDM user scope

Auto-enrollment failures with code **0x8018002b** and Event ID **76** usually mean **MDM user scope** is set to **None**, or the WIP/MAM scope is taking precedence on a BYOD device.

1. Sign in to the [Azure portal](https://portal.azure.com/) and select **Microsoft Entra ID**.
2. Select **Mobility (MDM and MAM) > Microsoft Intune**.
3. Set **MDM user scope** to **All**, or to **Some** and add the group that should auto-enroll.
4. Set **WIP/MAM user scope** to **None** (on a corporate-owned device MDM scope wins, but on BYOD the MAM scope wins — leave it None to force MDM enrollment).
5. Select **Save**.

### Step 4: Fix non-routable UPN suffixes (hybrid environments)

Event 76 / `0x8018002b` also occurs when the UPN uses an unverified or non-routable suffix such as `contoso.local`. Correct the suffix on-premises, then force a delta sync from the Microsoft Entra Connect server:

```powershell
Import-Module ADSync
Start-ADSyncSyncCycle -PolicyType Delta
```

Change the affected users' UPN suffix to a verified public domain (e.g. `contoso.com`) via **Active Directory Users and Computers** (`dsa.msc`) before running the sync.

### Step 5: Repair or fix the MDM Terms of Use URL

The error "we can't connect to the URL for your organization's MDM terms of use" points to a blank or incorrect Terms of Use URL. In **Microsoft Entra ID > Mobility (MDM and MAM) > Microsoft Intune**, select **Restore default MDM URLs**, confirm the **MDM terms of use URL** is `https://portal.manage.microsoft.com/TermsofUse.aspx`, then **Save**.

### Step 6: Trigger and validate enrollment on the client (Windows)

On a hybrid-joined Windows device, confirm join state first:

```cmd
dsregcmd /status
```

Confirm **AzureAdJoined** and **DomainJoined** are both **YES** and, under **SSO State**, **AzureAdPrt** is **YES**. If the tenant details show empty MDM URLs, the user isn't in MDM scope — revisit Step 3. Once join state is healthy, trigger the auto-enrollment scheduled task:

```cmd
gpupdate /force
```

## Troubleshooting

**Device cap reached ("DeviceCapReached").** The user has hit the device limit. In the Intune admin center, check **Devices > Enrollment restrictions > Device limit restrictions** for the limit, then **Users > All users >** select the user **> Devices** for the current count. Either remove stale devices or raise the limit under the **Default** device limit restriction (**Properties > Edit >** increase **Device limit**, maximum **15** per user). Removing stale device records is the preferred fix — raising the cap affects all users.

**"Something went wrong… 80180026."** Occurs when the legacy Intune PC software client (Intune PC agent) is still installed alongside modern MDM enrollment. Uninstall the legacy Intune PC agent, then retry.

**Auto MDM Enroll fails with 0x80180023 / `dmwappushservice` missing.** Confirm the `dmwappushservice` service exists via `services.msc`. If absent, export the `HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services\dmwappushservice` key from a healthy device on the same Windows build, merge it on the affected device, restart, remove the old Entra registration, and re-run `gpupdate /force`.

**Enrollment task never runs (error 2149056522 / Event ID 7016).** A leftover enrollment registry key can block the auto-enrollment task after a prior unenrollment. Check **Applications and Services Logs > Microsoft > Windows > Task Scheduler > Operational** for event 7016, then manually remove the stale MDM enrollment key under `HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Enrollments` (the GUID key with the most populated entries) and retry.

**Collect client logs when the cause is unclear.** On Windows, go to **Settings > Accounts > Access work or school**, select **Export your management logs**, and export the MDM diagnostic report. For a fuller report, use the **Info** button and create the advanced diagnostics report. Review the **DeviceManagement-Enterprise-Diagnostics-Provider/Admin** event log for the specific failure HRESULT.

**Company name contains special characters.** If policy creation or enrollment fails tenant-wide, remove special characters from the organization name in the Microsoft 365 admin center and save.

**Apple / Android variations.** For Apple Automated Device Enrollment (ADE), an "Expired or invalid token" or "Access denied" error means the ABM/ASM token must be renewed and Intune must still be listed as the MDM server in Apple Business/School Manager. For Android and iOS, confirm the platform is allowed under **Device platform restriction** and that any device-manufacturer or OS-version min/max limits aren't excluding the device.

## Prevention

- Set **MDM user scope** deliberately (All, or a dedicated enrollment group) and keep **WIP/MAM user scope** at **None** unless you specifically run MAM-only BYOD.
- Ensure every managed user has a routable UPN suffix (a verified public domain) — never `.local`.
- License users for Intune **before** they attempt enrollment; stage licenses via group-based assignment.
- Regularly remove stale and inactive device records so users don't silently hit the device cap. Device limit restrictions only count devices that contacted Intune within the last 90 days, but abandoned records still consume the cap.
- Standardize Windows enrollment on Microsoft Entra hybrid join (for domain-joined fleets) or Autopilot, and validate `dsregcmd /status` as part of build QA.
- Document your enrollment-restriction and device-limit policies, and audit them after any tenant change so a well-meaning edit doesn't block a whole platform.

Title: INT-005: Intune App Protection Policies (MAM) Issues
Content:
# Intune App Protection Policies (MAM) Issues

**Category:** Intune > App Protection
**Article Code:** INT-005
**Tier:** 3
**Audience:** Administrators / Technicians
**Estimated Resolution Time:** 30-90 minutes (plus up to 8 hours for policy propagation on already-signed-in accounts)

App Protection Policies (APP), also called Mobile Application Management (MAM), enforce data-protection controls — PIN, encryption, copy/paste and save-as restrictions, selective wipe — inside managed apps without requiring the device to be enrolled in MDM. Because MAM operates on user identity and app context rather than device state, its failure modes differ from device configuration or compliance issues. This article covers diagnosis and resolution for policies that fail to apply, apply inconsistently, or produce end-user error dialogs.

## Symptoms / When to Use

- A user reports no App PIN prompt, or unrestricted copy/paste/save-as, in Outlook, Teams, Word, Excel, PowerPoint, Edge, or OneDrive when the policy should restrict it.
- End users see dialogs such as **App not set up**, **Account not set up**, **Unable to register the app**, **Sign-in failed**, or **Accessing your organization's data** (wrong account).
- Data-transfer restrictions (open-in, save-as, cut/copy/paste) are not enforced, or are enforced on some apps but not others.
- **App protection status** in the admin center shows a user or app as **Not checked in**.
- A policy change (new PIN requirement, tightened save-as, revised access setting) was made hours ago but users still see the old behavior.
- A newly targeted user receives no policy at all.
- Selective wipe was requested but corporate data still appears in the app.
- On Windows, Edge repeatedly prompts for the work account after the "you're all set" page.

## Background

MAM policy is delivered to apps built with the **Intune App SDK** (or wrapped with the App Wrapping Tool). The app periodically calls the MAM service to retrieve the policy that the admin has targeted to the signed-in work or school account. Several structural facts drive most incidents:

- **Identity, not device.** Policy is evaluated for the work/school account signed into the app. If the user never signed in with the corporate account, or signed in with a personal or wrong corporate account, no policy applies. Only **one** work/school account per device can be MAM-managed at a time.
- **App context.** Multi-identity apps (Outlook, Word/Excel/PowerPoint, OneDrive) enforce policy only in the **work context**. New/unsaved documents and draft emails are treated as personal until saved to a corporate location such as OneDrive for Business, so "policy not applied" on a draft is by design.
- **User targeting only.** APP must be assigned to **user groups**, never device groups.
- **Company Portal dependency (Android).** On Android, much of the MAM enforcement logic lives in the Company Portal app. The device does not need to be enrolled, but the Company Portal app **must** be installed. On iOS/iPadOS it is not required for MAM.
- **Delivery timing.** The SDK checks every ~30 minutes for a **selective wipe** request. Changes to an **existing** policy for users already signed in may take **up to 8 hours** to surface. A newly targeted user can take **up to 24 hours** to appear in reports.
- **App status values.** Reporting shows each app as **Checked in** or **Not checked in**. "Not checked in" means the app has not yet contacted the service under that account.

## Resolution

Work the steps in order. Steps 1-4 are the standard Microsoft investigation flow; Steps 5-6 cover remediation and reporting.

### Step 1: Confirm prerequisites and licensing

MAM requires that the user has an Intune license and is a member of a security group that is targeted by an app protection policy which also targets the specific app in use.

Use the built-in troubleshooting pane to confirm licensing quickly:

1. In the [Microsoft Intune admin center](https://intune.microsoft.com), go to **Troubleshooting + support** > **Troubleshoot**.
2. Select **Select user**, choose the affected user, and confirm **Intune license** shows a green check.
3. If the app is Word, Excel, or PowerPoint, confirm the user also has a **Microsoft 365 Apps for business/enterprise** license and a managed save location (OneDrive) configured.

You can confirm the Intune license assignment with Microsoft Graph PowerShell:

```powershell
Connect-MgGraph -Scopes "User.Read.All"
Get-MgUserLicenseDetail -UserId "user@contoso.com" |
    Select-Object -ExpandProperty ServicePlans |
    Where-Object { $_.ServicePlanName -like "*INTUNE*" }
```

If no Intune service plan is returned, assign an Intune license in the Microsoft 365 admin center before continuing — nothing else will work without it.

### Step 2: Check app protection status in the portal

1. In the [Microsoft Intune admin center](https://intune.microsoft.com), go to **Apps** > **Monitor** > **App protection status**.
2. Select the **Assigned users** tile.
3. On the **App reporting** page, select **Select user**, search for the affected user, and choose **Select user**.
4. At the top of the pane, confirm the user is licensed for app protection and for Microsoft 365.
5. Review the per-device app list. Note the targeted apps, device types, policies, **device check-in status**, and **last sync time**.

If the app shows **Not checked in**, the app has not contacted the MAM service under the corporate account — move to Step 4 (sign-in) and Step 5 (force check-in). Remember a newly targeted user may not appear for up to 24 hours.

### Step 3: Verify targeting

Confirm the policy assignment reaches this user and this app.

1. In **Apps** > **App protection policies**, open the policy and review **Assignments**. Confirm the user's group is **Included** and not caught by an **Excluded** group.
2. Open **Group** > **All groups**, select the assigned group, choose **Members**, and confirm the affected user is present (check dynamic membership rules if applicable).
3. In the policy's **Apps** tab, confirm the specific app the user is running is in scope.

Enforce these constraints:

- The policy must be assigned to **user groups**, not device groups.
- On **Android Enterprise**, only **personally-owned work profiles** support APP.
- On iOS/iPadOS enrolled through **Automated Device Enrollment (ADE)**, **User Affinity** must be enabled or the app cannot authenticate the user.

You can enumerate configured policies and confirm assignment with Graph PowerShell:

```powershell
Connect-MgGraph -Scopes "DeviceManagementApps.Read.All"

# List all managed app (APP/MAM) policies in the tenant
Get-MgDeviceAppManagementManagedAppPolicy |
    Select-Object DisplayName, Id, "@odata.type"
```

### Step 4: Verify the user signed in with the correct corporate account

MAM only applies to the work/school account that is registered with the service, and only one such account per device is supported. A very common root cause is a pre-existing, unregistered account in the app (for example an account added before the policy existed, or a personal account).

Have the user:

1. Confirm they are signed into the app with the **exact** targeted UPN. The **Accessing your organization's data** dialog means a second, different work account was used.
2. If a stale or wrong account is present, sign out of the app, and if the wrong account was MAM-registered, remove it before signing back in with the correct UPN.
3. On multi-identity apps, verify they are operating in the **work context** (opening a corporate file / work mailbox), not a personal one.

### Step 5: Force a check-in and confirm the applied policy

Policy changes for an already-signed-in user can take up to 8 hours. To accelerate delivery:

- Have the user **sign out of the app and sign back in**, or **restart the device**.
- On **Android**, ensure the **Company Portal** app is installed and on the latest version, then open Company Portal and run **Settings** > **Sync**.
- Confirm the device has a stable network connection (the app must reach the MAM service).

To verify which policy the service believes is applied to a specific app registration, use Graph PowerShell against the **applied** and **intended** policy collections. "Applied" reflects what the app pulled at its last sync; "Intended" reflects what the admin currently targets — a mismatch confirms a propagation delay.

```powershell
Connect-MgGraph -Scopes "DeviceManagementApps.Read.All"

# Find the user's managed app registrations
$regs = Get-MgDeviceAppManagementManagedAppRegistration -All |
    Where-Object { $_.UserId -eq "<entra-object-id>" }

foreach ($r in $regs) {
    Write-Host "Registration:" $r.Id $r.AppIdentifier.PackageId

    # Policy actually applied at last sync
    Get-MgDeviceAppManagementManagedAppRegistrationAppliedPolicy `
        -ManagedAppRegistrationId $r.Id |
        Select-Object DisplayName, Id

    # Policy the admin currently intends
    Get-MgDeviceAppManagementManagedAppRegistrationIntendedPolicy `
        -ManagedAppRegistrationId $r.Id |
        Select-Object DisplayName, Id
}
```

If **Intended** lists the new policy but **Applied** does not, the configuration is correct and you are waiting on the up-to-8-hour propagation window — advise sign-out/sign-in rather than changing configuration.

### Step 6: Remediate

Based on findings:

- **No license:** assign the Intune (and, for Office apps, Microsoft 365) license.
- **User not in group / in excluded group:** correct group membership or exclusions.
- **Wrong or stale account registered:** remove the account from the app and re-register with the correct UPN.
- **Android without Company Portal:** install/update Company Portal.
- **Corrupt registration or a departed user:** issue a selective wipe (below).

To selectively remove corporate data from managed apps:

1. In the Intune admin center, go to **Apps** > **App selective wipe** > **Create wipe request**.
2. Select the user, then select the device, then select **Create**. A separate wipe request is tracked per protected app on that device.
3. For a departing user, use **Apps** > **App selective wipe** > **User-Level Wipe** > **Add** to wipe all apps on all of the user's devices. The user keeps receiving wipe commands at each check-in until you remove them from this list.

The wipe applies the next time the app runs and checks in; the SDK polls every ~30 minutes for a pending wipe.

## Troubleshooting

If the main path does not resolve the issue, work these variations against the specific symptom.

**End-user error dialogs (iOS/Android):**

- **App not set up** — no required APP is detected for the app. Confirm a policy for that platform is deployed to the user's group and targets that app (Steps 2-3).
- **Account not set up** — the account lacks an Intune license. Assign one.
- **Unable to register the app** — auto-enrollment with the MAM service failed. Clear the app's data, then collect logs via Company Portal or open a support ticket.
- **Sign-in failed / Failed app launch** — update the app and the Company Portal app; clear app data; confirm the correct UPN.
- **Accessing your organization's data** — a second, different work account was used; only one MAM account per device is allowed. Sign in with the account the sign-in screen pre-populates, or remove the existing MAM account first.
- **Device noncompliant (rooted/jailbroken)** — the platform check tripped; the device must be reset to factory defaults.

**Policy applies to some apps but not others:** the unaffected app is likely not built on the Intune App SDK, or is not included in the policy's **Apps** scope. Confirm the app is a supported managed app and is targeted.

**Data-transfer settings not enforced (open-in, share, save-as):**

- On **iOS**, Intune cannot control the OS share extension without device management; instead it **encrypts** corporate data before it leaves the app. Validate by attempting to open the exported file outside the managed app — it should be encrypted and unopenable. This is expected behavior, not a policy failure.
- On **Android**, native app associations can be changed by the user; use [data-transfer policy exceptions](https://learn.microsoft.com/intune/apps/app-protection-policies-exception) for specific approved apps.
- Confirm **Send org data to other apps** is set to **Policy managed apps** or **None** as intended.

**"Policy not applied" on new documents or draft emails:** multi-identity apps do not enforce MAM on new/unsaved WXP documents or Outlook drafts until saved to an identified corporate location. Not a defect.

**Windows / Edge repeatedly prompting for the work account after "you're all set":** MAM enrollment may still be processing, the user may have selected "this app only" on the heads-up page, or a pre-existing unregistered account exists in Edge. Wait a few minutes and retry in a new tab; if it persists, remove the unregistered account from the Edge profile and re-add it via the heads-up (registration) flow, then confirm MAM policy is applying to the account.

**Nothing applies to anyone in a newly created policy:** confirm assignment saved with an **Included** user group (not a device group), then allow up to 24 hours for the user to surface in reports; test with a deliberate restriction (for example, block copy/paste) rather than assuming absence of a prompt means failure.

**On-premises resources:** if APP is used with on-premises Exchange or Skype for Business, **Hybrid Modern Authentication** must be enabled or policy retrieval and access will fail.

## Prevention

- **Pilot before broad rollout.** MAM failures are silent to users — a misconfigured policy simply grants unrestricted access. Validate with a small pilot group who deliberately test each restriction, per Microsoft's [validation guidance](https://learn.microsoft.com/intune/app-management/protection/validate-policy-setup).
- **Assign to user groups only,** and keep include/exclude group logic simple and documented to avoid a user falling into both.
- **License first.** Ensure Intune (and Microsoft 365 for Office apps) licenses are provisioned before adding users to targeted groups.
- **Standardize the client baseline.** Require the latest managed app versions, and require Company Portal on Android; add both to your managed-app deployment baseline.
- **Set expectations on timing.** Document the up-to-8-hour propagation for policy changes and the 24-hour reporting lag so the service desk does not chase non-issues. Advise sign-out/sign-in to accelerate.
- **Enable User Affinity** on iOS/iPadOS ADE profiles and use **personally-owned work profiles** on Android Enterprise where MAM is required.
- **Monitor proactively.** Review **Apps** > **Monitor** > **App protection status** regularly and alert on **Not checked in** trends rather than waiting for user reports.
- **Have a de-provisioning runbook.** Use User-Level selective wipe for departing staff and remember to remove them from the wipe list only when the account is fully retired.

Title: INT-006: Intune Conditional Access Blocking Access
Content:
# Intune Conditional Access Blocking Access

**Category:** Intune > Conditional Access
**Article Code:** INT-006
**Tier:** 3
**Audience:** Administrators / Technicians (with end-user guidance in Troubleshooting)
**Estimated Resolution Time:** 30–90 minutes (longer if a compliance sync or re-enrollment is required)

## Symptoms / When to Use

Use this article when a user or service is unexpectedly blocked and the block traces back to a Conditional Access (CA) policy that references device compliance or an Intune control.

- User sees a browser error: "You can't get there from here" or "Your sign-in was successful but does not meet the criteria to access this resource," often citing a compliant or managed device requirement.
- Office/Microsoft 365 client (Outlook, Teams, OneDrive) repeatedly prompts for credentials, then fails, or shows "Need admin approval / device not compliant."
- Sign-in logs show a failure with one of these `AADSTS` codes:
  - `53000` – DeviceNotCompliant
  - `53001` – DeviceNotDomainJoined
  - `53002` – ApplicationUsedIsNotAnApprovedApp
  - `53003` – BlockedByConditionalAccess
  - `53009` – Application needs to enforce Intune protection policies
- A newly enrolled device is blocked even though Intune shows it as compliant.
- A spike in blocked sign-ins across many users after a policy change or a compliance policy tightening.
- Admins are locked out of the Entra or Intune portals after enabling a "Require compliant device" policy for **All users / All resources**.

## Background

Conditional Access is the enforcement engine; Intune is the signal source. Intune evaluates a device against its assigned **compliance policies** and reports a compliant/non-compliant state to Microsoft Entra ID. A Conditional Access policy with the grant control **Require device to be marked as compliant** (or **Require Microsoft Entra hybrid joined device**, **Require approved client app**, or **Require app protection policy**) reads that state at sign-in and grants or blocks access accordingly.

A block occurs when **every** condition in a CA policy is satisfied (user in scope, resource in scope, platform/client match) **and** the required grant control is not met. Common root causes:

- The device is genuinely non-compliant (failed a compliance rule such as OS version, encryption, or Defender status).
- The device is not enrolled in Intune, so no compliance state exists — Entra treats "no state" as not compliant.
- Compliance state has not yet synced to Entra after enrollment or a policy change (propagation lag).
- The user lacks an Intune license, so compliance is never evaluated.
- The setting **Mark devices with no compliance policy assigned as** is set to **Not compliant**, and the user has no compliance policy targeted.
- The app being accessed is a **service dependency** of another app that a stricter policy targets (for example, Teams depends on Exchange Online and SharePoint Online).
- Legacy authentication (Exchange ActiveSync, older clients) can't satisfy modern grant controls.

Because these policies can lock out administrators, always exclude break-glass accounts and stage new policies in **Report-only** mode before enforcing.

## Resolution

### Step 1: Collect the sign-in facts

Ask the user (or capture from the error page via **More details**):

- User principal name and display name
- Timestamp (approximate is fine)
- Target application
- Client type (browser vs. desktop/mobile client)
- Correlation ID / Request ID

These map directly to the sign-in log filters you'll use next.

### Step 2: Identify the blocking policy in the sign-in logs

1. Sign in to the [Microsoft Entra admin center](https://entra.microsoft.com) as at least **Reports Reader**.
2. Go to **Entra ID** > **Monitoring & health** > **Sign-in logs**.
3. Filter to the failed event using **Correlation ID** (most precise), or **Username** + **Date** + **Conditional Access = Failure**.
4. Open the event and select the **Conditional Access** tab. Policies that resulted in the block show a **Failure**/**Block** result. The left pane shows the values collected at sign-in (device state, platform, client app); the right pane shows whether they satisfied each policy's requirements.
5. Select the policy name (or the ellipsis > details) to see exactly which grant control failed — for example, "Require device to be marked as compliant: Failure."
6. Check the **Device Info** tab to confirm the device's **Compliant** and **Managed** status as Entra saw it at sign-in.

If the event detail is insufficient, use the sign-in diagnostic: on the event, go to **Basic info** > **Troubleshoot Event**.

### Step 3: Simulate the sign-in with the What If tool

Confirm which policies apply to the scenario without asking the user to retry repeatedly.

1. In the Entra admin center, go to **Entra ID** > **Conditional Access** > **Policies** > **What If**.
2. Supply the required conditions: **identity** (the user), **target resource** (use the specific App ID — app groups like "Office 365" won't match), **device platform**, and **client app**. Add optional conditions (location, sign-in risk, device state) to match the real sign-in as closely as possible.
3. Select **What If**. Review **Policies that apply** (with their grant/session controls) and **Policies that don't apply** (each with the first unmet condition).

Note: What If does **not** evaluate service dependencies. If you're testing Teams, separately test its dependencies (Exchange Online, SharePoint Online).

### Step 4: Enumerate policies with PowerShell (optional, for audit)

To review CA policy definitions in bulk, use the Microsoft Graph PowerShell SDK (module `Microsoft.Graph.Identity.SignIns`).

```powershell
Install-Module Microsoft.Graph.Identity.SignIns -Scope CurrentUser
Connect-MgGraph -Scopes "Policy.Read.All"

# List all policies with their state and grant controls
Get-MgIdentityConditionalAccessPolicy -All |
    Select-Object DisplayName, State,
        @{n='GrantControls';e={$_.GrantControls.BuiltInControls -join ','}} |
    Format-Table -AutoSize
```

Retrieve a single policy for detailed inspection:

```powershell
Get-MgIdentityConditionalAccessPolicy -ConditionalAccessPolicyId "<policy-id>" |
    Select-Object -ExpandProperty Conditions
```

Filter server-side by display name:

```powershell
Get-MgIdentityConditionalAccessPolicy -Filter "displayName eq 'Require compliant device - All users'"
```

The policy ID here is the GUID shown on the **Conditional Access** tab of the sign-in event and in the Entra policy blade URL.

### Step 5: Fix the device compliance state

If the block is legitimate (device is non-compliant), remediate the device rather than the policy.

1. In the [Intune admin center](https://intune.microsoft.com), go to **Devices** > **All devices** > select the device > **Device compliance**. Identify which compliance policy setting failed.
2. Remediate the failing setting on the device (enable BitLocker/FileVault, update OS, enable Defender, set a compliant passcode, etc.).
3. Force a compliance re-check:
   - **Windows:** open **Company Portal** > **Settings** > **Sync**, or run the sync from **Settings** > **Accounts** > **Access work or school** > select the account > **Info** > **Sync**.
   - **iOS/Android:** open **Company Portal** > **Devices** > select device > **Check settings** / **Check compliance**.
4. Confirm the device flips to **Compliant** in Intune, then wait for the state to propagate to Entra (see Step 6), and have the user retry.

### Step 6: Account for compliance propagation lag

A device that just became compliant in Intune is not instantly compliant to Entra CA. The compliance signal must sync to Microsoft Entra ID and the user's token must refresh.

- Allow a few minutes after the device reports compliant.
- Have the user sign out fully and sign back in (or restart the client app) to force a new token that carries the updated device claim.
- On the device, confirm it is Entra-registered/joined (`dsregcmd /status` on Windows — check `AzureAdJoined : YES` and `DeviceId`). Compliance can't be attributed without a device identity in Entra.

### Step 7: If the policy itself is misconfigured, remediate safely

If What If shows the policy is applying to users/resources it shouldn't, adjust the policy — but stage the change.

1. In the Entra admin center, open the policy under **Entra ID** > **Conditional Access** > **Policies**.
2. Correct the scope: tighten **Users** (exclude the affected group temporarily if appropriate), fix **Target resources**, or narrow **Conditions** (platforms, client apps, locations).
3. Ensure break-glass/emergency access accounts and **Directory Synchronization Accounts** are excluded.
4. Set **Enable policy** to **Report-only**, save, and validate impact using report-only results and the Insights and Reporting workbook before switching back to **On**.

To flip a policy state in an emergency (for example, to disable a policy locking everyone out), use PowerShell with write scope:

```powershell
Connect-MgGraph -Scopes "Policy.ReadWrite.ConditionalAccess"

$params = @{ state = "disabled" }   # valid: enabled | disabled | enabledForReportingButNotEnforced
Update-MgIdentityConditionalAccessPolicy `
    -ConditionalAccessPolicyId "<policy-id>" -BodyParameter $params
```

Re-enable it the same way with `state = "enabled"` once the fix is validated.

## Troubleshooting

If the main path doesn't resolve the block, work through these variations.

**"Intune says compliant, but the user is still blocked."**
- Confirm the user has an **Intune license** assigned — compliance isn't evaluated without one.
- On non-Knox Android, the user must tap **Get Started Now** in the quarantine/enrollment email before access is granted, even if already enrolled.
- On iOS/iPadOS, a pre-existing manually configured email profile can block the Intune email profile and mark the device non-compliant. Have the user remove the manual profile.
- The device may be stuck in a "checking compliance" state. Update Company Portal to the latest version, restart the device, and test on a different network.

**Service dependency blocks.**
The blocked app may be calling a resource covered by a different, stricter policy. In the sign-in log, compare the **Application** to the **Resource** it called (for example, Azure portal calling Azure Resource Manager, or Teams calling Exchange Online/SharePoint Online). Align the policy to cover all the dependent resources, or exclude the dependency deliberately. Check the **Audience** field under the Resource section to see every resource requested in the sign-in.

**Legacy authentication clients.**
Exchange ActiveSync and other legacy clients can't satisfy modern grant controls. For ActiveSync, the only supported condition is platform; MFA and most grant controls aren't honored. Move users to Outlook mobile (modern auth) or create a targeted policy that blocks legacy auth and a separate one for supported platforms.

**Admins locked out.**
If a "Require compliant device" policy for **All users / All resources** locked out administrators without an enrolled device:
- Sign in with a **break-glass account** that is excluded from all CA policies, then disable or scope the offending policy.
- If no break-glass account exists, use the PowerShell `Update-MgIdentityConditionalAccessPolicy` disable command in Step 7 from a session that is itself excluded, or open a Microsoft support case.
- Remember: **Require device to be marked as compliant** does not block Intune enrollment or the Company Portal, so users can still enroll to become compliant.

**Wrong error code interpretation.**
- `53001` (DeviceNotDomainJoined) points to a **hybrid joined** requirement, not compliance — the fixes differ.
- `53002` / `53009` indicate **approved app** or **app protection policy** controls; the user needs a supported app (e.g., Outlook mobile) with an Intune app protection policy, not device compliance.

**Guest/external users.**
CA policies can block B2B guests. Confirm whether an external-identities policy is in scope; guest devices are rarely Intune-managed, so a compliant-device requirement will block them unless external users are excluded or handled via cross-tenant access settings.

**End-user quick script (what to tell the user).**
Have the user: (1) restart the device, (2) open Company Portal and run **Sync / Check compliance**, (3) sign out of the failing app and sign back in, and (4) note the exact error and the **More details** link content for the ticket.

## Prevention

- **Always exclude break-glass accounts** and **Directory Synchronization Accounts** from every CA policy. Maintain at least two cloud-only emergency accounts excluded from all policies.
- **Stage every new or changed policy in Report-only mode.** Validate with report-only results, the What If tool, and the Conditional Access Insights and Reporting workbook before enforcing.
- **Never scope Block or Require-compliant-device to All users + All resources without exclusions.** Verify your own device is compliant before enabling a compliant-device policy.
- **Create the Intune compliance policy before the CA policy.** A "Require compliant device" control with no compliance policy behind it will block as intended only if devices actually have a policy assigned; confirm the **Mark devices with no compliance policy assigned as** setting matches your intent.
- **Adopt a naming convention** that encodes purpose, target, and scope (CA policies have no owner attribute) and keep an out-of-band owner registry.
- **Monitor proactively:** stream sign-in logs to Log Analytics, watch the "sign-ins requiring a compliant or managed device" health scenario, and review audit logs for policy changes.
- **Enable protected actions** so creating, modifying, or deleting CA policies requires step-up authentication.
- **Separate legacy-auth handling** into its own policy so ActiveSync and older clients don't produce confusing compliance blocks.

**Sources verified against Microsoft Learn:**
- Troubleshoot sign-in problems with Conditional Access — https://learn.microsoft.com/entra/identity/conditional-access/troubleshoot-conditional-access
- Troubleshoot Conditional Access Policies with the What If tool — https://learn.microsoft.com/entra/identity/conditional-access/what-if-tool
- Get-MgIdentityConditionalAccessPolicy (Microsoft.Graph.Identity.SignIns) — https://learn.microsoft.com/powershell/module/microsoft.graph.identity.signins/get-mgidentityconditionalaccesspolicy
- Troubleshoot Conditional Access (Intune) — https://learn.microsoft.com/troubleshoot/mem/intune/device-protection/troubleshoot-conditional-access
