Title: SPO-012: SharePoint Retention Labels and Policies Not Working
Content:
# SharePoint Retention Labels and Policies Not Working

**Category:** SharePoint > Compliance
**Article Code:** SPO-012
**Tier:** 3
**Audience:** Administrators / Technicians
**Estimated Resolution Time:** 30-90 minutes hands-on; up to 7 days for changes to fully propagate

## Symptoms / When to Use

Use this article when a Microsoft Purview retention policy or retention label does not behave as expected on SharePoint Online or OneDrive. Common signals:

- A published retention label does not appear in the **Apply label** picker in the SharePoint or OneDrive details pane, even after 1-7 days.
- An auto-apply label policy created days ago has not tagged any matching documents.
- A retention policy shows **(Error)** or a "taking longer than expected to deploy" message in the policy details pane in the Microsoft Purview portal.
- `Get-RetentionCompliancePolicy` returns a `DistributionStatus` stuck on **Pending** or reporting an error.
- Content that should be retained was deleted, or content that should be deletable cannot be removed ("This item is subject to retention" / delete blocked).
- A policy cannot be deleted and is stuck in **PendingDeletion**.
- End users report they cannot delete a library, list, or site, or cannot edit/delete a specific labeled file.

## Background

SharePoint and OneDrive retention is enforced by **Microsoft Purview Data Lifecycle Management** (retention policies) and **Records Management** (retention labels). Neither takes effect instantly. When you create or edit a policy, two phases occur: **distribution** (the policy definition is pushed to each targeted workload) and **application** (a background timer job evaluates content and applies the retention setting). Microsoft states this can take **up to 7 days** end to end. Published labels usually surface in SharePoint/OneDrive within 1 day but can take up to 7.

Most "not working" reports fall into one of these root causes:

1. **Propagation delay** — the change simply has not finished distributing/applying yet.
2. **Distribution error** — the policy failed to reach the workload (locked site, notification pipeline error, unsupported location).
3. **Indexing dependency** — SharePoint content must be **indexed** for retention to apply, and auto-apply KQL queries depend on crawled/managed properties existing.
4. **Precedence / principles of retention** — another policy or label with a stronger action is winning, so the observed behavior is actually correct.
5. **Records / deletion settings** — a "Keep" or record label is intentionally blocking deletion, which users misread as a bug.

Retention labels and retention policies use the **same** underlying cmdlets in **Security & Compliance PowerShell** (`Get/Set/New/Remove-RetentionCompliancePolicy` and the matching `-RetentionComplianceRule` cmdlets). App-scoped locations (Teams private channel messages, Viva Engage) use the `-AppRetentionCompliancePolicy` variants instead. Diagnosis almost always starts with checking `DistributionStatus`.

## Resolution

### Step 1: Confirm the change has had time to propagate

Before troubleshooting, confirm you are not simply inside the normal propagation window.

- **Published labels** (manual apply): typically appear in SharePoint/OneDrive within 1 day, allow up to 7.
- **Auto-apply label policies**: allow up to 7 days for labels to be applied to matching content.
- **Retention policies**: allow up to 7 days to distribute and apply.
- **Policy edits** (adding/removing sites): allow up to 24 hours.

If you are still inside these windows and the policy status is healthy, no action is required. If the window has passed, continue.

### Step 2: Connect to Security & Compliance PowerShell

All diagnostics run in Security & Compliance PowerShell, provided by the **ExchangeOnlineManagement** module. Install/update the module and connect.

```powershell
Install-Module -Name ExchangeOnlineManagement -Scope CurrentUser -Force
Import-Module ExchangeOnlineManagement
Connect-IPPSSession -UserPrincipalName admin@yourtenant.onmicrosoft.com
```

`Connect-IPPSSession` is the correct cmdlet for the Purview compliance endpoint. Do not use `Connect-ExchangeOnline` for these cmdlets.

### Step 3: Check the policy distribution status

Retrieve the policy and inspect its distribution state. The `DistributionStatus` tells you whether distribution succeeded, is pending, or errored; `DistributionResults` contains per-location detail.

```powershell
Get-RetentionCompliancePolicy -Identity "<policy name>" -DistributionDetail | FL DistributionStatus

Get-RetentionCompliancePolicy -Identity "<policy name>" -DistributionDetail |
    Select-Object -ExpandProperty DistributionResults
```

Interpretation:

- **Pending** — distribution is still running. Wait; do not make further edits until it clears.
- **Success** — distribution completed. If content still is not labeled, the issue is application/indexing/precedence (Steps 6-8), not distribution.
- **Error** — read `DistributionResults`. Only act on `DistributionStatus` errors; warnings can be ignored.

To list every policy that currently has an error in one pass:

```powershell
Get-RetentionCompliancePolicy -ErrorPolicyOnly -DistributionDetail |
    FL Name, DistributionStatus
```

For app-scoped policies (Teams private channel messages, Viva Engage), use the parallel cmdlet:

```powershell
Get-AppRetentionCompliancePolicy -Identity "<policy name>" -DistributionDetail | FL DistributionStatus
```

### Step 4: Retry distribution

If distribution errored (for example, `DistributionResults` shows `SiteInReadOnlyOrNotAccessible`, `PolicyNotifyError`, or a "taking longer than expected" message), force a redeployment. This is the single most common fix.

```powershell
Set-RetentionCompliancePolicy -Identity "<policy name>" -RetryDistribution
```

For app-scoped locations (Teams private channel messages, Viva Engage user/community messages):

```powershell
Set-AppRetentionCompliancePolicy -Identity "<policy name>" -RetryDistribution
```

After running this, the policy returns to **Pending** until sync completes. Running `Set-RetentionCompliancePolicy` triggers a full organization synchronization, which is a significant operation — retry one policy at a time and wait for it to reach **Success** before retrying the next.

Portal equivalent: **Microsoft Purview portal** > **Data Lifecycle Management** > **Microsoft 365** > **Retention policies** (or **Label policies**, or **Records Management** > **Label policies**). Select the policy **name** (not the checkbox) to open the details pane, then select **Retry**.

### Step 5: Resolve a locked site (SiteInReadOnlyOrNotAccessible)

If `DistributionResults` reports `SiteInReadOnlyOrNotAccessible`, the target site was locked (by an admin or a temporary automated process) and cannot accept the policy. Confirm and clear the lock, then retry.

```powershell
# Requires the Microsoft.Online.SharePoint.PowerShell module and SharePoint admin rights
Connect-SPOService -Url https://yourtenant-admin.sharepoint.com

Get-SPOSite -Identity https://yourtenant.sharepoint.com/sites/<site> | FL Url, LockState

# If LockState is ReadOnly or NoAccess, unlock it:
Set-SPOSite -Identity https://yourtenant.sharepoint.com/sites/<site> -LockState Unlock
```

Then rerun the retry from Step 4. Note that a site with `LockState` set to `NoAccess` or `ReadOnly` also blocks deletion of items even where retention would otherwise allow it.

### Step 6: Verify the label is actually published and applicable

If a **label** never appears for users, confirm the label policy targets the right location and is enabled.

- In the Purview portal: **Records Management** (or **Data Lifecycle Management**) > **Label policies** > open the policy > confirm SharePoint sites / OneDrive accounts are in scope and the status is **On (Success)**.
- Manual apply works only in the **modern** SharePoint experience, not classic. Have the user open the **details pane** on a selected item and choose the label under **Apply label**.
- For a group-connected Teams site, publish to the **Microsoft 365 Groups** location, not just SharePoint sites.

If a label needs to be applied without waiting for a published policy (for example, to test a single item), retention labels can also be applied directly through CSOM using `SetComplianceTagOnBulkItems` — but for normal operations, publish through a label policy.

### Step 7: Fix auto-apply label policies that match nothing

Auto-apply policies based on KQL/keywords depend on SharePoint search indexing. If matching documents are not being labeled:

1. Confirm the documents are **indexed**. Content that is not indexed cannot be matched. Force a reindex from **Document library settings** > **Advanced settings** > **Reindex Document Library**.
2. Confirm your KQL uses only **predefined managed properties** (for example `RefinableString00`–`RefinableString199`), not custom or crawled properties. Map custom columns to a refinable managed property in **SharePoint admin center** > **Search** > **Manage Search Schema**, then wait 24 hours before using it in a query.
3. Use the real managed property name in KQL (for example `RefinableString01`), never an alias.
4. Remember prefix wildcards (`cat*`) are supported but suffix (`*cat`) and substring (`*cat*`) are not.
5. Allow the full 7 days after any mapping or query change before concluding it failed.

### Step 8: Handle a policy stuck in PendingDeletion

If a policy cannot be deleted and reports **PendingDeletion**, force removal:

```powershell
Remove-RetentionCompliancePolicy -Identity "<policy name>" -ForceDeletion
```

## Troubleshooting

**"Settings not found" error.** The retention policy has no rule attached. Add one:

```powershell
New-RetentionComplianceRule -Name "<new rule name>" -Policy "<existing policy name>" -RetentionDuration Unlimited
```

Or in the portal, edit the policy and complete the **Retention settings** step.

**"You can't apply a hold here" / RecipientTypeNotAllowed.** You added a location type the policy does not support (typically a mailbox type mismatch). Remove the problematic location from the `New-`/`Set-RetentionCompliancePolicy` command and retry.

**Content was retained/deleted differently than the policy specifies.** This is usually correct behavior driven by the **principles of retention**: retention always wins over deletion, the longest retention period wins, explicit-scope policies beat org-wide ("all sites") policies, and a label's action takes precedence over a policy's. Enumerate every policy and label touching the item before assuming a defect. A scoped policy deleting after 5 years will override an org-wide policy retaining for 10.

**A user cannot delete a labeled file.** If the label is a **Keep** (retain) label or marks the item as a **record**, deletion is intentionally blocked. For SharePoint/OneDrive, the tenant setting **Deleting content labeled for retention** controls whether "keep"-labeled items can be deleted. Check or change it under **Purview** > **Settings** > **Records Management** > **Retention Labels** > **Deleting content labeled for retention** (separate toggles for SharePoint and OneDrive). Via PnP PowerShell the equivalent properties are `AllowFilesWithKeepLabelToBeDeletedSPO` and `AllowFilesWithKeepLabelToBeDeletedODB`:

```powershell
Connect-PnPOnline -Url https://yourtenant-admin.sharepoint.com -Interactive
Get-PnPTenant | Select-Object AllowFilesWithKeepLabelToBeDeletedSPO, AllowFilesWithKeepLabelToBeDeletedODB
```

If the label marks the item as a **regulatory record**, editing and deletion are always blocked and cannot be re-enabled — this is by design.

**Retained content is "gone" from the site.** For retain-and-delete or record scenarios, modified/deleted originals are copied to the hidden **Preservation Hold library**. A timer job runs every 7 days and, combined with the minimum 30-day hold, means content can take up to **37 days** to leave the Preservation Hold library, after which it moves through the second-stage Recycle Bin (93 days) before permanent deletion. Site collection admins can view and restore from the Preservation Hold library and second-stage Recycle Bin.

**Items excluded from search still get retention.** Configuring a library to not appear in search results does **not** exclude it from retention. Only unindexed content is skipped, and SharePoint sites must be indexed for retention to apply.

**Policy edit still not visible after 24 hours.** Re-run Step 3; a `Pending` status that never clears indicates a distribution error — go to Step 4/5.

**App-scoped vs. standard cmdlet confusion.** Using `Set-RetentionCompliancePolicy` against a Teams private channel/Viva Engage policy (or vice versa) fails or no-ops. Match the cmdlet family to the workload: `-RetentionCompliancePolicy` for Exchange, SharePoint, OneDrive, Microsoft 365 Groups, and Teams channel/chat; `-AppRetentionCompliancePolicy` for Teams private channel and Viva Engage.

## Prevention

- **Wait for Success before editing.** Always confirm `DistributionStatus` is not **Pending** before making another change to the same policy. Overlapping edits are a leading cause of stuck distributions.
- **Batch location changes.** Add or remove multiple sites in one command rather than repeated single edits, which each trigger a full sync:

```powershell
Set-RetentionCompliancePolicy -Identity "<policy name>" `
    -AddSharePointLocation "https://yourtenant.sharepoint.com/sites/finance","https://yourtenant.sharepoint.com/sites/legal"
```

- **Never pipe `Foreach-Object` into `Set-RetentionCompliancePolicy`** to add/remove locations — Microsoft explicitly warns against it. Pass a comma-separated list instead.
- **Plan for 7 days.** Set stakeholder expectations that retention changes are not immediate; schedule validation checks a week out.
- **Validate auto-apply queries in test mode** and confirm managed property mappings exist and are indexed before relying on KQL-based labeling.
- **Document precedence.** Maintain an inventory of which policies and labels target which sites so "unexpected" retention outcomes can be traced to the governing rule quickly.
- **Choose the right cmdlet family** for the workload from the start to avoid distribution errors.

## Sources

- https://learn.microsoft.com/troubleshoot/microsoft-365/purview/retention/resolve-errors-in-retention-and-retention-label-policies
- https://learn.microsoft.com/purview/create-retention-policies#how-long-it-takes-for-retention-policies-to-take-effect
- https://learn.microsoft.com/purview/retention-policies-sharepoint#how-retention-works-for-sharepoint-and-onedrive

Title: SPO-013: SharePoint Managed Metadata and Term Store Issues
Content:
# SharePoint Managed Metadata and Term Store Issues

**Category:** SharePoint > Metadata
**Article Code:** SPO-013
**Tier:** 2
**Audience:** Administrators / Technicians (with end-user guidance where noted)
**Estimated Resolution Time:** 30–90 minutes (longer for bulk term imports or CSOM remediation)

## Symptoms / When to Use

Use this article when you encounter any of the following:

- A **Managed Metadata column** shows no values, an empty picker, or "term not found" after a term was moved, renamed, deprecated, or deleted.
- Users cannot select terms because a **term set is missing, empty, or not marked available for tagging**.
- A **local (site-collection) term set** does not appear on a modern communication or Teams-connected site.
- **Import fails** with *"Not all terms were imported successfully. Please see the server log for more information."*
- **Filtering or sorting** on a Managed Metadata column returns no results (common on classic Tasks lists).
- A list/library created from a **template** shows blank or incorrect Managed Metadata values.
- Contributors report they **cannot add or edit terms** despite having site access.
- After a **tenant-to-tenant or SharePoint Server migration**, managed metadata columns are broken or point at the wrong store.

## Background

The **Managed Metadata Service (MMS)** stores a hierarchical taxonomy: **Groups** → **Term sets** → **Terms**. Terms are referenced by a unique GUID, not by their display text, so renaming a term does not break existing tagged items — but *deleting* or *deprecating* one does.

Term sets have two scopes:

- **Global term sets** are available to every site that subscribes to the MMS.
- **Local term sets** are created inside a single site collection (typically when a Managed Metadata column is built with "Customize your term set") and are visible only there.

Access is governed by three roles, independent of site permissions: **Term store admin** (full control, manages groups and languages), **Group manager** (manages contributors and term sets within a group), and **Contributor** (creates/edits terms). A user with Site Owner rights but no term store role cannot edit global terms — this is the most common "permission" complaint.

Term sets are also **Open** or **Closed** (whether users can add terms during tagging) and each term/term set has an **Available for tagging** flag. A disabled flag hides the term from pickers even though it exists.

Sources verified against Microsoft Learn:
- Open the Term Store Management Tool — https://learn.microsoft.com/sharepoint/open-term-store-management-tool
- Assign roles and permissions to manage term sets — https://learn.microsoft.com/sharepoint/assign-roles-and-permissions-to-manage-term-sets
- Create a default site collection term set if none is present — https://learn.microsoft.com/troubleshoot/sharepoint/administration/create-default-site-term-set

## Resolution

### Step 1: Confirm access to the term store

Global taxonomy edits require a SharePoint Administrator (or higher) role in Microsoft 365, or an explicit Term Store Admin assignment.

1. Go to the **SharePoint admin center** > **Content services** > **Term store**.
2. In the tree-view pane, select the taxonomy root.
3. Next to **Admins**, select **Edit** and confirm the technician's account is listed. Add it if missing, then **Save**.

For **local** term sets, open the tool at the site instead: **Site Settings** > **Site Administration** > **Term store management**.

### Step 2: Verify the term set exists and is available for tagging

1. In the Term store, expand the group and select the affected term set.
2. On the **Usage settings** tab, confirm **Available for tagging** is enabled. If it is cleared, select **Edit**, check **Enable**, and **Save**.
3. Select the individual term. On its **Usage settings** tab, confirm the term itself is also enabled for tagging.
4. If the term set is **Closed** and users need to add values ad hoc, change **Submission policy** to **Open** — or add the terms centrally.

A deprecated term stays valid on already-tagged items but disappears from the picker for new tagging. Re-enable it or add a replacement term as a **synonym** so historical values still resolve.

### Step 3: Restore a missing local term set (modern sites)

Modern communication sites and Teams-connected sites have no publishing feature, so the site-collection term store is not created until a Managed Metadata column forces it. If **Term store management** shows nothing at the site level:

1. On the site, select the **gear icon** > **Site contents**.
2. Open any list/library > **ellipsis** > **Settings**.
3. Under **Columns**, select **Create column**.
4. Name it (for example `LocalMMS`) and set the type to **Managed Metadata**.
5. Under **Term Set Settings**, choose **Customize your term set**, then **OK**.
6. Return to **Site Settings** > **Term store management** and confirm the local store now appears.

### Step 4: Repair a broken Managed Metadata column value

When a column shows blank after a term move/delete:

1. Confirm the target term still exists in the term store (Step 2). If it was deleted, recreate it or add it as a synonym under the surviving term.
2. Open the affected item, clear the column, re-select the correct term from the picker, and save. This rewrites the stored GUID.
3. For many items, re-tag in bulk: switch the library to **Grid view** (Edit in grid), or use a Power Automate flow / PnP PowerShell to set the field programmatically.

### Step 5: Import or migrate terms at scale

Small term sets import cleanly from the portal. Larger ones need the right tool:

1. In the Term store, select the target group, then **Import term set** (CSV) or the SKOS `.ttl` format.
2. Download the sample file, populate it, and upload. Keep CSV imports **under 5,000 terms**; keep SKOS imports **under ~20,000 terms**. (SKOS import requires a pay-as-you-go/Syntex license.)
3. For very large or complex taxonomies, export from the source and re-provision with PnP PowerShell. Note PnP PowerShell is community-supported, not covered by a Microsoft SLA:

```powershell
Install-Module PnP.PowerShell
Connect-PnPOnline -Url https://<tenant>-admin.sharepoint.com -Interactive

# Export an entire term group to XML from the source tenant
Export-PnPTermGroupToXml -Identity "Corporate Taxonomy" -Out .\taxonomy.xml

# Import it into the target tenant
Import-PnPTermGroupFromXml -Path .\taxonomy.xml
```

To read a term and confirm its GUID before/after a change:

```powershell
Get-PnPTerm -TermSet "Departments" -TermGroup "Corporate Taxonomy" -Includes Id,Name
```

If a portal CSV import fails on volume, split the file or perform the import via CSOM, which has no 5,000-term ceiling.

## Troubleshooting

**"Not all terms were imported successfully."** This is a known SharePoint Online limit: the portal term store tool rejects imports of 5,000+ terms. Split the CSV into sub-5,000-term files or import via CSOM. Verify the CSV is UTF-8 encoded and that property names contain none of the disallowed characters: `[ ] ; " < > | & \t`.

**Managed Metadata filtering returns nothing (classic Tasks list).** Edit the page, edit the list view Web Part, expand **Miscellaneous**, enable **Server Render**, and save. Repeat for each affected view. This is a documented SharePoint Online behavior.

**Template-created list shows blank Managed Metadata values.** List templates carry Lookup, Managed Metadata, and Person/Group columns correctly only within the *same* site where they were saved. On a different site collection or subsite they break. Recreate those columns after provisioning the list, or save the whole **site** as a template and create the new site in the same site collection.

**Contributor can't edit terms.** Site permissions do not grant term store rights. Assign the user a **Group manager** or **Contributor** role on the specific term group (SharePoint admin center > Term store > select group > **Edit** next to Group managers/Contributors).

**Migration broke the columns.** SPMT and the MMS support only **one default term store per site collection**. If multiple term stores are flagged default, columns cannot resolve. Set exactly one store as the default and clear the flag on the others, then revalidate.

**Term picker shows a term the column shouldn't allow (open term set).** Open term sets accept new values during tagging, and document-processing extractors add unmatched values to the term set root. Change the term set to **Closed** if you need strict control, then clean up stray root terms (move, merge, or convert to synonyms).

## Prevention

- **Restrict edit rights deliberately.** Keep the Term Store Admin list short and assign Group managers/Contributors per group rather than granting broad access.
- **Prefer global term sets** for anything reused across sites; reserve local term sets for genuinely single-site needs. Local sets cannot be shared and complicate migrations.
- **Never delete terms in production** — deprecate them and add replacements as synonyms so existing tagged items keep resolving.
- **Standardize one default site-collection term store** to avoid migration breakage.
- **Test imports in a staging term group** and stay under the 5,000-term portal limit; script bulk work with CSOM/PnP and version-control the export XML.
- **Document the taxonomy** (owners, stakeholders, contacts on each term set) using the built-in General tab fields so ownership is traceable.

Title: SPO-015: SharePoint Alerts Not Sending
Content:
# SharePoint Alerts Not Sending

**Category:** SharePoint > Alerts
**Article Code:** SPO-015
**Tier:** 2
**Audience:** Administrators / Technicians
**Estimated Resolution Time:** 30–90 minutes (longer if the root cause is Exchange mail flow or a service-side incident)

> **Retirement notice (read first):** Microsoft began removing classic SharePoint Alerts starting **July 2026**. Alerts may stop functioning entirely on tenants where the retirement has rolled out, regardless of configuration. Before spending time troubleshooting, confirm the tenant still supports alerts and set customer expectations. The durable replacement is a **rule** (list/library **Automate > Rules**) or a **Power Automate** flow. See the Prevention section. Reference: https://aka.ms/retirement/alerts/support

Classic SharePoint Online alerts email a user when items in a list or library are added, changed, or deleted. When they stop arriving, the cause is almost always one of: the user profile has no email address, the user lost permission to the object, alerts are disabled at the tenant, throttling, the target is an unsupported group type, or an Exchange/service-side mail issue. This article works those causes in order.

## Symptoms / When to Use

- A user created an alert on a list, library, or document but never receives notification email after an item is added, edited, or deleted.
- On creating an alert the user sees: *"You do not have an e-mail address. Alert has been created successfully but you will not receive notifications until valid e-mail or mobile address has been provided in your profile."*
- Existing alerts stopped arriving even though new alerts on a test library work.
- No alerts arrive for **any** user across multiple sites (points to tenant-wide disable or a service incident).
- Alerts sent to a distribution list or Microsoft 365 Group are silently not delivered.
- Task-list or workflow notification emails also fail (shared root cause: outgoing mail).

## Background

SharePoint Online alerts are generated by the alert subscription engine and delivered as email through Exchange Online. Delivery depends on a chain that must be intact end to end:

1. The subscribing user has a **valid work email** on their SharePoint user profile. This is normally populated from the mailbox; users **without an Exchange Online license** frequently have a blank profile email, which silently breaks delivery.
2. The user holds at least **Read** permission on the target list/library. Alerts respect item security; losing access silently stops the alert.
3. Alerts are **not disabled at the tenant**. `Set-SPOTenant -StopAlerts $true` turns alerts off for the entire organization.
4. The recipient is a **user or a mail-enabled security group**. Alerts to distribution lists and Microsoft 365 Groups are **not supported** and will not deliver.
5. Exchange Online accepts and delivers the message (not blocked by junk filtering, connectors, or a service incident), and the send is not being **throttled** for excessive immediate-alert volume.

Because the failure is silent at several links, work the chain top-down rather than guessing.

## Resolution

### Step 1: Confirm the user profile has a work email

This is the most common cause, especially for shared, service, or unlicensed accounts. As a SharePoint administrator:

1. Go to the SharePoint admin center (`https://<tenant>-admin.sharepoint.com`) **> More features > User profiles > Open**.
2. Select **Manage User Profiles**, search the affected user, and confirm **Work email** is populated with a valid, mail-enabled address.

If the field is blank, allow users to edit and replicate the property:

1. In **User profiles**, under **People**, select **Manage User Properties**.
2. Locate **Work email**, hover, open the drop-down, and select **Edit**.
3. Under **Edit Settings**, enable **Allow users to edit values for this property**.
4. Under **Policy Settings**, select **Replicable** (required so the value propagates to all site collections), then **OK**.

The most reliable long-term fix is assigning the account an **Exchange Online license** so the profile email populates automatically.

### Step 2: Verify the subscriber's permissions

Confirm the user has at least **Read** on the target object. Alerts fire only for items the subscriber can see.

1. On the list/library, open **Settings (gear) > Library/List settings > Permissions for this ... library**.
2. Confirm the user (directly or via a group) has a permission level of Read or higher.

If permissions are missing, grant access, then have the user delete and recreate the alert.

### Step 3: Confirm alerts are not disabled tenant-wide

If **no** user receives alerts anywhere, check the tenant `StopAlerts` flag. Connect with the SharePoint Online Management Shell:

```powershell
Connect-SPOService -Url https://<tenant>-admin.sharepoint.com
Get-SPOTenant | Select-Object StopAlerts
```

If `StopAlerts` is `True`, re-enable alerts:

```powershell
Set-SPOTenant -StopAlerts $false
```

`Set-SPOTenant` requires SharePoint administrator rights and the `Microsoft.Online.SharePoint.PowerShell` module. Reference: https://learn.microsoft.com/powershell/module/microsoft.online.sharepoint.powershell/set-spotenant

### Step 4: Test with a fresh alert

Isolate old-vs-new alert behavior. On a **test library**:

1. Have the user select **... > Alert me** (or **Automate > Alert me**) and create an immediate email alert.
2. Add, edit, or delete an item to trigger it.
3. Wait up to **15 minutes** — alerts are not instantaneous.

If the new alert arrives but old ones do not, the user's existing subscriptions are stale — proceed to Step 5. If even the new test alert fails after Step 1–3 are clean, escalate to Step-level troubleshooting below (Exchange/service).

### Step 5: Delete and recreate stale alerts

Corrupt or orphaned subscriptions are cleared by removing and recreating them.

- **End user:** on the site, **Settings (gear) > Alert me / Manage my alerts**, delete all listed alerts, then recreate the needed ones.
- **Site admin:** **Settings (gear) > Site settings > Site Administration > User alerts**. Select the affected **Display alerts for** user and **Delete Selected Alerts**. The user then recreates them.

## Troubleshooting

If alerts still fail after the main path, check these variations:

- **Unsupported recipient type.** Alerts cannot be delivered to **distribution lists** or **Microsoft 365 Groups**. Only individual users and **mail-enabled security groups** are supported. Re-point the alert to a supported recipient.
- **Throttling on high-volume immediate alerts.** If one address receives several thousand immediate alerts per hour across all subscriptions, SharePoint throttles delivery to protect service health. Switch heavy subscriptions from **immediate** to a **daily/weekly summary**, or consolidate them.
- **Junk/quarantine.** Confirm the alert mail is not landing in the user's **Junk Email** folder or Exchange **quarantine**. Add the SharePoint sender to allowed senders if needed.
- **Exchange mail flow.** If no SharePoint email of any kind is arriving, test general mail flow to the same mailbox. If ordinary email is also delayed or missing, the fault is Exchange, not SharePoint — investigate connectors, transport rules, and message trace in the Exchange admin center.
- **Service incident.** In the Microsoft 365 admin center, check **Health > Service health** for active SharePoint or Exchange advisories before deeper troubleshooting. A tenant-wide, all-user failure with clean configuration is frequently a service-side issue or the alerts retirement rollout.
- **Custom email content expected.** Native alerts cannot use custom templates. If the customer needs branded or conditional notifications, that requires Power Automate or SharePoint Designer workflows — it is not an alert bug.

If Steps 1–5 are clean and a fresh test alert still fails on a non-retired tenant, collect the last known good time and exact reproduction steps, then open a Microsoft support case.

## Prevention

- **Migrate off classic alerts.** With retirement underway (July 2026), move business-critical notifications to **list/library Rules** (**Automate > Manage rules**) for simple add/change conditions, or **Power Automate** flows (**Automate > Power Automate**, or a scheduled reminder flow on a date column) for anything richer. These are the supported forward path.
- **License mailboxes that need alerts.** Ensure any account expected to receive notifications has an Exchange Online license so its profile email stays populated.
- **Use supported recipients.** Target individual users or mail-enabled security groups; never distribution lists or Microsoft 365 Groups.
- **Prefer summary over immediate** for high-churn lists to avoid throttling.
- **Document alert ownership** so that when staff change roles or lose object permissions, their alerts are reviewed and reassigned rather than silently failing.
- **Baseline mail flow.** Keep Exchange Online mail flow and anti-spam allow-lists healthy; most "SharePoint alert" failures are actually email delivery failures.

**Tags:** sharepoint, alerts, notifications, sharepoint-online, email, set-spotenant, stopalerts, power-automate, exchange-online, troubleshooting, user-profile, permissions

Title: SPO-016: SharePoint Content Types Not Applying or Syncing
Content:
# SharePoint Content Types Not Applying or Syncing

**Category:** SharePoint > Content Types
**Article Code:** SPO-016
**Tier:** 3
**Audience:** Administrators / Technicians
**Estimated Resolution Time:** 30–90 minutes (plus up to 1 hour of tenant-side propagation delay)

Content types published from the content type hub (or the SharePoint admin center Content type gallery) do not always appear on target sites, lists, and libraries on the schedule administrators expect. This article covers diagnosis and remediation for SharePoint Online, with a secondary section for SharePoint Server hybrid/on-premises syndication.

## Symptoms / When to Use

- A content type published in the **Content type gallery** (SharePoint admin center) does not appear on a target site or in a list/library.
- Changes to an existing published content type (new columns, renamed columns, updated document template) are not reflected on consuming sites even after waiting.
- A newly created site does not receive content types you expected to be inherited from a hub site.
- A column added to a content type in the hub shows up on some sites but not others, or appears with the wrong (default browser) language name.
- End users report the content type is missing from the **+ New** menu on a document library.
- Page scheduling controls disappear after a content type was republished, or site-level customizations to a content type were silently overwritten.
- The Content type gallery in the SharePoint admin center throws "An unexpected error has occurred" or "You need permission to access this site."
- (On-premises) The **Content type subscriber** timer job runs but consuming site collections never receive updates; content type publishing error logs show failures.

## Background

SharePoint has two distinct distribution models for content types, and they behave very differently.

**1. Classic content type publishing (syndication).** The content type hub lives at `/sites/ContentTypeHub`. Content types created in the SharePoint admin center Content type gallery are stored here. When you publish a content type, a timer-driven job packages it and distributes it to subscribing site collections. This is an eventual, asynchronous "push" — nothing is instant. In SharePoint Online the propagation is fully managed by Microsoft and can take **15 minutes or more**, and for larger tenants considerably longer. On SharePoint Server the push is driven by two timer jobs: the **Content type hub** job (default: daily — packages unpublished/changed content types) and the **Content type subscriber** job (default: hourly — pulls the packages from the hub and applies them to the local content type gallery of each subscribing site collection).

**2. Modern "pull as needed" model.** Microsoft has shifted SharePoint Online away from "push everywhere" toward "pull as needed." Rather than every site collection receiving every published content type, a site or list can pull a specific published content type from the hub on demand via the Microsoft Graph `getCompatibleHubContentTypes` and `addCopyFromContentTypeHub` APIs (exposed as Graph PowerShell cmdlets). Separately, the **Push content types to a hub** feature (Microsoft Syntex, pay-as-you-go licensed) auto-adds content types to new lists/libraries on sites associated with a chosen hub site.

Two consequences follow directly from this architecture:

- **Publishing is one-directional and destructive to local edits.** When a content type is republished from the gallery, it overwrites changes made to that content type at the site level. A well-known example: enabling page scheduling adds a `PublishStartDate` field at the site level; republishing the `Site Page` content type from the gallery strips it, breaking scheduling until the content type is republished again after re-enabling scheduling.
- **A content type is only added to a library if the type is compatible.** A pushed/pulled content type is added to a document library only if it derives (directly or indirectly) from the **Document** content type, and to a list only if it does **not** derive from Document. Type mismatches are a common silent failure.

Most "not syncing" tickets are actually propagation-delay, permission, subscription-scope, or compatibility issues rather than genuine faults.

## Resolution

### Step 1: Confirm the content type is actually published

Publishing status is the most common miss. A content type that was created or edited but never published (or that was edited and not **re**-published) will never propagate.

1. Go to the SharePoint admin center, expand **Content services**, and select **Content type gallery**. (Direct link: `https://go.microsoft.com/fwlink/?linkid=2185074`.) Sign in with a Global Administrator or SharePoint Administrator account. The gallery is not available to accounts holding only the Global Reader role.
2. Under the **Site content type** column, select the content type.
3. In the menu bar, select **Publish** to open the **Manage Publishing** panel.
4. Choose the correct action and select **Save**:
   - **Publish** — first-time publish; makes the content type available for download to all sites.
   - **Republish** — pushes updates to a content type that was already published. **You must republish after every edit** — editing alone does not propagate.
   - **Unpublish** — removes it; existing copies on other sites are converted to local content types.

You can perform the same operation directly in the hub at `https://<tenant>.sharepoint.com/sites/ContentTypeHub`.

### Step 2: Wait for (and account for) propagation delay

After publishing or republishing, allow **at least 15 minutes**, and up to an hour on larger tenants, before treating non-appearance as a fault. Do not repeatedly republish during this window — it queues additional work and does not speed anything up.

For the **Push content types to a hub** (Syntex) feature specifically: the first time a content type is pushed to an existing hub and its already-associated sites, it can take **up to an hour** — measured from when the hub or associated site is next visited — for settings to update. New hub associations after that reflect within a few minutes.

### Step 3: Verify the target actually subscribes / is in scope

In the modern model a site does not automatically receive every published content type. Confirm the delivery path that applies:

- **Syntex push model:** In the Content type gallery, select the content type, select **Edit**, then **Choose hub sites**, and confirm the target's hub site is selected. This feature requires a Syntex pay-as-you-go license. Only new lists/libraries created after association receive the type automatically.
- **Pull model:** The target site or list must explicitly pull the content type (Step 4). Nothing arrives until it does.
- **Compatibility:** Confirm the content type derives from **Document** if the target is a document library, or does **not** derive from Document if the target is a list. A mismatch is silently skipped.

### Step 4: Force a targeted pull with Microsoft Graph PowerShell

When you need a specific published content type on a specific site or list immediately, pull it rather than waiting for propagation. This uses the documented Microsoft Graph PowerShell `Microsoft.Graph.Sites` module.

Install/import and connect with the required scope (`Sites.Manage.All`, or `Sites.FullControl.All`):

```powershell
Install-Module Microsoft.Graph.Sites -Scope CurrentUser
Import-Module Microsoft.Graph.Sites
Connect-MgGraph -Scopes "Sites.Manage.All"
```

List the hub content types that are compatible with the target site (or list):

```powershell
# Compatible hub content types for a site
Get-MgSiteContentTypeCompatibleHubContentType -SiteId $siteId

# Compatible hub content types for a specific list
Get-MgSiteListContentTypeCompatibleHubContentType -SiteId $siteId -ListId $listId
```

Pull (add or sync) a specific published content type by its content type ID into the site or list:

```powershell
$params = @{ contentTypeId = "0x0101" }

# Pull into a site
Add-MgSiteContentTypeCopyFromContentTypeHub -SiteId $siteId -BodyParameter $params

# Pull into a specific list
Add-MgSiteListContentTypeCopyFromContentTypeHub -SiteId $siteId -ListId $listId -BodyParameter $params
```

Re-running `Add-Mg...CopyFromContentTypeHub` for a content type that already exists on the target **syncs** the latest published version — a reliable way to force a stubborn update onto one site without republishing to the whole tenant.

### Step 5: Add the content type to the list or library (make it visible to users)

Getting a content type onto a *site* does not put it on the **+ New** menu of a library. Content types must be allowed on the list, and the type added to it.

Via the browser (end-user / site owner path):
1. Open the library, then **Settings (gear) > Library settings > More library settings**.
2. Under **General Settings > Advanced settings**, set **Allow management of content types** to **Yes**, then **OK**.
3. On the settings page, under **Content Types**, select **Add from existing site content types**, choose the content type, and select **Add**.

If the content type is present at the site level but does not appear in the "add from existing" picker, it has not finished syncing to the site — return to Step 4 and pull it directly to the site first.

### Step 6: Confirm the result

1. Open the target library and confirm the content type appears under the **+ New** menu.
2. Create a test item/document from the content type and confirm the expected columns and document template are present.
3. For an updated content type, verify the specific change (new column, renamed column) is present on an existing item's edit form.

## Troubleshooting

**Content type gallery throws an error or "You need permission to access this site."** The most common cause is permissions. Confirm the operator is a Global or SharePoint Administrator. Then browse to `https://<tenant>.sharepoint.com/sites/contenttypehub/_layouts/15/mngsiteadmin.aspx` and verify that **Company Administrator** and **SharePoint Service Administrator** are listed as site collection administrators; add the specific user as an individual administrator there if needed. Global Reader cannot open the gallery.

**Edit made but nothing propagates.** Editing a content type does not distribute it. You must **Republish** (Step 1). This is the single most frequent cause of "not syncing" tickets.

**A column name shows in the wrong language after sync.** When you rename a site column that is part of a published content type, the target site and the browser must be in the **same** language for the updated column name to render correctly after the sync completes. Have the user set their browser language to match the site language, or update the display name in each target language.

**Site-level customizations disappeared after a republish.** Republishing overwrites site-level content type changes. The canonical case is page scheduling: republishing `Site Page` removes the `PublishStartDate` field. To restore, go to the content type hub Pages library, set **Scheduling > Enable scheduling** to **On**, then in the Content type gallery select the affected content type (e.g. **Site Page**), **Publish > Republish > Save**. Allow 15+ minutes. Repeat for each affected content type. As a rule, make content type changes centrally in the gallery, not per-site, precisely because republishing clobbers local edits.

**Content type reaches the site but not a specific library.** Check compatibility (Step 3): a Document-derived type cannot be added to a non-document list, and vice versa. Also confirm the library has **Allow management of content types** enabled (Step 5).

**Newly created content type won't push to a hub (Syntex).** For the **Push content types to a hub** feature to work, the content type must **already be published** first. Publish it in the gallery, then use **Edit > Choose hub sites**.

**SharePoint Server / hybrid — subscriber job runs but nothing updates.** On SharePoint Server the flow depends on the Managed Metadata service connection and two timer jobs. First confirm the consuming web application's Managed Metadata service connection has both **Consumes content types from the Content Type Gallery at <URL>** and **Push-down Content Type Publishing updates from the Content Type Gallery to sub-sites and lists using the content type** enabled (Central Administration > Application Management > Manage service applications > the Managed Metadata connection > **Properties**).

Then force the jobs from the SharePoint Management Shell. Run the hub packaging job first, then the subscriber job:

```powershell
# Run on a SharePoint Server farm (SharePoint Management Shell)
Get-SPTimerJob | Where-Object { $_.DisplayName -like "*Content Type Hub*" } | Start-SPTimerJob
Get-SPTimerJob | Where-Object { $_.DisplayName -like "*Content Type Subscriber*" } | Start-SPTimerJob
```

Filtering by `DisplayName` avoids depending on the internal job name. Watch the run status in **Central Administration > Monitoring > Check job status**.

**Diagnose which content types failed to publish (on-premises).** The content type hub keeps a publishing error log. From the content type hub site collection, open **Site settings > Content type publishing** (under Site Collection Administration) to see the subscriber's last refresh and any content types that failed, then republish the failing types from the hub.

**Nothing works and the delay is unreasonable.** If a content type still has not propagated after an hour on SharePoint Online, force a targeted pull with Graph (Step 4) for the affected site/list as a workaround, and open a Microsoft support case if tenant-wide publishing appears stalled — the push side is Microsoft-managed and not directly controllable in SharePoint Online.

## Prevention

- **Make all content type changes centrally in the Content type gallery / hub, then republish.** Avoid editing published content types at the site level — a future republish will overwrite those edits without warning.
- **Always Republish after editing.** Build "Republish and note the timestamp" into your change checklist so the propagation window is tracked.
- **Budget for propagation.** Communicate the 15-minutes-to-1-hour expectation to stakeholders and schedule changes outside peak hours. Do not repeatedly republish while waiting.
- **Match the base type to the target.** Derive from **Document** for libraries, from **Item** (not Document) for lists. Document this in the content type's description.
- **Standardize the delivery model per environment.** Decide whether you are using classic gallery publishing, the Syntex push-to-hub feature, or on-demand Graph pulls, and apply one model consistently rather than mixing them.
- **Keep hub administration permissions tight and correct.** Ensure Global/SharePoint Administrators are site collection admins on `/sites/contenttypehub` so gallery access does not fail intermittently.
- **Handle multilingual column renames deliberately** — provide display names for every site language rather than relying on a single-language rename.
- **On SharePoint Server, monitor the Content type hub and Content type subscriber timer jobs** and review the content type publishing error log on the hub after each publishing cycle.
- **Script recurring pulls where propagation is unreliable.** For critical sites, a small Graph PowerShell runbook that re-runs `Add-Mg...CopyFromContentTypeHub` after a publish guarantees the target is synced without waiting on tenant-wide push.

Title: SPO-017: SharePoint Site Collection Admin Access Issues
Content:
# SharePoint Site Collection Admin Access Issues

**Category:** SharePoint > Administration
**Article Code:** SPO-017
**Tier:** 2
**Audience:** Administrators / Technicians
**Estimated Resolution Time:** 15-45 minutes

Guidance for diagnosing and restoring site collection administrator (now called "site admin") access in SharePoint Online. Covers the SharePoint admin center portal, the SharePoint Online Management Shell, and PnP PowerShell, plus the edge cases that commonly block access on live tenants.

## Symptoms / When to Use

- A user reports "Access Denied" or "You need permission to access this site" on a site they should administer.
- A departed employee was the only site admin and the site now has no working administrator.
- A group-connected team site lost all owners, so no one can manage membership or settings.
- A SharePoint or Global Administrator can see a site in the admin center but cannot open it or its Site Settings.
- Membership changes made in the admin center do not appear to take effect for a user.
- A OneDrive needs to be accessed for data recovery or offboarding, but no admin is assigned.
- You need to bulk-verify or reset site admins across many site collections.

## Background

SharePoint Online distinguishes several roles that are easy to confuse:

- **SharePoint Administrator / Global Administrator** — tenant-level roles that grant access to the SharePoint admin center. Critically, these admins do **not** automatically have access to the content of every site or OneDrive; they can *grant themselves* access, but until they do, opening a site can return Access Denied.
- **Primary site admin (owner)** — the single account listed as the primary administrator of a site collection. Set via the `-Owner` property.
- **Additional site admins (site collection administrators)** — one or more accounts with full control of the site collection. There is no fixed limit, unlike on-premises SharePoint Server, which allowed only one primary and one secondary.
- **Site owners group** — a SharePoint permission group. For group-connected sites this maps to the Microsoft 365 group owners.

Most "admin access" incidents come from one of three root causes: the only admin left the organization, a group site lost its owners, or a tenant admin assumed their role grants automatic content access. The fix is almost always to assign a valid site admin using tenant-admin credentials, then have that account act on the site.

Two important constraints: `Set-SPOUser` is **not supported with granular delegated admin privileges (GDAP)**, which affects partner/CSP scenarios, and you must connect to the tenant **admin** URL (not the site URL) for these cmdlets to work.

## Resolution

### Step 1: Confirm your tenant-admin role and connect

Confirm the operator holds the SharePoint Administrator or Global Administrator role (Microsoft 365 admin center > Roles). Then connect the SharePoint Online Management Shell to the tenant **admin** endpoint:

```powershell
# Install once if needed:
# Install-Module -Name Microsoft.Online.SharePoint.PowerShell -Scope CurrentUser
Connect-SPOService -Url https://contoso-admin.sharepoint.com
```

Replace `contoso` with your tenant name. The URL must end in `-admin.sharepoint.com`.

### Step 2: Inspect current admins on the site

Before changing anything, capture who currently has access. `Get-SPOUser` lists users and security groups on a site collection:

```powershell
Get-SPOUser -Site https://contoso.sharepoint.com/sites/marketing -Limit All |
    Where-Object { $_.IsSiteAdmin -eq $true } |
    Select-Object DisplayName, LoginName, IsSiteAdmin
```

If this returns no valid admins, or only disabled/deleted accounts, proceed to add one.

### Step 3: Add a site collection administrator (PowerShell)

Use `Set-SPOUser` with `-IsSiteCollectionAdmin $true`. This is the fastest way to restore access:

```powershell
$tenant = "contoso"
$site   = "marketing"
$user   = "opalc"
Set-SPOUser -Site https://$tenant.sharepoint.com/sites/$site `
    -LoginName $user@$tenant.com -IsSiteCollectionAdmin $true
```

The account is now an additional site admin with full control. Verify by re-running the `Get-SPOUser` check from Step 2 or by having the user open the site.

### Step 4: Change the primary admin (owner) if needed

Adding an admin does not change the *primary* owner. If the primary must be reassigned (for example, the listed owner has left), set the `-Owner` property with `Set-SPOSite`:

```powershell
Set-SPOSite -Identity https://contoso.sharepoint.com/sites/marketing `
    -Owner joe.healy@contoso.com -NoWait
```

`-NoWait` returns immediately instead of blocking until the operation completes.

### Step 5: Portal alternative (SharePoint admin center)

If PowerShell is unavailable, use the admin center. This is often faster for a single site:

1. Go to the [SharePoint admin center](https://go.microsoft.com/fwlink/?linkid=2185219) and sign in with an account holding admin permissions.
2. Select **Sites** > **Active sites** (or open the **Active sites** page directly).
3. In the left column, select the site.
4. Select **Membership** on the command bar to open the details panel.
5. For a group-connected team site you can add/remove group owners and additional site admins; for other sites you can add/remove site admins and change the primary admin.
6. Add or change roles, then select **Save**.

Note: removing someone as *primary* admin leaves them listed as an *additional* admin — remove them from both if full removal is intended.

## Troubleshooting

**A tenant admin still gets Access Denied.** A SharePoint/Global Administrator role does not grant automatic content access. Use Step 3 to add that admin as a site admin, then reopen the site.

**The account is an external/guest user.** Guest login names use a mangled format. Match it exactly:

```powershell
Set-SPOUser -Site https://contoso.sharepoint.com/sites/benefits `
    -LoginName adelev_fabrikam.onmicrosoft.com#ext#@contoso.onmicrosoft.com `
    -IsSiteCollectionAdmin $true
```

**The site is a OneDrive.** OneDrive is a personal site collection. Add an admin via the admin center: **More features** > **User profiles** > **Open** > **Manage User Profiles**, find the user, right-click > **Manage site collection owners**. Never remove the user as admin of their own OneDrive — it breaks many experiences.

**`Set-SPOUser` fails under a partner/CSP login.** `Set-SPOUser` is not supported with GDAP. Sign in with an in-tenant admin account, or use the admin center portal instead.

**Connected to the wrong URL.** If cmdlets fail with connection errors, confirm you connected to `https://<tenant>-admin.sharepoint.com`, not the site URL.

**Membership changes do not appear immediately.** Permission and role changes can take time to propagate; token/cache refresh (sign out and back in) usually resolves apparent delays.

**A group-connected site has no owners.** Restoring a SharePoint site admin gives site control, but Microsoft 365 group ownership is managed separately. Add group owners in the Microsoft 365 admin center (or the site's **Membership** panel) so Teams, Planner, and the group mailbox regain an owner.

**Bulk assignment across many sites.** Iterate over sites, connected as a tenant admin:

```powershell
$sites = Get-SPOSite -Limit All
foreach ($s in $sites) {
    Set-SPOUser -Site $s.Url -LoginName admin@contoso.com -IsSiteCollectionAdmin $true
}
```

**PnP PowerShell alternative.** If your tooling standardizes on PnP PowerShell (community-supported, no Microsoft SLA), connect to the admin site and manage admins there:

```powershell
Connect-PnPOnline -Url https://contoso-admin.sharepoint.com -Interactive -ClientId <your-client-id>
Set-PnPSiteCollectionAdmin -Owners "opalc@contoso.com" `
    -Url https://contoso.sharepoint.com/sites/marketing
```

## Prevention

- **Assign at least two site admins** on every business-critical site so a single departure never orphans a site.
- **Prefer group/security groups over individuals** as owners where possible, so membership survives personnel changes.
- **Include SharePoint site admin reassignment in the offboarding runbook.** Before disabling a leaver's account, transfer primary ownership with `Set-SPOSite -Owner` and add a replacement admin.
- **Enable site ownership policies** (SharePoint admin center > Policies > Site lifecycle management) to automatically detect and remediate ownerless sites.
- **Do not rely on tenant-admin roles for day-to-day site access.** Grant explicit site admin rights and remove them when the task is done to follow least privilege.
- **Audit periodically.** Script a monthly `Get-SPOUser` / `Get-SPOSite` sweep to flag sites with fewer than two valid, enabled admins.

**Tags:** sharepoint, site-collection-admin, access-denied, set-spouser, set-sposite, powershell, pnp, sharepoint-admin-center, permissions, offboarding
