Title: SPO-018: SharePoint Hub Site Association Problems
Content:
# SharePoint Hub Site Association Problems

**Category:** SharePoint > Hub Sites
**Article Code:** SPO-018
**Tier:** 3
**Audience:** Administrators / Technicians
**Estimated Resolution Time:** 30–90 minutes (plus up to 2–4 hours for tenant propagation)

## Symptoms / When to Use

Use this article when hub site association is failing, missing, or behaving inconsistently. Typical signals:

- A site owner clicks **Settings > Site information > Hub site association**, but the dropdown is empty or the target hub is not listed.
- `Add-SPOHubSiteAssociation` fails with **"File not found"**, **"This site is already a HubSite"**, or **"This site is currently associated with a HubSite."**
- A newly associated site does not show the shared hub navigation bar, hub theme, or roll-up content on the hub home page.
- `Register-SPOHubSite` fails because the target site is already joined to another hub.
- Hub navigation and theme appear on modern pages but are missing on classic pages of a team site.
- In multi-geo tenants, association from another geo location fails when a URL is passed to `-HubSite`.
- A hub-to-hub (parent hub) association was set in the admin center, but cross-hub search results or roll-ups do not appear.
- Changes were made 10 minutes ago and "nothing happened" — the expected propagation delay has not elapsed.
- A site owner cannot associate their site with a hub even though they own the site (permissions/rights scoping issue).

## Background

A SharePoint hub site connects related sites into a "hub family." When a site is **associated** with a hub, it inherits the hub's shared top navigation and theme, its content rolls up into hub web parts configured for "all sites in the hub," and it joins the hub's search scope. Association never changes site permissions — roll-ups are security-trimmed, so users only see content they already have rights to.

Key structural rules that drive most association problems:

- **A site can belong to only one hub at a time.** To move a site to a different hub, the existing association must be removed (or overwritten) first.
- **A site that is already associated with a hub cannot itself be registered as a hub.** You must remove its association before running `Register-SPOHubSite`.
- **Hubs are public by default.** Any user who owns a site can associate it with any hub — *unless* the hub admin has scoped join rights to specific users or security groups via `Grant-SPOHubSiteRights`. If rights are scoped, owners outside that list cannot associate and will not see the hub in the picker.
- **Tenant limit: 2,000 hub sites** per organization. Hub-to-hub associations count against this limit. There is no limit on the number of member sites per hub.
- **Propagation is not instant.** Registering a hub and some association changes can take **up to 2–4 hours** to fully appear across the tenant.
- **Classic team sites** show hub navigation and hub settings only on modern pages (libraries, lists, site contents). This is expected, not a bug.
- **Multi-geo:** when associating across geo locations, you must pass the hub site's **Site ID (GUID)** to `-HubSite`. A URL will fail.

The primary tooling is the **SharePoint Online Management Shell** (module `Microsoft.Online.SharePoint.PowerShell`). PnP PowerShell and CLI for Microsoft 365 provide equivalent commands and are useful fallbacks. All hub cmdlets require SharePoint Administrator (or Global Administrator) privileges.

## Resolution

### Step 1: Connect with an administrator context

Install/update the SharePoint Online Management Shell, then connect. Replace `contoso` with your tenant name.

```powershell
# One-time install (or update) of the module
Install-Module -Name Microsoft.Online.SharePoint.PowerShell -Force

# Connect to the SharePoint admin endpoint
Connect-SPOService -Url https://contoso-admin.sharepoint.com
```

If you prefer PnP PowerShell:

```powershell
Install-Module -Name PnP.PowerShell -Force
Connect-PnPOnline -Url https://contoso.sharepoint.com -Interactive
```

### Step 2: Confirm the current state before changing anything

List every hub in the tenant and confirm the target hub exists and is registered:

```powershell
Get-SPOHubSite
```

Inspect the specific hub, including who has join rights and whether approval is required:

```powershell
Get-SPOHubSite -Identity https://contoso.sharepoint.com/sites/Marketing
```

Check the member site's current association. The `HubSiteId` value tells you whether it is already attached to a hub (a non-zero GUID) or free (`00000000-0000-0000-0000-000000000000`):

```powershell
Get-SPOSite -Identity https://contoso.sharepoint.com/sites/Research -Detailed |
    Select-Object Url, HubSiteId, IsHubSite
```

Capture the hub's Site ID now — you will need the GUID for multi-geo and for GUID-based association:

```powershell
(Get-SPOHubSite -Identity https://contoso.sharepoint.com/sites/Marketing).SiteId
```

### Step 3: Associate the site with the hub

Standard association by URL:

```powershell
Add-SPOHubSiteAssociation -Site https://contoso.sharepoint.com/sites/Research `
    -HubSite https://contoso.sharepoint.com/sites/Marketing
```

If the site is already attached to a **different** hub and you want to move it, `Add-SPOHubSiteAssociation` will re-point it (it overwrites the existing association). If you hit an error, remove the old association first (Step 4) and re-run.

In a **multi-geo** tenant, or any time a URL fails, associate by the hub's Site ID:

```powershell
Set-SPOSite -Identity https://contoso.sharepoint.com/sites/Research `
    -HubSiteId <hub-site-guid>
```

`Set-SPOSite -HubSiteId` is the most reliable programmatic path because it accepts the GUID directly and works cleanly across geos.

PnP equivalent:

```powershell
Add-PnPHubSiteAssociation -Site https://contoso.sharepoint.com/sites/Research `
    -HubSite https://contoso.sharepoint.com/sites/Marketing
```

CLI for Microsoft 365 equivalent:

```bash
m365 spo hubsite connect --url https://contoso.sharepoint.com/sites/Research --hubSiteId <hub-site-guid>
```

### Step 4: Remove or change an existing association

To detach a site from its current hub:

```powershell
Remove-SPOHubSiteAssociation -Site https://contoso.sharepoint.com/sites/Research
```

Detaching by clearing the hub ID (equivalent, GUID-based):

```powershell
Set-SPOSite -Identity https://contoso.sharepoint.com/sites/Research `
    -HubSiteId 00000000-0000-0000-0000-000000000000
```

This is the required first step before you can register a previously associated site as its own hub.

### Step 5: Fix "This site is already a HubSite" when registering

If you need the site to *become* a hub but it is already associated with another hub, remove the association first, then register:

```powershell
Remove-SPOHubSiteAssociation -Site https://contoso.sharepoint.com/sites/Research
Register-SPOHubSite -Site https://contoso.sharepoint.com/sites/Research `
    -Principals owner@contoso.com
```

`-Principals` scopes who may associate their sites with the new hub. Pass one or more users or mail-enabled security groups; leave it broad only if any owner should be allowed to join.

### Step 6: Grant or scope association rights

If site owners report the hub is missing from their association picker, the hub likely has scoped join rights. Grant the `Join` right to the affected users or a mail-enabled security group:

```powershell
Grant-SPOHubSiteRights -Identity https://contoso.sharepoint.com/sites/Marketing `
    -Principals nestorw@contoso.com `
    -Rights Join
```

To revoke access:

```powershell
Revoke-SPOHubSiteRights -Identity https://contoso.sharepoint.com/sites/Marketing `
    -Principals nestorw@contoso.com
```

To make the hub public again, revoke all explicitly-granted principals — a hub with no scoped principals is joinable by any site owner.

### Step 7: Portal path (no PowerShell)

For technicians without shell access, use the SharePoint admin center:

1. Go to **Sites > Active sites** in the SharePoint admin center.
2. Select the member site (select the row, not the URL).
3. On the command bar, select **Hub**. The menu offers **Associate with a hub**, **Change hub association**, or **Unregister as hub site**, depending on the site's current state.
4. Choose the target hub and select **Save**.

End users who own the site can self-associate at **Settings (gear) > Site information > Hub site association**, then pick the hub and select **Save** — provided they have Join rights.

### Step 8: Verify

Re-check the member site and confirm `HubSiteId` now matches the hub's `SiteId`:

```powershell
Get-SPOSite -Identity https://contoso.sharepoint.com/sites/Research -Detailed |
    Select-Object Url, HubSiteId
```

Then load the member site in a browser and confirm the shared hub navigation bar appears at the top and the hub theme applied. Allow for propagation delay before declaring failure.

## Troubleshooting

**"File not found" from `Add-SPOHubSiteAssociation`.** Either the member site URL or the hub URL is wrong, the hub is not actually registered, or the site was recently created/renamed and hasn't propagated. Verify both URLs resolve, confirm the hub appears in `Get-SPOHubSite`, and re-run.

**"This site is currently associated with a HubSite."** You are trying to register an already-associated site as a hub. Run `Remove-SPOHubSiteAssociation` first (Step 5).

**"This site is already a HubSite."** The target of your association command is itself a registered hub. A hub cannot be associated *as a member* of another hub through `Add-SPOHubSiteAssociation` — hub-to-hub linking is a separate parent-hub association (see below).

**Association succeeded but navigation/theme did not appear.** Wait — propagation can take up to 2–4 hours. If it persists beyond that: confirm the page is a **modern** page (classic team-site pages never show hub nav), hard-refresh/clear cache, and verify the hub owner has actually built the hub navigation (associating a site does not auto-add it to the hub's nav menu).

**Owner can't see the hub in the picker.** Join rights are scoped. Run `Get-SPOHubSite -Identity <hub>` to see granted principals, then `Grant-SPOHubSiteRights ... -Rights Join` for the owner or their security group (Step 6). Note the `Rights` parameter only accepts the value `Join`.

**Multi-geo association fails with a URL.** Pass the hub's Site ID (GUID) to `-HubSite`, or use `Set-SPOSite -HubSiteId <guid>`. URLs are not honored for cross-geo hub targets.

**Roll-up web parts on the member site are empty.** Roll-ups are security-trimmed. If the viewer lacks permission to the source content, it will not appear — this is by design, not an association fault. Confirm with an account that has access to the member sites.

**Hub-to-hub (parent hub) search/roll-up not working.** Parent hub associations are configured in the admin center, not via `Add-SPOHubSiteAssociation`: select the hub site > **Hub > Edit hub site settings**, then set the **Parent hub association** field and **Save**. Cross-hub connections work up to three levels of association. Important: web parts configured for "all sites in the hub" continue to show only the original hub's members — parent-hub association expands *search*, not roll-up web parts. Also, navigation links to associated hubs are not added automatically; a hub owner must add them in edit mode.

**Approval-gated joins.** If a hub was configured with `Set-SPOHubSite -RequiresJoinApproval $true`, an association request may be pending approval rather than failing. Check the hub's join-approval flow, or temporarily disable it:

```powershell
Set-SPOHubSite -Identity https://contoso.sharepoint.com/sites/Marketing `
    -RequiresJoinApproval $false
```

**Hitting the 2,000 hub ceiling.** `Register-SPOHubSite` will fail once the tenant reaches 2,000 hubs (hub-to-hub associations count too). Audit with `Get-SPOHubSite | Measure-Object` and unregister unused hubs with `Unregister-SPOHubSite`.

**PnP/CLI fallback.** If the SharePoint Online Management Shell behaves inconsistently, reproduce the operation with `Add-PnPHubSiteAssociation` / `Get-PnPHubSite` or `m365 spo hubsite connect` to isolate whether the issue is client-side or tenant-side.

## Prevention

- **Standardize on GUID-based association** (`Set-SPOSite -HubSiteId`) in automation and scripts. It avoids URL-resolution and multi-geo pitfalls entirely.
- **Document hub Site IDs** in your runbook alongside URLs so cross-geo and scripted associations are copy-paste reliable.
- **Plan the hub topology before building.** Decide member sites vs. hubs vs. parent-hub tiers up front; remember a site can only be in one hub and cannot be both associated and a hub simultaneously.
- **Scope join rights deliberately.** Use `Grant-SPOHubSiteRights` with mail-enabled security groups rather than naming individuals, so access follows group membership and survives staff changes.
- **Prefer modern communication or team-site templates** for member sites. Avoid classic team sites where hub navigation only partially renders.
- **Set expectations on propagation.** Tell requesters that hub changes can take up to 2–4 hours; this prevents duplicate "it's broken" tickets.
- **Monitor the 2,000-hub limit** with a scheduled `Get-SPOHubSite` inventory, and unregister abandoned hubs promptly.
- **Never assume association changes permissions.** Assemble the hub family first, then adjust member-site permissions (or add a shared "read" group) so roll-ups surface as intended.

**Tags:** sharepoint, hub-sites, hub-association, spo, powershell, Add-SPOHubSiteAssociation, Set-SPOSite, HubSiteId, Register-SPOHubSite, Grant-SPOHubSiteRights, multi-geo, hub-navigation, pnp-powershell
Tags: sharepoint, hub-sites, hub-association, spo, powershell, Add-SPOHubSiteAssociation, Set-SPOSite, HubSiteId, Register-SPOHubSite, Grant-SPOHubSiteRights, multi-geo, hub-navigation, pnp-powershell

Title: SPO-019: SharePoint Site Slow Performance
Content:
# SharePoint Site Slow Performance

**Category:** SharePoint > Performance
**Article Code:** SPO-019
**Tier:** 2
**Audience:** Administrators / Technicians
**Estimated Resolution Time:** 45–120 minutes (longer if remediating large lists or page redesign)

Slow SharePoint Online sites are almost always the sum of several small problems — oversized images, too many web parts, structural navigation, un-indexed large lists, or CDN not being used — rather than a single fault. This article gives a repeatable, evidence-based workflow for diagnosing the cause and remediating both the tenant/admin layer and the individual page/list layer.

## Symptoms / When to Use

- A modern site or communication site page takes several seconds (or longer) to render, while other sites in the same tenant load quickly.
- Users report the home page or a specific hub page is "always spinning."
- A list or library throws **"The number of items in this list exceeds the list view threshold, which is 5000 items."**
- Sorting or filtering a column fails with **"Cannot show the value of the filter."**
- Page load is slow only on first (cold) load and fast on refresh — points to caching/CDN.
- Slowness correlates with a specific web part (news, highlighted content, embedded iframe) or with structural (mega-menu) navigation.
- Slowness is isolated to one geographic office, or only over VPN.

## Background

Perceived performance in modern SharePoint is measured as **End User Perceived Latency (EUPL)** — how fast the page renders in the browser. Modern pages do most rendering client-side, so the biggest levers are payload size and the number of network calls a page makes.

Microsoft publishes concrete per-page limits for modern portal/communication sites:

- **20 or fewer web parts** per page (total, OOTB + custom).
- **4 or fewer dynamic web parts** per page (web parts that query SharePoint each load, e.g. News).
- **Images 300 KB or smaller**, ideally served from a CDN.
- **Fewer than 100 items** in site navigation.
- **Fewer than 5,000 pages/news items** per site.

For lists and libraries, the **List View Threshold is 5,000 items** — the maximum number of items a single database operation (a view, sort, or filter) can process during business hours. This is a hard, non-configurable limit in SharePoint Online. Views that scan more than 5,000 items are throttled. The limit to add or remove a column index is 20,000 items, so index columns *before* a list grows past that point.

The Office 365 CDN offloads static assets (JS, CSS, fonts, images) to edge servers close to the user, cutting cold-load time. The SharePoint Framework `*/CLIENTSIDEASSETS` origin is required for SPFx solutions to load correctly.

## Resolution

### Step 1: Reproduce and baseline with the Page Diagnostics for SharePoint tool

Install the **Page Diagnostics for SharePoint** browser extension (Microsoft Edge or Chrome). It analyzes modern portal and classic publishing pages against Microsoft's baseline rules. It does **not** work on system pages (e.g. `allitems.aspx`) or App pages — run it on the actual site/portal page.

1. Open the slow page, then open the extension and select **Start**.
2. Let the page fully load, then select **Stop** (the tool waits for delayed loading by design).
3. Review the **Diagnostic tests** tab. Results are bucketed:
   - **Attention required** (red): outside baseline, actively hurting performance.
   - **Improvement opportunities** (yellow): may be contributing.
   - **No action required** (green): within baseline.
4. Record the header metrics for comparison after each change:
   - **SPRequestDuration** — server-side processing time (high values often mean structural navigation, many API calls, or large images).
   - **SPIISLatency** — time before SharePoint begins serving the page.
   - **Page load time** — total request-to-render time.
5. For a true cold-load number, clear the browser cache (or use a private/InPrivate window with the extension allowed) before clicking **Start**. Compare against a warm reload to see what is being cached.

To hand off to Microsoft Support, enable HAR export **before** clicking Start, then use the **Network Trace** tab → **Export to HAR**. Note the **Correlation ID** shown in the tool. HAR files contain URLs (potential PII) — follow your data-handling policy before sharing.

### Step 2: Remediate the page (image, web part, and navigation issues)

Work the red items first, re-running the tool after each change (test 2–3 times and average — load times vary with network conditions).

- **Large images detected (>300 KB):** Re-compress and resize images for web before upload. Modern pages auto-generate renditions, but very large source images degrade rendering.
- **Too many web parts / dynamic web parts:** Reduce to ≤20 total and ≤4 dynamic. Split dense pages into multiple pages.
- **Too many search requests (>3 per page):** Consolidate Highlighted Content / Search web parts and rely on their caching.
- **Structural (mega-menu) navigation:** Structural navigation forces per-request enumeration. Where the page is slow and menus are large, prefer simpler navigation and keep site navigation under 100 items.

### Step 3: Fix the large-list throttling (List View Threshold)

If the slowness is a list/library throwing the 5,000-item error or failing to sort/filter:

1. Open the list → **Settings gear** → **List settings** → **Indexed columns**, and add an index on the column(s) you filter or sort by. (Add indexes while the list is under 20,000 items.)
2. Edit the default view (or create a new one) so it returns **fewer than 5,000 items** using a filter on an **indexed** column. For example, filter on a `Status` or `Modified` indexed column.
3. Use folders or metadata to partition large libraries so no single view scans more than 5,000 items.
4. Reduce the **item limit per page** in the view settings so paging stays under the threshold.

There is no PowerShell cmdlet in SharePoint Online to raise the 5,000 threshold — it is fixed. Remediation is always through indexing, filtered views, and partitioning.

### Step 4: Confirm the Office 365 CDN is enabled

A missing or disabled CDN is a common cause of slow cold loads and broken SPFx assets. Connect with the SharePoint Online Management Shell (`Microsoft.Online.SharePoint.PowerShell` module, tenant admin required):

```powershell
Connect-SPOService -Url https://<tenant>-admin.sharepoint.com
```

Check current CDN state:

```powershell
Get-SPOTenantCdnEnabled -CdnType Public
Get-SPOTenantCdnEnabled -CdnType Private
Get-SPOTenantCdnOrigins -CdnType Public
Get-SPOTenantCdnPolicies -CdnType Public
```

If Public CDN is disabled, enable it (default origins are provisioned automatically):

```powershell
Set-SPOTenantCdnEnabled -CdnType Public -Enable $true
```

Repeat for Private CDN if your org hosts user-content images there:

```powershell
Set-SPOTenantCdnEnabled -CdnType Private -Enable $true
```

Verify the SPFx origin exists — if it is missing, SPFx web parts fail silently:

```powershell
Get-SPOTenantCdnOrigins -CdnType Public
```

If `*/CLIENTSIDEASSETS` is not listed, add it:

```powershell
Add-SPOTenantCdnOrigin -CdnType Public -OriginUrl */CLIENTSIDEASSETS
```

CDN propagation can take up to 15 minutes for new origins. Re-run the Page Diagnostics tool afterward — the CDN test should move to green.

### Step 5: Re-baseline and confirm improvement

Re-run the Page Diagnostics tool on the same page. Compare **Page load time**, **SPRequestDuration**, and the count of red/yellow items against the Step 1 baseline. Confirm with the reporting user from a representative client and network before closing.

## Troubleshooting

- **CDN cmdlets not recognized:** You are likely in the wrong module. `*-SPOTenantCdn*` cmdlets require the SharePoint Online Management Shell (`Microsoft.Online.SharePoint.PowerShell`), not the PnP or Graph modules. Install/import it, then `Connect-SPOService` before running any cmdlet.

- **CLI for Microsoft 365 alternative:** If your team uses the cross-platform CLI instead of PowerShell:

  ```bash
  m365 spo cdn get --type Public
  m365 spo cdn set --type Public --enabled true
  m365 spo cdn origin list
  ```

  Note: the CLI is community-supported (PnP) with no Microsoft SLA.

- **Page Diagnostics tool shows an error / won't run:** It only analyzes SharePoint in Microsoft 365 site pages. It errors on system pages, App pages, and non-SharePoint pages. Confirm you are on a modern site page or classic publishing page, and update the extension to the latest version (2.0.0+ supports modern pages).

- **CDN test fails on a classic team site:** Classic team sites without the publishing feature cannot use the CDN, so that single test failure is expected and can be ignored. Do **not** enable the publishing feature solely for CDN — it increases page load time. All other tests still apply.

- **Slow only for one office or over VPN:** This is a network path issue, not a SharePoint page issue. Confirm the client egresses to the nearest Microsoft front door (avoid backhauling M365 traffic through a central proxy/VPN). Compare **Page load time** (network-affected) against **SPRequestDuration** (server-side) — if server time is low but page time is high, the bottleneck is the network.

- **Cold slow / warm fast:** Caching or CDN gap. Verify the CDN is enabled (Step 4) and that assets are served from the CDN in the Network Trace tab (items >1000 ms show red).

- **Sort/filter still fails after indexing:** The index must exist on the exact column being filtered, and the resulting view must return under 5,000 items. Adding an index requires the list be under 20,000 items; if larger, filter to a smaller working set first or partition the data.

## Prevention

- Set a standard: **≤20 web parts and ≤4 dynamic web parts per page**, images **≤300 KB**, navigation **<100 items**. Review new portal pages with the Page Diagnostics tool before publishing.
- **Index list columns early** (while lists are under 20,000 items) on any column used for filtering, sorting, or grouping. Design views to stay under 5,000 items from day one.
- Keep the **Office 365 CDN enabled** tenant-wide and confirm the `*/CLIENTSIDEASSETS` origin after any SPFx work.
- Optimize and compress images before upload; host shared static assets (logos, CSS, JS) on the CDN.
- Prefer simple/hub navigation over large structural mega-menus on high-traffic pages.
- Keep sites under **5,000 pages/news items** and archive stale content.
- Ensure clients use local internet egress to Microsoft 365 rather than routing M365 traffic through centralized VPN/proxy.

Title: TMS-062: Microsoft Teams Chat History Missing or Not Loading
Content:
# Microsoft Teams Chat History Missing or Not Loading

**Category:** Teams > Messaging
**Article Code:** TMS-062
**Tier:** 1
**Audience:** Technicians / End Users
**Estimated Resolution Time:** 10–30 minutes

## Symptoms / When to Use

Use this article when a user reports that Teams chat history is missing, blank, or won't load:

- A one-on-one or group chat shows no prior messages, or "Couldn't load messages."
- History disappears after a client update, sign-out, or device change.
- Messages appear on mobile but not desktop (or vice versa).
- Search finds a message but clicking it opens an empty conversation.

## Background

Teams stores chat messages in a cloud substrate (Exchange/SharePoint-backed compliance storage), so history is **not** lost just because a client is misbehaving — it is almost always a client cache, sync, or policy issue, not data loss. The most common causes are a corrupt local cache, a stale authentication token, a retention policy that legitimately removed old messages, or the user viewing a different account/tenant than expected.

## Resolution

### Step 1: Confirm the account and network

- Verify the user is signed into the **correct tenant/account** (top-right profile). Guest/multi-tenant users often land in the wrong context.
- Confirm connectivity; a degraded connection shows partial history. Check https://portal.office.com/servicestatus for a Teams incident.

### Step 2: Force a client refresh

- Press **Ctrl+R** (or right-click the Teams tray icon → Quit, then relaunch).
- New Teams: Settings → **General** and confirm the app is up to date.

### Step 3: Clear the Teams cache (resolves most cases)

**New Teams (Windows):**
```powershell
# Quit Teams first, then clear cached data
Get-Process ms-teams -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue | Stop-Process -Force
Remove-Item "$env:LOCALAPPDATA\Packages\MSTeams_8wekyb3d8bbwe\LocalCache\*" -Recurse -Force -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue
```

**Classic Teams (Windows):**
```powershell
Get-Process Teams -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue | Stop-Process -Force
Remove-Item "$env:APPDATA\Microsoft\Teams\*" -Recurse -Force -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue
```

**macOS (classic):** quit Teams, then remove `~/Library/Application Support/Microsoft/Teams`.

Relaunch and sign in; history re-syncs from the cloud (may take a minute).

### Step 4: Verify on a second client

Sign in to https://teams.microsoft.com in a browser. If history **is** present in the web client, the problem is confirmed local (cache), and Step 3 resolves it. If history is **missing everywhere**, proceed to Step 5.

### Step 5: Check retention/compliance policy (admin)

If messages are genuinely gone across all clients, a retention policy may have deleted them by design.
```powershell
Connect-IPPSSession
Get-RetentionCompliancePolicy | Where-Object {$_.TeamsChatLocation -ne $null} |
  Select Name, Enabled, TeamsChatLocation
Get-RetentionComplianceRule | Select Name, RetentionDuration, RetentionComplianceAction
```
A rule with a short `RetentionDuration` and a Delete action explains missing older messages. Adjust the policy if the retention window is shorter than the business requires.

## Troubleshooting

- **Only group chat affected:** the user may have been removed and re-added; history before re-add can be hidden for that member.
- **Search opens empty chat:** almost always cache — clear per Step 3.
- **Corporate device with app management:** an Intune app-config or conditional access token expiry can block sync; re-authenticate.

## Prevention

- Keep Teams auto-updating; most sync bugs are fixed in newer builds.
- Set Teams chat retention deliberately (compliance center) and document the window so "missing" old chats are understood as policy, not failure.
- Encourage users to sign out cleanly before switching devices.

**Tags:** teams, chat, history, cache, retention, sync, troubleshoot

Title: TMS-063: Teams Meeting Recording Missing or Failed
Content:
# Teams Meeting Recording Missing or Failed

**Category:** Teams > Meetings
**Article Code:** TMS-063
**Tier:** 2
**Audience:** Administrators / Technicians
**Estimated Resolution Time:** 20–60 minutes (longer if a recording must be recovered from recycle bin or async media storage)

## Symptoms / When to Use

- A user reports the **Record** button is missing or greyed out (a lock icon may appear on it) during a meeting.
- Recording started successfully but the finished file never appeared in the meeting chat, the **Recordings and Transcripts** tab, or the organizer's OneDrive.
- The recap page shows: *"The recording is currently unavailable. Please check with organizer whether it's still being uploaded, has expired, or has been deleted."*
- Users receive an upload/error banner at the end of a recorded meeting.
- Channel meeting recordings can't be found by attendees, or can be viewed but not downloaded.
- Webinar or town hall recordings fail to publish or don't appear in the event's VOD.

## Background

Teams uses **convenience recording**: the capture happens in Microsoft 365 and the finished `.mp4` is uploaded to the organizer's storage, not the user's local machine. Storage location depends on meeting type:

- **Non-channel (private) meetings** → the recording initiator's / organizer's **OneDrive** under `/My files/Recordings`.
- **Channel meetings** → the **SharePoint** site backing the channel, in the **Recordings** folder under **Documents**.

Recording therefore requires three conditions to all be true: the user is licensed and policy-enabled to record; **both** the organizer and the recording initiator have recording permission; and the destination OneDrive/SharePoint is provisioned with available quota. Failures cluster into three buckets — the **Record button never appears** (license/policy), the **upload fails** (storage/quota), or the file **existed but is gone** (expiration/deletion).

If upload fails because the organizer, co-organizers, and initiator lack a OneDrive account or the quota is full, Teams temporarily writes the file to **async media storage**. No automatic retry occurs. The organizer has **21 days** to download it before it is permanently deleted. Recordings also expire on a schedule (default **120 days**), after which they move to the recycle bin and are eventually purged.

## Resolution

### Step 1: Confirm the meeting type and expected location

Ask the user whether this was a private meeting or a channel meeting, then check the correct location directly.

- Non-channel: `<organizer's OneDrive>/My files/Recordings`
- Channel: in Teams, open the channel > **Files** > **Recordings** > **Open in SharePoint**, or browse the SharePoint site `Documents/<Channel name>/Recordings`.

In high-volume chats the recording link sometimes fails to render. Have the user scroll to the top of the chat and back down to force a refresh before assuming the file is missing.

### Step 2: Connect to Teams PowerShell

Most policy checks require the MicrosoftTeams module.

```powershell
Connect-MicrosoftTeams
```

### Step 3: Verify the user's recording policy

The Record button is controlled by `AllowCloudRecording` on the assigned Teams meeting policy. Identify the user's effective policy and confirm the flag is `True`.

```powershell
# Show which meeting policy is assigned to the user
Get-CsUserPolicyAssignment -Identity "user@contoso.com" -PolicyType TeamsMeetingPolicy

# Inspect the recording-related settings on that policy (Global shown as example)
Get-CsTeamsMeetingPolicy -Identity Global |
    Select-Object Identity, AllowCloudRecording, AllowLocalRecording, ChannelRecordingDownload, NewMeetingRecordingExpirationDays
```

If `AllowCloudRecording` is `False`, enable it on the appropriate policy:

```powershell
# Org-wide default
Set-CsTeamsMeetingPolicy -Identity Global -AllowCloudRecording $true

# Or a custom policy
Set-CsTeamsMeetingPolicy -Identity "Your Policy Name" -AllowCloudRecording $true
```

Portal equivalent: **Teams admin center** > **Meetings** > **Meeting policies** > select the policy > toggle **Meeting recording** **On** > **Save**.

Remember that **both** the organizer and the recording initiator need recording permission. If a presenter can't record, check the organizer's policy too, not just the presenter's.

### Step 4: Assign a corrected policy if needed

If the user is on the wrong policy, grant the correct one:

```powershell
Grant-CsTeamsMeetingPolicy -Identity "user@contoso.com" -PolicyName "Your Policy Name"
```

Policy changes can take time to propagate to clients. Have the user sign out and back in, or leave and rejoin the meeting.

### Step 5: Confirm OneDrive/SharePoint storage is provisioned and has quota

An upload with no destination or a full quota is the most common cause of a "recorded but missing" file. Verify the organizer has OneDrive provisioned and space available.

```powershell
# Requires the Microsoft.Online.SharePoint.PowerShell module
Connect-SPOService -Url "https://contoso-admin.sharepoint.com"

# Check the user's OneDrive usage and quota (URL uses _ for . and @)
Get-SPOSite -Identity "https://contoso-my.sharepoint.com/personal/user_contoso_com" |
    Select-Object Url, StorageQuota, StorageUsageCurrent
```

Budget roughly **400 MB per hour** of recording. If the quota is near full, free space or raise the limit, then have the organizer re-attempt an upload from async media storage (see Step 6) within the 21-day window.

### Step 6: Run the built-in diagnostics

Microsoft 365 admins can run targeted diagnostics from the admin center (not available for GCC High, 21Vianet, or Germany):

- **Missing Recording Diagnostic** — in the Microsoft 365 admin center **Need Help?** search box, run the diagnostic, then enter the **meeting URL** (from the invite) and the **date recorded**. It confirms whether the recording completed and uploaded.
- **Meeting Recording Support Diagnostic** — validates the user's license and meeting policy prerequisites. Search **Diag: Teams 1:1 Call Recording** for call-recording issues specifically.
- **Teams Meeting Recording Test** (`https://aka.ms/MRCA-TMR`) — user-level check that the account meets all requirements to record.

## Troubleshooting

**Record button still missing after enabling the policy.** Confirm the client is on the latest Teams update, then have the user rejoin or try the Teams web client. Verify this is a *meeting*, not a 1:1 call — call recording is governed separately by `AllowCloudRecordingForCalls` on the Teams **calling** policy, not `AllowCloudRecording`. Hover the lock icon on the button; the tooltip states the specific blocking reason.

**Recording exists but attendees can't download it (channel meetings).** This is expected when `ChannelRecordingDownload` is set to `Block` — files land in a `Recordings\View only` folder where members can view but not download. Confirm and change if unintended:

```powershell
Get-CsTeamsMeetingPolicy -Identity Global | Select-Object ChannelRecordingDownload
Set-CsTeamsMeetingPolicy -Identity Global -ChannelRecordingDownload Allow
```

**Recording expired / recap says "unavailable."** Recordings move to the **recycle bin** of their storage location at expiration. Recover from the OneDrive (private meetings) or SharePoint site (channel meetings) recycle bin — first-stage, then site-collection second-stage. Recovery is time-sensitive; once purged from the recycle bin, files **cannot** be recovered. Note that expiration is set at creation time; changing `NewMeetingRecordingExpirationDays` does not affect existing files.

**Webinar or town hall recording missing.** These are governed by the **events** policy, not the meeting policy, and publish through VOD. Verify:

```powershell
Set-CsTeamsEventsPolicy -Identity <policy name> -RecordingForWebinar Enabled
Set-CsTeamsEventsPolicy -Identity <policy name> -RecordingForTownhall Enabled
```

Town hall and webinar VOD recordings are stored in SharePoint Embedded containers and can only be located/deleted via **Teams admin center** > **Analytics and reports** > **Usage reports** (Town hall / Webinar usage reports). Only the event organizer manages them from their calendar.

**Shared mailbox meetings.** A meeting organized by a shared mailbox without a Teams license follows the **Global** policy. If Global has `AllowCloudRecording $false`, those meetings can't be recorded. Assign a Teams license to the shared mailbox before applying a custom policy.

**Copilot dependency.** If an organizer turns off Microsoft 365 Copilot in their meeting options, recording and transcription are disabled together. Check the organizer's meeting options if recording silently fails to start.

## Prevention

- Keep `AllowCloudRecording $true` on the policies that need it, and audit policy assignments periodically with `Get-CsUserPolicyAssignment`.
- Proactively monitor OneDrive/SharePoint quota for heavy recorders; alert well before the limit given the ~400 MB/hour footprint.
- Set an intentional expiration policy that matches retention requirements. Use `-NewMeetingRecordingExpirationDays -1` (PowerShell only) for "never expire" where compliance requires it; for true compliance retention, apply **Microsoft Purview** retention labels rather than relying on the expiration feature.
- Educate users that recordings save to the cloud (OneDrive/SharePoint), not their PC, and that they have only **21 days** to rescue a recording from async media storage after a failed upload.
- Standardize on the latest Teams client via update management to avoid client-side record-button regressions.

**Tags:** teams, meeting recording, cloud recording, AllowCloudRecording, onedrive, sharepoint, ChannelRecordingDownload, recording expiration, recording missing, powershell, teams admin center, webinar, town hall, diagnostics

Title: TMS-068: Teams Channel Moderation and Posting Permissions
Content:
# Teams Channel Moderation and Posting Permissions

**Category:** Teams > Channels
**Article Code:** TMS-068
**Tier:** 2
**Audience:** Administrators / Technicians (with team owner / end-user guidance)
**Estimated Resolution Time:** 15–30 minutes per channel; 30–60 minutes for a scripted rollout across multiple teams

## Symptoms / When to Use

- A team owner wants an **announcements-only** channel where members can read but not start new posts.
- Members are replying to broadcast posts that should be read-only (e.g., leadership updates, incident notifications).
- Guests are posting in a channel that should be restricted to internal staff.
- A connector or bot must be the only source of new posts (e.g., a live-site/monitoring channel), and human members should not start threads.
- A class or training team needs only instructors/moderators to open new discussions.
- You need to standardize posting permissions across many channels/teams programmatically rather than clicking through each one.
- A user reports "I can't start a new conversation in this channel" and you need to confirm whether moderation is the cause.

## Background

By default, standard (non-private) channels are **unmoderated**: any team member can start posts, reply, and react. Team owners can enable moderation to control who starts new posts and whether members may reply.

Two independent controls exist:

1. **Who can start a new post** — mapped to the Graph property `userNewMessageRestriction`, with values `everyone`, `everyoneExceptGuests`, or `moderators`.
2. **Reply and submission permissions** — mapped to `replyRestriction` (`everyone` or `authorAndModerators`), plus `allowNewMessageFromBots` and `allowNewMessageFromConnectors`.

When moderation is turned **On**, only moderators can start new posts. **Team owners are moderators by default and cannot be removed.** Owners can promote members to moderator; moderators can add or remove other moderators within that channel.

Important scope limits:

- Moderation applies to **standard channels only**. It is **not available for the General channel or private channels**.
- Configuration is done from the **Teams desktop or web client** (Manage channel), or via **Microsoft Graph / Graph PowerShell**.
- The `MicrosoftTeams` PowerShell module's `Set-TeamChannel` cmdlet only updates a channel's display name and description — it does **not** expose moderation settings. Use the Graph route below for scripting.

## Resolution

### Step 1: Exclude guests without full moderation (owner, GUI)

This is the lightest control and does not require turning moderation on.

1. Open the channel in Teams (desktop or web).
2. Select **More options (…)** next to the channel name > **Manage channel**.
3. Under **Who can start a new post?**, select **Everyone except guests can start a new post**.

Members and owners can still post; guests are blocked from starting new posts.

### Step 2: Turn on moderation for an announcements-style channel (owner, GUI)

1. In the channel, select **More options (…)** > **Manage channel**.
2. Under **Channel moderation**, select **On**. Only moderators can now start new posts.
3. Under **Who are the moderators?**, select **Manage**, then add or remove team members as moderators. Owners are always moderators.
4. Under **Team member permissions**, set the checkboxes for what non-moderators may do:
   - Allow members to **reply** to channel messages (clear this for a true read-only announcements channel).
   - Allow members to **pin** channel messages.
   - Allow **bots** to submit channel messages.
   - Allow **connectors** to submit channel messages.

### Step 3: Configure moderation at scale with Graph PowerShell

For bulk or repeatable configuration, use the **Microsoft.Graph.Beta.Teams** module. The moderation properties are exposed by `Update-MgBetaTeamChannel` through the `moderationSettings` object.

Install and connect with a delegated scope that can write channel settings:

```powershell
Install-Module Microsoft.Graph.Beta.Teams -Scope CurrentUser

Connect-MgGraph -Scopes "ChannelSettings.ReadWrite.All"
```

Resolve the team (group) ID and channel ID you want to modify:

```powershell
# Find the team by display name
$team = Get-MgGroup -Filter "displayName eq 'Company Announcements'"
$teamId = $team.Id

# List channels to grab the target channel's Id
Get-MgTeamChannel -TeamId $teamId | Select-Object DisplayName, Id
$channelId = (Get-MgTeamChannel -TeamId $teamId `
    -Filter "displayName eq 'Announcements'").Id
```

Apply moderation so only moderators post, members may still reply, and connectors/bots are allowed:

```powershell
Import-Module Microsoft.Graph.Beta.Teams

$params = @{
    moderationSettings = @{
        userNewMessageRestriction     = "moderators"
        replyRestriction              = "everyone"
        allowNewMessageFromBots       = $true
        allowNewMessageFromConnectors = $true
    }
}

Update-MgBetaTeamChannel -TeamId $teamId -ChannelId $channelId `
    -BodyParameter $params
```

For a strict read-only announcements channel (no member replies), set `replyRestriction` to `authorAndModerators`:

```powershell
$params = @{
    moderationSettings = @{
        userNewMessageRestriction     = "moderators"
        replyRestriction              = "authorAndModerators"
        allowNewMessageFromBots       = $false
        allowNewMessageFromConnectors = $false
    }
}

Update-MgBetaTeamChannel -TeamId $teamId -ChannelId $channelId `
    -BodyParameter $params
```

To exclude guests only (moderation effectively off, but guests blocked from new posts):

```powershell
$params = @{
    moderationSettings = @{
        userNewMessageRestriction = "everyoneExceptGuests"
        replyRestriction          = "everyone"
    }
}

Update-MgBetaTeamChannel -TeamId $teamId -ChannelId $channelId `
    -BodyParameter $params
```

To turn moderation **off** and restore default open posting, set `userNewMessageRestriction` back to `everyone`.

### Step 4: Provision a new channel with moderation baked in

When creating channels programmatically, set moderation at creation time with `New-MgBetaTeamChannel`:

```powershell
$params = @{
    displayName               = "Announcements"
    description               = "Read-only company announcements"
    membershipType            = "standard"
    moderationSettings = @{
        userNewMessageRestriction     = "moderators"
        replyRestriction              = "authorAndModerators"
        allowNewMessageFromBots       = $true
        allowNewMessageFromConnectors = $true
    }
}

New-MgBetaTeamChannel -TeamId $teamId -BodyParameter $params
```

### Step 5: Verify the applied settings

Confirm the change either in the client (**Manage channel** should now reflect the new state) or by reading the channel back through Graph and inspecting the moderation object.

```powershell
$channel = Get-MgBetaTeamChannel -TeamId $teamId -ChannelId $channelId
$channel.ModerationSettings | Format-List
```

## Troubleshooting

- **No "Channel moderation" option appears.** Confirm the channel is a **standard** channel. Moderation controls are hidden for the **General** channel and **private/shared** channels by design.
- **"Manage channel" is not visible or is read-only.** Only **team owners** (or existing channel moderators) can change moderation. Members see a read-only view. Verify the user's team role.
- **PowerShell error: parameter `-ModerationSettings` / property not recognized.** You are likely using the wrong module. Moderation properties are documented on the **beta** cmdlets (`Update-MgBetaTeamChannel`, `New-MgBetaTeamChannel`) in **Microsoft.Graph.Beta.Teams**. The `MicrosoftTeams` module's `Set-TeamChannel` does not support moderation — it only renames a channel or sets its description.
- **`Connect-MgGraph` succeeds but the update returns 403 / Forbidden.** The signed-in account needs `ChannelSettings.ReadWrite.All` (delegated) plus effective rights over the team (team owner). For app-only automation, grant `ChannelSettings.ReadWrite.Group` or `ChannelSettings.ReadWrite.All` and admin-consent it.
- **Changes don't appear immediately in the client.** Teams caches channel state. Have the user refresh, or fully restart the client. Propagation can lag a few minutes.
- **Guests can still post after selecting "Everyone except guests."** Confirm the user is actually a guest (external) identity and not a member. Also confirm tenant-level guest access is enabled/consistent; a member account added via B2B may still resolve as a member.
- **Members can't reply after moderation is on.** That is expected when `replyRestriction = authorAndModerators` (or the "Allow members to reply" checkbox is cleared). Re-enable replies if the intent was announcements with discussion.

## Prevention

- **Standardize with templates.** Define a small set of channel profiles (open, guests-excluded, announcements-only, connector-driven) and apply them with the Step 3 scripts so behavior is consistent across teams.
- **Assign at least two moderators** per moderated channel. Owners are moderators by default, but naming explicit backups prevents a single point of failure if an owner leaves.
- **Document the intent** in the channel description (e.g., "Announcements — replies disabled") so members understand why they can't post.
- **Review periodically.** Include moderated channels in quarterly Teams governance reviews to confirm the moderator list and restrictions still match business need.
- **Prefer beta cmdlets deliberately.** Moderation properties currently live in the Microsoft Graph beta surface; pin the `Microsoft.Graph.Beta.Teams` module version in your automation and retest after upgrades, since beta APIs can change.
- **Test on a pilot team first** before a tenant-wide rollout, and validate both the owner GUI view and the end-user experience.

Title: TMS-069: Teams App Installation Blocked or Failing
Content:
# Teams App Installation Blocked or Failing

**Category:** Teams > Apps
**Article Code:** TMS-069
**Tier:** 2
**Audience:** Administrators / Technicians
**Estimated Resolution Time:** 15–45 minutes (plus up to 24 hours for tenant-side propagation)

## Symptoms / When to Use

Use this article when a user cannot add, install, or open a Microsoft Teams app (Microsoft, third-party, or line-of-business/custom), and one or more of the following is observed:

- The app is missing from the Teams app store, or the **Add** button is greyed out or absent.
- User sees "This app has been blocked by your IT admin," "App isn't available," or "You don't have permission to add this app."
- A previously working app disappears from a user's app bar or stops loading.
- Admin has uploaded a custom (LOB) app but users cannot find or install it.
- The **Upload a custom app** / **Upload an app to your org's app catalog** option is missing for developers.
- The app is marked **Blocked by publisher** or **Blocked** on the **Manage apps** page.
- Users are submitting app requests that never reach an approver, or requests appear but the app stays unavailable after approval.

## Background

App availability in Teams is governed by several independent gates. An app is only installable when **every** applicable gate allows it; **any one** blocking gate prevents installation. The gates are:

1. **Org-wide app settings** (on the **Manage apps** page) — a tenant-level switch for Microsoft apps, third-party apps, and custom apps.
2. **App status** — each app is individually **Allowed** or **Blocked** at the org level.
3. **User-level access** — controlled by either **App permission policies** (legacy) or **App centric management / unified app management** (current). These decide which users may use a given app.
4. **App setup policies** — govern whether a user can **upload custom apps** (sideload) and which apps are pinned/pre-installed.
5. **Team-level setting** — **Allow members to upload custom apps**, set per team by the team owner.

Microsoft is migrating tenants from **App permission policies** to **App centric management (ACM)** (also referenced as unified app management, UAM). On migrated tenants the permission-policy page is read-only and per-user access is defined per app instead. Government clouds (GCC, GCCH, DoD) block all third-party apps by default. Custom LOB apps have their own org-wide sideloading toggle that is separate from the third-party control.

Microsoft explicitly recommends that all app permission and setup **policy creation/modification** be performed in the Teams admin center (TAC), not PowerShell — the `New-`/`Set-CsTeamsAppPermissionPolicy` cmdlets may report success but do not apply to the tenant. PowerShell is supported for **viewing** policies and **assigning** existing policies to users.

## Resolution

Work the gates top-down. You need **Teams Administrator** (or higher) to change these settings.

### Step 1: Confirm the app's org-level status

1. Sign in to the Microsoft Teams admin center: `https://admin.teams.microsoft.com`
2. Go to **Teams apps** > **Manage apps**.
3. Search for the app and check the **Status** column.
4. If it shows **Blocked**, select the app, then choose **Allow** (or open the app details page and set the **Status** toggle to **Allowed**).
5. If it shows **Blocked by publisher**, the developer requires admin configuration first — follow the publisher's setup guidance before allowing it.

### Step 2: Check org-wide app settings

1. On the **Manage apps** page, select **Actions** > **Org-wide app settings**.
2. Confirm the relevant category is enabled:
   - **Microsoft apps** — allow Microsoft-published apps.
   - **Third-party apps** — must be **On** for any non-Microsoft store app (off by default in GCC/GCCH/DoD).
   - **Custom apps** — the **Let users interact with custom apps in preview** / sideloaded-apps toggle must be **On** for LOB apps.
3. Save. Changes can take a few hours to propagate.

### Step 3: Grant user-level access

**If your tenant uses App centric management (recommended / current):**

1. Open the app's details page on the **Manage apps** page.
2. On the **Users and groups** (availability) setting, choose **Everyone**, or **Specific users or groups** and add the affected users/groups, then **Save**.
3. **No one** is equivalent to a blocked app — change it if access is needed.

**If your tenant still uses App permission policies (legacy):**

1. Go to **Teams apps** > **Permission policies**.
2. Edit the **Global (Org-wide default)** policy or a custom policy so the app is allowed, then **Save**. Create/edit the policy here in TAC — not in PowerShell.
3. Assign a custom policy to a user with PowerShell if needed:

```powershell
Connect-MicrosoftTeams
Grant-CsTeamsAppPermissionPolicy -Identity "user@contoso.com" -PolicyName "HR App Access"
```

To inspect which policy a user has:

```powershell
Get-CsOnlineUser -Identity "user@contoso.com" | Select-Object DisplayName, TeamsAppPermissionPolicy
```

### Step 4: Enable custom app upload (sideloading), if applicable

For developers/testers who need to upload a custom app package:

1. Go to **Teams apps** > **Setup policies** > **Global (Org-wide default)** (or a custom policy).
2. Set **Upload custom apps** to **On** and **Save**.
3. Assign the setup policy to the target users:

```powershell
Connect-MicrosoftTeams
Grant-CsTeamsAppSetupPolicy -Identity "dev@contoso.com" -PolicyName "Developers"
```

You can also toggle the org-wide custom-apps interaction switch via PowerShell (this is the **Custom apps** control in Org-wide app settings):

```powershell
Set-CsTeamsSettingsCustomApp -IsSideloadedAppsInteractionEnabled $true
```

Setup-policy propagation and custom app upload activation can take up to 24 hours.

### Step 5: Verify and test

1. Have the user fully restart Teams (sign out, or clear cache) after propagation.
2. Confirm the app now shows **Add** in the store and installs.
3. For pre-installed/pinned apps, confirm the app appears on the app bar per the assigned setup policy.

## Troubleshooting

If the app is still blocked after the steps above, check these variations:

- **Two admin centers out of sync (unmigrated tenants):** Until UAM migration completes, allow/block status must match in both the Teams admin center and the **Integrated apps** page of the Microsoft 365 admin center (`https://admin.microsoft.com` > **Settings** > **Integrated apps**). A block in either place wins.
- **Propagation delay:** Most changes take a few hours; custom app upload can take up to 24 hours. Do not assume failure immediately after a change.
- **Team-level override:** For an app being added inside a specific team, the team owner may have cleared **Allow members to upload custom apps** under **Manage team** > **Settings** > **Member permissions**. This blocks upload even when the setup policy allows it.
- **Policy precedence:** A user can receive policies via direct assignment and group assignment. Direct (user-level) assignment wins; otherwise the group assignment with the highest rank (lowest number) applies. Confirm the effective policy with `Get-CsOnlineUser`.
- **ACM migration state:** If the **Permission policies** page displays a banner saying policies no longer apply, the tenant is on ACM — manage access per app (Step 3, first option) rather than editing policies.
- **Government cloud:** In GCC/GCCH/DoD, third-party apps are off by default; enabling a single app also requires the third-party org-wide setting be turned on where permitted.
- **Blocked by publisher / conditional access:** Some apps require Microsoft Entra admin consent or app configuration. Check **Entra ID** > **Enterprise applications** for a pending consent request, and review Conditional Access policies that may block the app's service principal.
- **Cmdlet reports success but nothing changes:** Expected behavior for `New-`/`Set-CsTeamsAppPermissionPolicy`. Make these changes in TAC instead.

## Prevention

- Standardize on **App centric management** and define per-app availability (Everyone / Specific users or groups / No one) rather than maintaining many permission policies.
- Keep the Teams admin center and Microsoft 365 **Integrated apps** allow/block lists synchronized until UAM migration is complete.
- Vet and allow business-critical apps proactively so users don't hit blocks; use the **User requests** tab on the **Manage apps** page to triage and approve requests promptly.
- Restrict custom app upload to a dedicated developer setup policy instead of enabling it org-wide.
- Document approved apps and any GCC/government-cloud constraints in your tenant runbook, and communicate the up-to-24-hour propagation window to requesters to avoid premature escalations.

Title: TMS-070: Teams Presence Status Stuck or Incorrect
Content:
# Teams Presence Status Stuck or Incorrect

**Category:** Teams > Presence
**Article Code:** TMS-070
**Tier:** 1
**Audience:** Administrators / Technicians
**Estimated Resolution Time:** 10–30 minutes

Presence in Teams is calculated by the service from user activity, calendar state, and manually set status. It is not something an admin edits directly — there is no cmdlet to "set" a user's presence. Fixes target the client, the subscription, and the calendar/EWS pipeline that feed it.

## Symptoms / When to Use

- Status stays **Away** after the user resumes activity on an unlocked device.
- Status is stuck on **Out of Office** or **In a meeting** with no matching calendar event.
- A contact shows **Status unknown** or never updates for other users.
- Presence differs between desktop, web, and mobile clients.
- Presence indicator is missing or wrong inside Outlook.

## Background

Each client maintains a **presence subscription**. When a device is locked, sleeps, or is idle for 5+ minutes, presence flips to Away. If the subscription expires and isn't re-created on resume (common on macOS and when a mobile client is also signed in), the stale status persists. Calendar-driven states (**In a meeting**, **Out of Office**) depend on the Teams presence service reaching the mailbox over **Exchange Web Services (EWS)**; if EWS access is blocked or the mailbox is on-premises, presence lags or sticks. Outlook presence additionally requires Teams installed, running, and registered as the default IM provider.

## Resolution

### Step 1: Reset presence from the client

Have the user manually reset their status: select the profile picture > current status > **Reset status**. This forces the client to re-publish and re-create the subscription.

### Step 2: Sign out of secondary clients

If Teams is signed in on another device (phone, second desktop), presence may reflect that device's last state. Sign out of Teams on all secondary devices, then confirm the primary device.

### Step 3: Restart / clear the client cache

Fully quit Teams (not just close the window) and reopen. If it persists, clear the client cache. For new Teams on Windows:

```powershell
Get-Process -Name ms-teams -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue | Stop-Process -Force
Remove-Item -Path "$env:LOCALAPPDATA\Packages\MSTeams_8wekyb3d8bbwe\LocalCache" -Recurse -Force -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue
```

Sign back in and re-check presence.

### Step 4: Run the presence connectivity test

For calendar-based states, run the **Teams Presence Based on Calendar Events** test in the Remote Connectivity Analyzer as the affected user:

```text
https://testconnectivity.microsoft.com/tests/TeamsCalendarPresence/input
```

Sign in as the user, complete the verification code, accept the terms, and select **Perform Test**. Review any warnings or failures it reports.

### Step 5: Run the admin self-help diagnostic

As a Global or Teams admin, open the **Teams Presence** diagnostic, which runs inside the Microsoft 365 admin center:

```text
https://aka.ms/TeamsPresenceDiag
```

Enter the affected user's email under **Username or Email**, select **Run Tests**, and follow the remediation links. (Not available for GCC, GCC High, 21Vianet, or Germany.)

## Troubleshooting

**Status unknown for a contact.** Confirm the contact has signed in to Teams, hasn't set **Appear offline**, and that their email and Teams sign-in address match. If the addresses differ, correct them, then have the contact sign out and back in.

**Stuck on "Out of Office" or never shows "In a meeting."** This points at EWS. In Exchange Online PowerShell, confirm EWS is enabled for the mailbox:

```powershell
Get-CASMailbox -Identity user@contoso.com | Format-List EwsEnabled
```

If it returns `False`, re-enable it:

```powershell
Set-CASMailbox -Identity user@contoso.com -EwsEnabled $true
```

For on-premises or hybrid mailboxes, expect delays up to an hour; ensure the Exchange REST API URL is published externally, since the presence service does not fall back to the EWS endpoint.

**Coexistence with Skype for Business.** In Islands mode, presence can appear inconsistent by design. Check the user's assigned mode:

```powershell
Get-CsOnlineUser -Identity user@contoso.com | Select-Object UserPrincipalName, TeamsUpgradeEffectiveMode
```

**Presence wrong only in Outlook.** Verify Teams is running and registered as the default IM app. In the registry under `HKEY_CURRENT_USER\Software\IM Providers`, `DefaultIMApp` (REG_SZ) should equal `Teams`. Or run the guided fix from the Get Help app.

## Prevention

- Keep the Teams desktop client current; presence-subscription fixes ship in client updates.
- Discourage users from staying signed in on idle secondary devices.
- Ensure `EwsEnabled` stays `$true` and required Microsoft 365 endpoints are allowed through proxies/firewalls.
- Migrate on-premises mailboxes to Exchange Online to eliminate presence-delay behavior.
- Educate users to use **Reset status** before opening a ticket for a single stale indicator.

Title: TMS-071: Teams Direct Message Not Delivering
Content:
# Teams Direct Message Not Delivering

**Category:** Teams > Messaging
**Article Code:** TMS-071
**Tier:** 1
**Audience:** Administrators / Technicians
**Estimated Resolution Time:** 15–30 minutes

A user sends a one-to-one (direct) chat message in Microsoft Teams and it never reaches the recipient. This is almost always a policy, tenant boundary, or account-state issue rather than a client bug. Work the checks below in order.

## Symptoms / When to Use

- A direct message shows sent but the recipient never sees it, or the sender cannot start a chat with a specific person.
- The recipient does not appear in search, or appears but cannot be selected.
- "You can't send messages to this person" or a similar chat-blocked banner appears.
- Chat works internally but fails when messaging an external (federated) user.
- Only some users are affected — points to a per-user messaging policy or Information Barrier segment.

## Background

Teams direct-message delivery depends on several server-side gates, any one of which can silently drop or block a chat:

- **Teams messaging policy** — `AllowUserChat` controls whether a user can use one-to-one/group chat. If set to `False`, chat is disabled for that user.
- **Information Barriers (IB)** — Purview IB policies can block communication between defined segments. Blocked pairs cannot search, select, or message each other.
- **External access (federation)** — messaging a user in another tenant requires external access to be enabled and, if scoped, the partner domain to be allowed.
- **Account state** — disabled, unlicensed, or not-yet-provisioned recipient accounts will not receive messages.

## Resolution

### Step 1: Connect to Teams PowerShell

Install (if needed) and connect with an account holding Teams Administrator rights.

```powershell
Install-Module -Name MicrosoftTeams -Scope CurrentUser
Connect-MicrosoftTeams
```

### Step 2: Confirm the sender's messaging policy allows chat

Find which messaging policy is assigned to the affected user, then inspect that policy's `AllowUserChat` value.

```powershell
Get-CsOnlineUser -Identity "user@contoso.com" |
  Select-Object DisplayName, TeamsMessagingPolicy

# Inspect the named policy (blank/Global = the tenant default)
Get-CsTeamsMessagingPolicy -Identity Global |
  Select-Object Identity, AllowUserChat, AllowUserDeleteMessage
```

If `AllowUserChat` is `False`, either move the user to a policy that permits chat or update the policy. Assign a working policy per user:

```powershell
Grant-CsTeamsMessagingPolicy -Identity "user@contoso.com" -PolicyName "AllowChatPolicy"
```

To flip the setting on the assigned policy itself (affects everyone on that policy):

```powershell
Set-CsTeamsMessagingPolicy -Identity "AllowChatPolicy" -AllowUserChat $true
```

Repeat Step 2 for the **recipient** — both parties need chat enabled.

### Step 3: Rule out Information Barriers

If the block is between two specific internal users, check whether an IB policy separates them.

```powershell
Get-InformationBarrierRecipientStatus -Identity meganb -Identity2 alexw
```

Review the output for an applied policy (`*ExoPolicyId`). If IB is blocking them by design, no fix is needed. If the block is unexpected, confirm policy application status and, if a recent change hasn't taken effect, reapply.

```powershell
Get-InformationBarrierPoliciesApplicationStatus
Start-InformationBarrierPoliciesApplication
```

### Step 4: Check external access for cross-tenant chat

If the recipient is in another organization, verify external access in **Teams admin center > Users > External access**. Confirm external access is **On** and, if you use an allow list, that the recipient's domain is listed. Both tenants must permit external access for the chat to route.

### Step 5: Validate the recipient account

In **Microsoft 365 admin center > Users > Active users**, confirm the recipient is enabled, has a Teams-enabling license (for example Microsoft 365 E3/E5 or Teams Essentials), and has signed into Teams at least once. New or recently licensed accounts may take time to provision; undelivered messages appear once the recipient first signs in.

## Troubleshooting

- **Message sent but not appearing:** the recipient may not have opened Teams recently. Messages surface after they sign in — confirm before escalating.
- **Cross-tenant chat still fails after Step 4:** the *remote* tenant may block external access or your domain specifically. This is outside your control; have the recipient's admin verify their external access settings.
- **Messaging a Skype for Business / on-premises account:** delivery fails if the recipient is Offline or Do Not Disturb, or if either party is not on Teams. Both users must be on Teams and the recipient in an active presence state.
- **Only one direction fails:** re-run Step 2 against the party who cannot receive — asymmetric policy assignment is common.
- **Policy change not reflected:** messaging-policy assignments can take up to a few hours to propagate. Have the user sign out and back in.

## Prevention

- Standardize on a small set of messaging policies with `AllowUserChat = $true` and assign via group-based policy assignment to avoid per-user drift.
- Document intended Information Barrier segments so expected blocks aren't mistaken for faults.
- Set external-access domain allow lists deliberately and review them when onboarding new partners.
- Verify Teams licensing and first sign-in as part of new-user provisioning.

Title: TMS-072: Teams Notifications Not Working
Content:
# Teams Notifications Not Working

**Category:** Teams > Notifications
**Article Code:** TMS-072
**Tier:** 1
**Audience:** Technicians (with Administrator escalation)
**Estimated Resolution Time:** 10–30 minutes

## Symptoms / When to Use
- User receives no banner, sound, or badge alerts for chats, @mentions, or channel activity.
- Notifications appear in the Teams activity feed but never as desktop/OS banners or sounds.
- Alerts work on one client (e.g., mobile) but not another (desktop or web).
- A specific app or channel stopped notifying after a policy or client change.
- Notifications are delayed rather than missing (often OS Focus/Do Not Disturb).

## Background
Teams notifications pass through three layers, and any one can suppress them:

1. **OS layer** — Windows Focus Assist / notification settings, or macOS Notification Center and Focus. If the OS blocks Teams, no banner or sound appears regardless of Teams settings.
2. **Teams client layer** — per-user settings under **Settings > Notifications and activity**, including per-app and per-channel overrides, Quiet Hours, and the Windows-vs-Teams notification style toggle.
3. **Tenant policy layer** — the Teams Notifications and Feeds policy (`TeamsNotificationAndFeedsPolicy`) controlling suggested/trending feeds and related behavior.

Most Tier-1 cases resolve at the OS or client layer. Confirm those before touching tenant policy.

## Resolution

### Step 1: Confirm the OS is not blocking Teams
On **Windows**, open **Settings > System > Notifications**, ensure notifications are **On**, confirm **Microsoft Teams** is enabled in the app list, and turn off **Do not disturb** / **Focus**.

On **macOS**, open **System Settings > Notifications > Microsoft Teams**, set **Allow notifications** on, choose **Banners** or **Alerts**, and confirm a **Focus** mode is not suppressing Teams.

### Step 2: Check Teams client notification settings
In the Teams desktop client, go to **Settings and more (…) > Settings > Notifications and activity**. Verify:
- **Sound**, **Banner**, and **Feed** are enabled for **Chat messages** and **Mentions**.
- **Quiet hours / Quiet time** is not active.
- Under **Show notifications for**, per-app overrides (e.g., a muted app) are not set to off. Select **Edit** next to the app to restore **Banner and feed**.

Check the affected channel directly: open the channel, select **… > Channel notifications**, and set it to **All activity** or **Custom** as needed.

### Step 3: Set the notification style to Teams built-in
Still under **Notifications and activity**, set the notification style to **Teams built-in** (rather than **Windows**). The Windows style depends on Action Center and is a frequent cause of missing banners after upgrades to the new Teams client.

### Step 4: Clear cache / restart the client
Fully quit Teams (right-click the tray/dock icon and **Quit**, not just close the window) and relaunch. If banners still fail on the new Teams client for Windows, reset it:

```cmd
winget upgrade "Microsoft Teams"
```

For a macOS-specific issue where a custom Teams notification sound reverts to the default system sound, clear the Notification Center cache (admin):

```bash
pkill -9 NotificationCenter
```

Non-admin macOS users: restart the device (**Apple menu > Restart**).

### Step 5: Verify tenant policy (Administrator)
If multiple users are affected, inspect the assigned Teams Notifications and Feeds policy in the **MicrosoftTeams** PowerShell module:

```powershell
Connect-MicrosoftTeams
Get-CsTeamsNotificationAndFeedsPolicy -Identity Global
```

To re-enable a feed setting that was disabled by policy:

```powershell
Set-CsTeamsNotificationAndFeedsPolicy -Identity Global -SuggestedFeedsEnabledType EnabledUserOverride
```

To review or reassign per-user policy, use the **Teams admin center** at **Users > Manage users > [user] > Policies**, or confirm the effective policy with `Get-CsUserPolicyAssignment`.

## Troubleshooting
- **Only mobile is silent:** Check the Teams mobile app under **Settings > Notifications**, and confirm the phone OS allows Teams push and that battery optimization is not force-stopping Teams in the background.
- **Only web is silent:** Browser notifications must be allowed for `teams.microsoft.com` in the browser's site permissions; incognito/private windows block them.
- **App notifications missing (Viva, Power BI, custom apps):** These follow per-app settings under **Notifications and activity > Apps**. Some app sections only appear after the first notification arrives. Viva Connections/SharePoint News notifications have no org-wide admin toggle.
- **Intune-managed devices:** An app protection policy set to **Block org data** strips notification content, and a Managed Apps configuration key (e.g., `com.microsoft.teams.chat.notifications.IntuneMAMOnly` = `0`) disables them entirely. Check **Intune > Apps > Protection / Configuration**.
- **Still nothing after all layers checked:** Sign out and back in to refresh the client token, or clear the Teams cache directory.

## Prevention
- Standardize new-hire setup to enable OS notifications for Teams and set the client notification style to **Teams built-in**.
- Document any tenant Notifications and Feeds policy changes so muted feeds are traceable.
- When deploying Intune app protection policies, confirm the org-data notification setting matches the intended user experience before broad assignment.
- Advise users that Quiet Hours and OS Focus modes suppress alerts, and show them where to toggle these.

Title: TMS-073: Teams Search Not Returning Results
Content:
# Teams Search Not Returning Results

**Category:** Teams > Search
**Article Code:** TMS-073
**Tier:** 1
**Audience:** Technicians / Administrators
**Estimated Resolution Time:** 10–30 minutes

Microsoft Teams search returns nothing (or stale/partial results) for messages, people, or files. In most Tier-1 cases this is a client-side cache or index problem and clears with a cache reset and re-sign-in. This article covers the quick fix and the checks that narrow down tenant-side causes.

## Symptoms / When to Use

- Search bar returns zero results for messages you know exist.
- Search shows old results but not recent messages, chats, or files.
- A specific person or external contact does not appear in people search.
- Results appear on Teams web (teams.microsoft.com) but not in the desktop client, or vice versa.
- "Something went wrong" or an endlessly spinning search pane.

## Background

Teams search is served by a Microsoft-hosted substrate index, not by the local client. The desktop client keeps a local cache of recent content and index state. When that cache is corrupt or out of date, search can fail even though the service-side index is healthy — which is why a single-user problem is usually client cache, and a tenant-wide problem is usually service or policy.

Two other common causes are worth knowing up front. People search for **external federated contacts** has strict requirements: the searcher's mailbox must be in Exchange Online, the contact must have a phone number in its contact record, and you must search by **email address, not display name**. Separately, indexing has a propagation lag — brand-new messages can take a few minutes to become searchable.

## Resolution

### Step 1: Confirm scope (web vs. desktop, one user vs. many)

Have the user sign in at [https://teams.microsoft.com](https://teams.microsoft.com) and repeat the search. If web search works but desktop does not, the problem is the local client — go to Step 2. If it fails everywhere for one user, continue through the steps. If it fails for many users at once, check **Microsoft 365 admin center > Health > Service health** for an active Teams advisory before troubleshooting clients.

### Step 2: Restart and clear the Teams client cache

Fully quit Teams first. Right-click the Teams icon in the taskbar and select **Quit**.

**New Teams (Windows)** — reset the app (Start > Settings > Apps > Installed apps > Microsoft Teams (work or school) > Advanced options > **Reset**), or delete the cache folder manually:

```cmd
%userprofile%\appdata\local\Packages\MSTeams_8wekyb3d8bbwe\LocalCache\Microsoft\MSTeams
```

Delete all files and folders in that directory, then restart Teams.

**Classic Teams (Windows)** — delete the cache folder:

```cmd
%appdata%\Microsoft\Teams
```

**New Teams (macOS)** — quit Teams (Cmd-Q), then in Terminal:

```bash
rm -rf ~/Library/Group\ Containers/UBF8T346G9.com.microsoft.teams
rm -rf ~/Library/Containers/com.microsoft.teams2
```

Restart Teams. The first launch after a cache clear is slower while the cache rebuilds. Re-test search.

### Step 3: Sign out and sign back in

If clearing the cache did not resolve it, sign out completely (profile picture > **Sign out**), quit Teams, then sign back in. This forces the client to re-authenticate and re-sync index state with the substrate.

### Step 4: Allow for indexing lag

If only *recent* items are missing, wait 5–15 minutes and re-run the search. Newly sent messages and newly created files are not searchable until the substrate finishes indexing them.

## Troubleshooting

**External contact not found:** Confirm all three requirements are met — the searcher's mailbox is on Exchange Online, the external contact has a phone number, and the search uses the contact's **email address**. Then run the admin diagnostics:

- **Teams Federation** self-help diagnostic in the Microsoft 365 admin center: [https://aka.ms/TeamsFederationDiag](https://aka.ms/TeamsFederationDiag)
- **Teams Federation and Interoperability** test in the Remote Connectivity Analyzer: [https://testconnectivity.microsoft.com/tests/TeamsFederation/input](https://testconnectivity.microsoft.com/tests/TeamsFederation/input)

(Neither diagnostic is available in GCC / GCC High / 21Vianet environments.)

**Tenant-wide failure:** Check Service health for a Teams or Microsoft Search advisory. Do not clear caches on multiple machines chasing a service-side incident.

**Cache clear did not help:** Update to the latest Teams build (new Teams auto-updates; verify no pending restart), then confirm the OS date/time and time zone are correct — clock skew breaks token validation and can silently break search sync.

**File search only:** File results come from SharePoint/OneDrive. If chats and people search work but files do not, treat it as a SharePoint search issue rather than a Teams client issue.

## Prevention

- Keep Teams on the current supported build; avoid blocking the new-Teams auto-update channel.
- On VDI/non-persistent images, follow Microsoft's Teams cache folder exclusion guidance so search index state is not wiped every logon.
- Educate users that external contacts are found by email address, not name, and that new content has a short indexing delay.
- For recurring single-user issues, standardize on the cache-clear + re-sign-in sequence in Step 2 before escalating.
