Title: TMS-074: Teams File Sharing and Access Errors
Content:
# Teams File Sharing and Access Errors

**Category:** Teams > Files
**Article Code:** TMS-074
**Tier:** 2
**Audience:** Administrators / Technicians (with end-user guidance in Prevention)
**Estimated Resolution Time:** 20–60 minutes (longer if propagation delays or guest re-invites are involved)

Microsoft Teams stores channel files in the connected SharePoint site's document library and chat files in the sender's OneDrive. Almost every "can't open," "no access," or "something went wrong" error in the Teams **Files** tab is really a SharePoint or OneDrive permission/sharing problem surfacing through the Teams UI. Diagnose at the storage layer, not the Teams client.

## Symptoms / When to Use

- Files tab returns **"There was a problem reaching this app"** or **"We can't get your files, we're working on getting them back."**
- Guests see **"Something went wrong — Attempted to perform an unauthorized operation."**
- Chat recipient gets **"You don't have access to this file."**
- **"The object specified does not belong to a list"** when opening a channel's Files tab.
- Users can view files but can't get a working share link, or **Share** options are greyed out.
- External recipients report expired links or "access denied" after previously having access.
- New team members can't see files that existing members can.

## Background

Teams does not have its own file store. Understanding the mapping is the whole job:

- **Channel (standard) files** live in the team's SharePoint site, in the **Shared Documents** library, in a folder named after the channel.
- **Chat / meeting files** live in the sender's **OneDrive for Business** under *Microsoft Teams Chat Files*.
- **Private and shared channel files** live in separate, dedicated SharePoint sites with their own permissions inherited from channel membership.

Permission consequences:

- A team is backed by a **Microsoft 365 Group**. Group owners become SharePoint **site owners**; group members become **site members**. Manage permissions through Teams, not SharePoint, for standard teams — for private/shared channels this is mandatory (SharePoint shows them read-only).
- **External/guest access** to Teams files is governed by the **SharePoint and OneDrive external sharing settings**, not by a Teams-only switch. If SharePoint external sharing is off (or more restrictive than the site needs), guests are blocked even though the person appears in the team.
- The **Shared Documents** library name is load-bearing. Renaming it breaks the Teams Files tab.
- Orphaned groups (no owner) break the Files tab entirely.

## Resolution

Work top-down: confirm the storage location, then site permissions, then external sharing, then site-collection quirks.

### Step 1: Identify the backing SharePoint site

In the affected channel, open the **Files** tab and select **Open in SharePoint** (or the "..." menu > Open in SharePoint). Note the site URL — you'll need it for the cmdlets below. For chat-file errors, the backing store is the sender's OneDrive, not a team site.

### Step 2: Connect the SharePoint Online Management Shell

Run PowerShell as an admin and connect with a SharePoint Administrator account. The admin URL is your tenant name plus `-admin`.

```powershell
Install-Module -Name Microsoft.Online.SharePoint.PowerShell -Scope CurrentUser
Connect-SPOService -Url https://contoso-admin.sharepoint.com/
```

### Step 3: Verify site-level permissions and membership

Confirm the user is actually a member/owner of the team. In Teams, open **Manage team > Members**. Missing members almost always explains "some users can't see files." Add the user as a member (or owner) — this syncs to SharePoint automatically.

Check the site's effective sharing state:

```powershell
Get-SPOSite -Identity https://contoso.sharepoint.com/sites/ProjectX | Format-List Url,SharingCapability,Owner
```

If the group is **orphaned** (no owner), the Files tab throws "There was a problem reaching this app." Assign an owner in the Microsoft 365 admin center under **Teams & groups > Active teams and groups**, then reopen the Files tab.

### Step 4: Confirm external sharing (guest access errors)

Guest "unauthorized operation" errors mean SharePoint external sharing is off or too restrictive. Check the organization level first.

Portal path: **SharePoint admin center > Policies > Sharing**. Set SharePoint external sharing to **New and existing guests** (or **Existing guests** / **Anyone** as policy allows). Remember: the OneDrive slider can be equal to or more restrictive than SharePoint, never more permissive.

Then confirm the specific site is not more restrictive than the org. The site setting must be equal to or more restrictive than the tenant setting:

```powershell
Set-SPOSite -Identity https://contoso.sharepoint.com/sites/ProjectX -SharingCapability ExternalUserAndGuestSharing
```

Valid `SharingCapability` values:

- `Disabled` — external sharing off
- `ExistingExternalUserSharingOnly` — only guests already in the directory
- `ExternalUserSharingOnly` — new and existing authenticated guests
- `ExternalUserAndGuestSharing` — authenticated guests plus "Anyone" (anonymous) links

Also confirm group owners are allowed to add guests: **Microsoft 365 admin center > Settings > Org settings > Microsoft 365 Groups** — enable *Let group owners add people outside the organization to groups*. If this was off, guests were never actually added to the group even if invited.

Sharing changes can take up to an hour to propagate; restricting access removes guest access within about an hour as well.

### Step 5: Fix a renamed document library

"The object specified does not belong to a list" means the library was renamed from **Shared Documents**. Revert it with PnP PowerShell (site owner permissions required):

```powershell
Install-Module -Name PnP.PowerShell -Scope CurrentUser
Connect-PnPOnline -Url "https://contoso.sharepoint.com/sites/ProjectX" -Interactive
$list = Get-PnPList 'Renamed Documents'
$list.RootFolder.MoveTo('Shared Documents')
$list.Update()
```

Run `Get-PnPList` with no parameters first to see the current (renamed) library name.

### Step 6: Fix chat-file "You don't have access" errors

This is caused by **Limited-access user permission lockdown mode** being active on the sender's OneDrive site collection — do not enable this on OneDrive. Have the file owner deactivate it: **OneDrive > Settings (gear) > OneDrive Settings > More Settings > Site Collection Features**, locate **Limited-access user permission lockdown mode**, and select **Deactivate**. As an alternative, re-share the file with **Specific people** from the OneDrive web UI to regenerate a valid permission.

### Step 7: Run the Microsoft 365 self-diagnostic

For "We can't get your files" and guest-access errors, run the built-in tenant diagnostic. In the **Microsoft 365 admin center**, use the **Help & support / Run Tests** experience (linked from the relevant Microsoft troubleshooting articles) to auto-populate the Teams file-access diagnostic. It checks group ownership, sharing settings, and library health in one pass. Not available for GCC, 21Vianet, or Germany clouds.

## Troubleshooting

If the main path doesn't resolve it, check these variations:

- **Private/shared channel files:** Permissions come from channel membership only. Adding someone to the parent team does not grant access to a private channel. Add them to the channel itself; SharePoint permissions for these sites are read-only.
- **"Sharing options are greyed out":** Verify both org-level (**Policies > Sharing**) and site-level sharing allow external sharing. For OneDrive, check **Microsoft 365 admin center > Users > Active users > [user] > OneDrive > Manage external sharing** and confirm *Let people outside your organization access your site* is on.
- **Domain restrictions:** If sharing works for some external domains but not others, an allow/block list is in play. Check `Get-SPOTenant | Format-List Sharing*` and the site's `SharingDomainRestrictionMode` / `SharingAllowedDomainList`.
- **Expired guest links:** Verification-code guests re-authenticate on a cycle (default 30 days); external users can be set to expire via `ExternalUserExpirationInDays`. Re-share to reissue.
- **Conditional Access / device compliance:** An unmanaged-device or location policy can block SharePoint even when sharing is correct — the user gets access-denied in the browser, not just Teams. Review Entra Conditional Access sign-in logs.
- **Propagation delay:** After any sharing change, wait up to 60 minutes and have the user fully close and reopen Teams (or use the web client) before re-testing.
- **Cache corruption (single user):** If only one user is affected on one machine, clear the Teams cache and retry via `teams.microsoft.com` to rule out the client.

## Prevention

- **Manage all team permissions through Teams**, not the SharePoint site — direct SharePoint edits desync from the M365 Group and cause intermittent access loss.
- **Never rename the Shared Documents library** and never enable Limited-access user permission lockdown mode on OneDrive.
- **Keep every group/team owned by at least two owners** to prevent orphaning; audit with a recurring orphaned-group report.
- **Set org-level external sharing to the least-permissive level that meets business need** and raise it per-site only where required — the site setting can be more restrictive than the org, never more permissive.
- **Prefer "Specific people" sharing links** over "Anyone" links; reserve "Anyone" for sites that genuinely need anonymous access and always set link expiration and view-only where possible.
- **Educate end users** that Teams file errors are usually membership/sharing issues: confirm they're a team member and that the recipient's link type matches the audience before escalating.

Title: TMS-075: Teams Desktop Client Stuck Loading
Content:
# Teams Desktop Client Stuck Loading

**Category:** Teams > Client
**Article Code:** TMS-075
**Tier:** 1
**Audience:** Technicians
**Estimated Resolution Time:** 10–25 minutes

New Teams (or classic Teams) opens to a blank window or spinner and never finishes loading. Most cases are a corrupt local cache and clear in a few minutes. Work the steps in order and stop when the client loads.

## Symptoms / When to Use

- Teams desktop opens to a white/blank window or a perpetual loading spinner.
- Splash screen appears, then the window closes immediately or hangs.
- Client is stuck on "Loading Teams…" while the web client (teams.microsoft.com) works fine.
- Restarting the app does not help; the browser client and mobile app are unaffected.
- No sign-in error code is shown (if a `0xCAA…` code appears, use the sign-in KB instead).

## Background

The desktop client caches auth tokens, config, and rendered content locally. New Teams (MSTeams, an MSIX/Store app) stores this under `LocalCache`; classic Teams uses `%appdata%\Microsoft\Teams`. A corrupt or locked cache is the most common cause of a hang after the splash screen.

Loads that fail *before* the cache is even read usually point to blocked network endpoints, a reparse-point/redirected AppData folder, or an out-of-date client. The main path below (restart → clear cache → reset) resolves the large majority of Tier-1 cases.

## Resolution

### Step 1: Fully quit Teams

A background process keeps cache files locked, so the app must be fully stopped before clearing anything.

Right-click the Teams icon in the system tray and select **Quit**, then confirm no process remains:

```powershell
Get-Process -Name ms-teams, Teams -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue | Stop-Process -Force
```

### Step 2: Clear the client cache (New Teams — Windows)

Delete the local cache folder, then relaunch. Teams rebuilds the cache on next start (first launch will be slower than usual).

```cmd
%userprofile%\appdata\local\Packages\MSTeams_8wekyb3d8bbwe\LocalCache\Microsoft\MSTeams
```

Paste the path into **Win+R** (or File Explorer), delete all files and folders inside the directory, then restart Teams.

For **classic Teams**, use this path instead and delete its contents:

```cmd
%appdata%\Microsoft\Teams
```

For **macOS** (New Teams), quit Teams, open Terminal, and run:

```bash
rm -rf ~/Library/Group\ Containers/UBF8T346G9.com.microsoft.teams
rm -rf ~/Library/Containers/com.microsoft.teams2
```

Restart Teams and let it fully load. If it now works, stop here.

### Step 3: Reset the New Teams app

If clearing the cache did not help, reset the app package. This clears all app data including local personalization (chats and files are server-side and are not lost).

1. Open **Settings** > **Apps** > **Installed apps**.
2. Search for **Microsoft Teams**, select the **…** menu, and choose **Advanced options**.
3. Under **Reset**, select **Reset**.
4. Restart Teams and sign in.

### Step 4: Confirm the client is current

An outdated build can hang on load. In a working Teams window, select **Settings and more (…)** next to your profile picture > **Check for updates**. Teams updates in the background; restart when prompted and retry.

## Troubleshooting

If the client still will not load after Steps 1–4:

- **Blocked endpoints.** A firewall or proxy blocking Teams endpoints causes loads to hang or time out. Confirm the device can reach the required [Microsoft 365 URLs and IP ranges](https://learn.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/enterprise/urls-and-ip-address-ranges). Test from the same network in a browser at `https://teams.microsoft.com` — if the web client also hangs, treat it as a network issue.

- **Redirected AppData / reparse points.** On roaming or folder-redirected profiles, New Teams can fail to launch when the Cookies/Cache shell folders or the TEMP/TMP variables point to a reparse point. Check with:

  ```powershell
  (gp ([environment]::getfolderpath("Cookies"))).Attributes -match 'ReparsePoint'
  (gp ([environment]::getfolderpath("InternetCache"))).Attributes -match 'ReparsePoint'
  ```

  If either returns **True**, repoint the folder to a non-redirected local path (see the launch-issues KB linked below).

- **Full reinstall.** As a last resort, uninstall Teams, delete the cache folder from Step 2, and reinstall the latest client (run the installer **as administrator**). Sign back in afterward.

- **Collect logs before escalating.** If the issue persists, gather client logs (**Ctrl+Alt+Shift+1** with Teams focused) and open a ticket referencing this article.

## Prevention

- Keep clients on auto-update; discourage users from pinning old versions.
- Exclude Teams cache paths from aggressive folder redirection and roaming profiles; use per-machine local cache in VDI.
- Ensure Teams endpoints are allowlisted on firewalls and proxies before deploying to new sites.
- After tenant identity or Conditional Access changes, have users sign out and back in rather than force-quitting mid-load.

Title: TMS-076: Teams Mobile App Crashing
Content:
# Teams Mobile App Crashing

**Category:** Teams > Mobile
**Article Code:** TMS-076
**Tier:** 1
**Audience:** Technicians (end-user coordination required)
**Estimated Resolution Time:** 10–25 minutes

The Microsoft Teams mobile app closes unexpectedly on iOS or Android. This is almost always a client-side issue — corrupt cache, an outdated build, or an Intune App Protection policy conflict — and resolves without a tenant change.

## Symptoms / When to Use

- Teams closes immediately on launch ("opens and closes") or after a few seconds.
- Crash occurs on a specific action: opening a chat, joining a call, sharing a file, or loading a tab.
- Only one user or a small group is affected; Teams desktop/web works for the same account.
- App freezes and is killed by the OS, or shows a blank/white screen then exits.
- Started after an OS update, a Teams app update, or a new Intune app protection policy.

## Background

Teams mobile is a hybrid app: native shell plus web-based content. Crashes usually stem from a corrupt local cache, an app build that is incompatible with the current OS version, or a Mobile Application Management (MAM) App Protection policy blocking a required function (for example, save-as, copy/paste, or a conditional launch action). Because cache and app data live only on the device, clearing them — not a server change — is the first-line fix. Tenant-wide crashes affecting many users point instead to a service incident (check the Microsoft 365 admin center Service Health dashboard) or a bad policy rollout.

## Resolution

### Step 1: Confirm scope and check service health

Rule out a broad outage before touching the device. In the Microsoft 365 admin center, go to **Health** > **Service health** and check **Microsoft Teams** for an active advisory. If a single user is affected, continue below.

### Step 2: Force close and update the app

Have the user fully close Teams (swipe it out of the app switcher — do not just background it) and reopen. If it still crashes, update to the latest build:

- **iOS:** App Store > profile icon > scroll to **Microsoft Teams** > **Update**.
- **Android:** Play Store > profile icon > **Manage apps & device** > **Update** on Microsoft Teams.

Also apply pending OS updates (**Settings > General > Software Update** on iOS; **Settings > System > System update** on Android). Version mismatches between Teams and the OS are a common crash cause.

### Step 3: Clear Teams app data (cache)

Clearing app data removes the corrupt local cache. The user signs back in afterward; no chat history is lost (it is stored server-side).

- **iOS:** Open the device **Settings** app > **Teams** > toggle **Clear App Data** on. Reopen Teams and sign in.
- **Android:** In Teams, go to **Settings** > **Data and storage** > **Clear app data** > **Clear data**. If Teams will not open at all, clear it from the OS: **Settings** > **Apps** > **Teams** > **Storage** > **Clear cache**, then **Clear storage/data**.

Launch Teams and confirm the crash is gone.

### Step 4: Reinstall the app

If clearing data did not help, uninstall and reinstall Teams. This is the only reliable way to fully purge corrupt app data on iOS.

- **iOS:** Press and hold the Teams icon > **Remove App** > **Delete App**, then reinstall from the App Store.
- **Android:** **Settings** > **Apps** > **Teams** > **Uninstall**, then reinstall from the Play Store.

Have the user sign in again and re-approve any Intune enrollment prompt.

## Troubleshooting

**Crash only on a specific action (call, file open, tab):** Suspect an Intune App Protection policy. In the **Microsoft Intune admin center** (intune.microsoft.com), go to **Apps** > **App protection policies** and review the policy targeting the user for restrictive conditional launch or data-transfer settings that could block the action.

**Need crash logs for a support case:** Collect Teams app diagnostics through Intune. In the **Microsoft Intune admin center**, go to **Troubleshooting + support** > **Troubleshoot** > select the user > **Summary** > **App protection**, find Teams, use the **...** menu > **Collect diagnostics**. The device must be covered by an Intune App Protection policy and tenant diagnostic collection must be enabled under **Tenant administration** > **Device diagnostics**.

**Still crashing after reinstall:** Test the same account on Teams web or another device to isolate account vs. device. Check available device storage (a nearly full device causes crashes) and confirm the device OS is on a supported version for the current Teams release.

## Prevention

- Keep Teams and the device OS on current, supported versions; enable automatic app updates.
- Stage new Intune App Protection policy changes to a pilot group before tenant-wide deployment.
- Advise users to periodically clear cache (Step 3) rather than letting app data grow unbounded.
- Monitor Service Health so widespread mobile issues are identified as service-side, not device-side.

**Tags:** teams, mobile, crash, ios, android, cache, app-data, intune, app-protection, mam, troubleshooting, tier-1

Title: TMS-077: Teams Live Events Setup and Streaming Issues
Content:
# Teams Live Events Setup and Streaming Issues

**Category:** Teams > Live Events
**Article Code:** TMS-077
**Tier:** 3
**Audience:** Administrators / Technicians
**Estimated Resolution Time:** 45 minutes – 3 hours (longer when eCDN provisioning or a full event dry run is required)

> **Retirement notice:** Microsoft is retiring Teams live events in July 2026. Events already scheduled are supported through February 28, 2027. For new large-scale events, plan a migration to **Teams town hall** (or Webinar for smaller interactive sessions). This article covers live events for tenants still running them and for supporting in-flight events through the retirement window.

## Symptoms / When to Use

Use this article when you encounter any of the following:

- A user reports the **"New live event"** option is missing from the Teams calendar **+ New meeting** dropdown.
- An organizer receives a *"You don't have permission to schedule live events"* or *"Live events aren't enabled"* message.
- Producers using an external encoder (Teams Encoder production) cannot connect the RTMP/RTMPS feed, or the encoder connects but no preview appears in the producer window.
- Attendees cannot join a scheduled event, see *"The live event hasn't started"* indefinitely, or the video buffers/stalls for viewers on the corporate network.
- Anonymous or external attendees are blocked from a public event that should be open to everyone.
- Recording, captions, or Q&A are unavailable when the organizer expected them.
- Multiple viewers at one office location report degraded playback while remote viewers are fine (network congestion / missing eCDN).
- The tenant needs live events configured for an integration (for example Dynamics 365 Customer Insights – Journeys) that requires public, anonymous-accessible events.

## Background

A Teams live event is a one-to-many broadcast: a small group of organizers, producers, and presenters delivers content to a large view-only audience. Two production models exist:

- **Teams (Quick Start) production** — everything runs inside the Teams client. Presenters share webcam, screen, or content directly.
- **External app or device (Teams Encoder) production** — a hardware or software encoder pushes a single-bitrate **RTMP or RTMPS** stream into Teams, which handles transcoding for adaptive bitrate delivery. This model is used for studio-grade town-hall-style events driven by a media mixer.

The delivery stack is **Azure Media Services** for transcoding plus **Azure CDN** for public distribution. Inside the enterprise, an **enterprise content delivery network (eCDN)** — Microsoft eCDN or a certified partner (Hive, Kollective, Ramp) — is layered on top to keep many concurrent viewers from saturating the corporate WAN.

Two distinct control planes govern the feature:

1. **Live events policies** (`CsTeamsMeetingBroadcastPolicy`) — per-user policies that decide who can schedule events, who can attend, recording behavior, and transcription. This is where "the option is missing" problems almost always originate.
2. **Live events settings** (`CsTeamsMeetingBroadcastConfiguration`) — a single org-wide configuration for the attendee support URL and the third-party video distribution (eCDN/SDN) provider.

Key platform limits to keep in mind: max **720p** output resolution, up to **10,000** concurrent attendees, up to **15** concurrent live/pre-live events per tenant, and a **4-hour** maximum event length. Events created with an external encoder have no redundancy and are not recoverable if a failover occurs, so encoder-based events demand extra pre-flight care.

## Resolution

All PowerShell below uses the **Microsoft Teams PowerShell module**. Install it and connect before running any cmdlet:

```powershell
Install-Module -Name MicrosoftTeams -Scope CurrentUser
Connect-MicrosoftTeams
```

### Step 1: Confirm the organizer is licensed and in a supported coexistence mode

Creating live events requires an Enterprise (E1/E3/E5) or Education (A3/A5) license assigned to the **organizer**, and the tenant coexistence/upgrade mode must allow scheduling Teams meetings (**Islands**, **Meetings First**, or **Teams Only**). Attendees do not need a license for a public event.

Check the user's assigned coexistence mode:

```powershell
Get-CsOnlineUser -Identity "user@contoso.com" | Select-Object DisplayName, TeamsUpgradeEffectiveMode
```

If a license was only just assigned, allow 30–60 minutes for it to take effect before the live event option appears.

### Step 2: Verify the live events policy allows scheduling

The most common cause of a missing "New live event" option is a policy where scheduling is disabled. Inspect the policy assigned to the user (start with Global if you don't know which one applies):

```powershell
Get-CsTeamsMeetingBroadcastPolicy -Identity Global
```

Confirm `AllowBroadcastScheduling` is `True`. To check a named (custom) policy:

```powershell
Get-CsTeamsMeetingBroadcastPolicy -Identity "SalesLiveEvents"
```

To find which policy a specific user is assigned:

```powershell
Get-CsOnlineUser -Identity "user@contoso.com" | Select-Object DisplayName, TeamsMeetingBroadcastPolicy
```

If scheduling is off in the Global policy and you want everyone to have it, enable it:

```powershell
Set-CsTeamsMeetingBroadcastPolicy -Identity Global -AllowBroadcastScheduling $true
```

**Portal equivalent:** Teams admin center > **Meetings** > **Live events policies** > select **Global (Org-wide default)** or the custom policy > set **Live events scheduling** to **On** > **Save**.

### Step 3: Grant the correct policy to the user

If the organizer is on a restrictive custom policy, either move them to the Global policy or to a policy that allows scheduling.

Move a user back to the Global policy (assigning `$null` removes any per-user override so the Global policy applies):

```powershell
Grant-CsTeamsMeetingBroadcastPolicy -Identity "user@contoso.com" -PolicyName $null -Verbose
```

Assign a specific enabling policy:

```powershell
Grant-CsTeamsMeetingBroadcastPolicy -Identity "user@contoso.com" -PolicyName "EnableBroadcastSchedulingPolicy" -Verbose
```

To create a scheduling-enabled policy for a subset of users:

```powershell
New-CsTeamsMeetingBroadcastPolicy -Identity "EnableBroadcastSchedulingPolicy"
Set-CsTeamsMeetingBroadcastPolicy -Identity "EnableBroadcastSchedulingPolicy" -AllowBroadcastScheduling $true
```

For large groups, assign by security group rather than user-by-user:

```powershell
New-CsGroupPolicyAssignment -GroupId "<security-group-object-id>" `
  -PolicyType TeamsMeetingBroadcastPolicy -PolicyName "EnableBroadcastSchedulingPolicy"
```

Policy changes can take time to replicate to the client; allow a few hours and have the user restart Teams before concluding it failed.

### Step 4: Set who can attend, recording, and captions

Attendee visibility controls whether the event can be public (anonymous) or is restricted. Set it in the policy that governs the organizer:

```powershell
# Allow public events open to anyone, including anonymous users
Set-CsTeamsMeetingBroadcastPolicy -Identity Global -BroadcastAttendeeVisibilityMode Everyone
```

Valid `-BroadcastAttendeeVisibilityMode` values include `Everyone`, `EveryoneInCompany`, `EveryoneInCompanyAndExternal`, and `InvitedUsersInCompanyAndExternal`. Use the most restrictive value that meets the requirement — reserve `Everyone` for genuinely public events.

Control recording (applies to events produced in Teams):

```powershell
# Options: AlwaysEnabled | AlwaysDisabled | UserOverride
Set-CsTeamsMeetingBroadcastPolicy -Identity Global -BroadcastRecordingMode UserOverride
```

Enable live captions/subtitles for attendees (Teams-produced events):

```powershell
Set-CsTeamsMeetingBroadcastPolicy -Identity Global -AllowBroadcastTranscription $true
```

> **GCC High / DoD:** Live events policies **must** be configured through PowerShell — the Teams admin center policy UI is not available for these clouds.

### Step 5: Configure org-wide live event settings (support URL and eCDN)

The attendee support URL and the video distribution provider are org-wide settings, not per-user policy. Set the support URL:

```powershell
Set-CsTeamsMeetingBroadcastConfiguration -SupportURL "https://support.contoso.com/liveevents"
```

**Portal equivalent:** Teams admin center > **Meetings** > **Live event settings** > enter the **Support URL** > **Save**.

To configure an eCDN/SDN provider, use the portal (this is provider-specific and not fully exposed via a single cmdlet):

1. Open the Teams admin center and go to **Meetings** > **Live event settings** (`https://admin.teams.microsoft.com/broadcasts/settings`).
2. Toggle **Video distribution provider** to **On**.
3. Select the provider (Microsoft eCDN, Hive, Kollective, or Ramp) from the dropdown.
4. Fill in the fields your provider requires (some providers do not use every field). Leave **Custom Support URL** as-is unless directed.
5. Select **Save**. Changes can take **up to 24 hours** to apply; Microsoft eCDN provisioning specifically takes **4–24 hours**.
6. Use **Verify setup** / **Verify** to validate against an existing video in the tenant. A **Success** message confirms correct configuration.

> **Critical:** Pre-scheduled events created **before** eCDN finishes provisioning will **not** use the eCDN. Re-create those events after provisioning completes so they pick up the distribution provider.

### Step 6: Set up the external encoder (Teams Encoder production)

For encoder-based events, retrieve the ingest details from the event and configure the encoder:

1. In the Teams **Calendar**, open the scheduled live event and expand the invite details.
2. In the **RTMP in details** section, use **Get RTMP** to copy the ingest URL and **Get RTMP key** to copy the stream key.
3. Enter the URL and key into the encoder's streaming output settings.
4. Configure the encoder to the recommended settings:

```text
Ingest:      Single-bitrate RTMPS or RTMP
Video codec: H.264, Profile High (Level 4.0), Progressive, 16:9
Resolution:  1280x720 @ up to 5 Mbps (CBR)  |  1920x1080 @ up to 10 Mbps (CBR or VBR)
Frame rate:  29.97 or 30 fps
Keyframe:    GOP 2 seconds, with an IDR frame at the start of each GOP
Audio codec: AAC-LC, 192 kbps, 48 kHz (44.1 kHz acceptable)
```

5. Join the event as a **Producer**, start streaming from the encoder, wait a few seconds for the feed to appear in the presenter area, select it into the queue, choose **Send Live**, then **Start** to begin the broadcast.
6. At the end, always select **Stop event** in Teams **before** disconnecting the encoder.

Both an audio and a video stream must be present or Teams will not play the content back. Do not change encoder settings after it starts pushing — disconnect via the producer controls and restart setup if a change is required.

### Step 7: Open the required network paths

Confirm the following before the event, on the network that hosts the encoder and on viewer networks:

- **RTMP ingest (encoder outbound):** allow domain `*.rtmpingest.mcr.teams.microsoft.com` on **ports 1935 (RTMP) and 1936 (RTMPS)**.
- **Viewer download (bypass proxy / SSL inspection):** `*.bmc.cdn.office.net` and `*.ml.cdn.office.net` should bypass proxy servers and have SSL inspection disabled.
- **General Teams:** all endpoints in the Microsoft 365 URLs and IP address ranges must be reachable.
- Ensure the encoder site's **upload** bandwidth comfortably exceeds the stream bitrate (double the bitrate is a good planning target).

## Troubleshooting

**"New live event" still missing after enabling the policy.** Confirm the change actually landed on the user's assigned policy (`Get-CsOnlineUser ... | Select TeamsMeetingBroadcastPolicy`), not just Global. Verify license and coexistence mode from Step 1. Have the user fully sign out and back in — policy propagation to the client can take several hours. Note that the Teams desktop client does not support live events on Surface Hub; on Surface Hub, users can only join as viewers via the Edge browser.

**Encoder will not connect to the ingest URL.** Re-copy the RTMP URL **and** key (a stale or truncated key is the usual culprit). Confirm ports 1935/1936 and `*.rtmpingest.mcr.teams.microsoft.com` are open on the encoder's network. Test from a network outside the corporate VPN/firewall to isolate a blocking device. Some encoders implement RTMPS in a way Teams does not accept — fall back to RTMP on 1935 or confirm the encoder is on Microsoft's supported/tested list.

**Encoder connects but no producer preview.** Allow several seconds after the feed starts. Confirm both audio and video streams are being sent (video-only or audio-only feeds will not preview or play). Refresh the producer page in Teams — leaving/reloading the page does not stop the event.

**"Maximum number of events reached" when starting.** The tenant hit the 15 concurrent event limit. A Teams admin can stop lower-priority events to free capacity for a high-priority one.

**Feed is glitchy, dropping frames, or low quality.** This is almost always upload bandwidth or encoder configuration. Verify the site's upload speed exceeds the configured bitrate, use a wired connection, match the recommended encoder settings exactly, watch encoder CPU load, and update encoder firmware/software. Restarting the encoder mid-stream will briefly error for viewers, who then must reload.

**Viewers see an error after the event ends.** The encoder was disconnected before **Stop event** was selected. Always stop the event in Teams first.

**Some viewers fine, others at one site buffering.** Localized congestion. If no eCDN is deployed, plan roughly 2 Mbps of download per concurrent viewer per location and deploy Microsoft eCDN or a partner eCDN. Confirm the CDN bypass domains (`*.bmc.cdn.office.net`, `*.ml.cdn.office.net`) are not being routed through a proxy or SSL-inspected.

**Anonymous/external attendees blocked from a public event.** Confirm `BroadcastAttendeeVisibilityMode` is `Everyone` on the organizer's policy (Step 4) **and** that the event itself was created with the "Everyone" permission. Both the policy and the per-event setting must allow anonymous access. Note anonymous users cannot be added as producers or presenters.

**Viewers in China cannot join.** Azure CDN, which live events depend on, may be unreachable in China. A VPN back to the corporate network is typically required for those users.

**VPN forced-tunnel degrading playback.** For clients on a forced-tunnel VPN, configure a split-tunnel exception so attendee CDN traffic (`*.ml.cdn.office.net`, TCP/UDP 443) goes direct rather than over the VPN.

## Prevention

- **Plan the migration to Teams town hall now.** With live events retiring in July 2026, build new large-scale events on town hall and reserve live events for in-flight commitments only.
- **Standardize policy design.** Keep one clearly named policy per audience (for example, `EventProducers-Enabled`) and assign by security group with `New-CsGroupPolicyAssignment` rather than per user. Keep the Global policy at your least-privileged default.
- **Provision eCDN well ahead of any large event.** Because provisioning takes 4–24 hours and pre-scheduled events do not adopt eCDN retroactively, enable it early and re-create any events scheduled before provisioning completed.
- **Run a full dry run** on the actual production network at least a day before, at least an hour before for high-scale events. Validate encoder connectivity, producer preview, recording, captions, and a test viewer join.
- **Pre-stage network access:** open RTMP ingest ports/domains, exempt the CDN download domains from proxy and SSL inspection, and confirm upload bandwidth headroom (target double the stream bitrate) at the encoder site.
- **Use wired connections and CBR** on encoders, keep firmware current, and never alter encoder settings once the stream is pushing.
- **Document the event support URL** org-wide so attendees always have a working contact path during an event.

Title: TMS-078: Teams Meeting Breakout Rooms Not Working
Content:
# Teams Meeting Breakout Rooms Not Working

**Category:** Teams > Meetings
**Article Code:** TMS-078
**Tier:** 2
**Audience:** Administrators / Technicians (with end-user guidance)
**Estimated Resolution Time:** 15-45 minutes (plus up to 24 hours for policy propagation)

## Symptoms / When to Use

Use this article when an organizer reports one or more of the following:

- The **Rooms** (breakout rooms) icon is missing from the meeting control bar during a live meeting.
- The **Breakout rooms** option does not appear under **More options** when editing a scheduled meeting.
- Breakout rooms can be created but cannot be **opened**, or participants are not moved into their assigned rooms.
- A presenter cannot be appointed as a **breakout room manager**, or the appointed manager sees no controls.
- Pre-assignment of participants is unavailable ("Assign participants" greyed out).
- The feature works for some organizers but not others in the same tenant.
- Breakout rooms are missing after the organizer joined from Teams web, a mobile device, or a Teams Room.

## Background

Breakout rooms are gated at three layers. A failure at any layer produces the symptoms above:

1. **Tenant policy.** The `CsTeamsMeetingPolicy` assigned to the **organizer** controls availability via the `AllowBreakoutRooms` parameter (Boolean, default `True`). The policy that matters is the organizer's, not the attendee's. If the organizer holds a custom or restricted policy with the setting disabled, no one in that meeting gets breakout rooms.
2. **Client and role.** Only a **meeting organizer, co-organizer, or an appointed breakout room manager** can create and manage rooms. Managers must be a **presenter in the organizer's own organization** — external/guest presenters cannot be made managers. Creation and management require **Teams on desktop** (Windows or macOS). The Teams web client and mobile apps can *participate* in rooms but cannot create or manage them.
3. **Meeting state.** Pre-meeting configuration only surfaces **after meeting invites have been sent**. Automatic participant assignment must be done up front — you cannot switch to automatic assignment later in the meeting.

Policy changes are not instant. Assignment of a Teams meeting policy typically applies within a few hours but can take **up to 24 hours** to fully propagate. The affected user must also fully restart Teams to pick up the change.

## Resolution

Work top-down: confirm the organizer's policy first, then role/client, then meeting configuration.

### Step 1: Connect to Microsoft Teams PowerShell

Install (once) and connect using the MicrosoftTeams module.

```powershell
Install-Module -Name MicrosoftTeams -Scope CurrentUser -Force
Connect-MicrosoftTeams
```

### Step 2: Identify the policy assigned to the organizer

Breakout room availability follows the organizer. Confirm which meeting policy that user holds.

```powershell
Get-CsUserPolicyAssignment -Identity "organizer@contoso.com" -PolicyType TeamsMeetingPolicy
```

If no per-user policy is returned, the user inherits the **Global (Org-wide default)** policy.

### Step 3: Check the AllowBreakoutRooms setting on that policy

Inspect the specific policy identified in Step 2 (replace `Global` with the policy name if a custom one is assigned).

```powershell
Get-CsTeamsMeetingPolicy -Identity "Global" | Select-Object Identity, AllowBreakoutRooms
```

`AllowBreakoutRooms` must be `True`. If it is `False`, continue to Step 4.

### Step 4: Enable breakout rooms on the policy

Update the policy in place. This affects every user assigned to it.

```powershell
Set-CsTeamsMeetingPolicy -Identity "Global" -AllowBreakoutRooms $true
```

If you must not change a shared policy for all its users, create a dedicated policy instead:

```powershell
New-CsTeamsMeetingPolicy -Identity "Allow-BreakoutRooms" -AllowBreakoutRooms $true
```

### Step 5: Assign the policy to the affected organizer

Only needed if you created a new policy in Step 4.

```powershell
Grant-CsTeamsMeetingPolicy -Identity "organizer@contoso.com" -PolicyName "Allow-BreakoutRooms"
```

To roll the change out to a group rather than individual users, use group-based assignment:

```powershell
New-CsGroupPolicyAssignment -GroupId "<group-object-id>" -PolicyType TeamsMeetingPolicy -PolicyName "Allow-BreakoutRooms" -Rank 1
```

### Step 6: Confirm the effective assignment and have the user restart Teams

```powershell
Get-CsUserPolicyAssignment -Identity "organizer@contoso.com" -PolicyType TeamsMeetingPolicy
```

Instruct the organizer to fully quit Teams (right-click the tray icon > **Quit**, not just close the window) and relaunch. Allow up to 24 hours if the icon still does not appear.

### Step 7: Verify the portal setting (GUI alternative)

If you prefer the admin center or need to confirm PowerShell changes landed:

1. Go to the [Teams admin center](https://admin.teams.microsoft.com/).
2. Navigate to **Meetings** > **Meeting policies**.
3. Open the policy assigned to the organizer.
4. Under **Meeting engagement**, confirm **Breakout rooms** is **On**.
5. Select **Save**.

### Step 8: Validate the meeting-level configuration

Have the organizer confirm the client-side prerequisites:

- They are joined on **Teams desktop** (Windows/macOS), signed in as the organizer or co-organizer.
- For pre-meeting setup, the meeting **invites have already been sent** — open the event > **More options** > **Breakout rooms**.
- To delegate, the intended manager is a **presenter within the organization**; then in the meeting select **Rooms** > **Rooms settings** > enable **Assign presenters to manage rooms**.

## Troubleshooting

**Icon present but rooms won't open.** Only **one** breakout room manager can control the rooms at a time. If a manager was appointed, the organizer must select **Rooms** > **Manage rooms** to take control back. Rooms also cannot open before the meeting has actually started.

**Participants aren't auto-moved into rooms.** Check **Rooms settings** > **Automatically move people to rooms**. When off, participants must click **Join** manually. When a time limit is set with auto-move off, participants choose whether to rejoin the main meeting.

**Cannot pre-assign or automatically assign later.** Automatic assignment is only offered at creation and only when invites were sent beforehand. If the meeting is already running without it, assign participants manually instead.

**Manager appointment fails.** The user must be an in-tenant **presenter** first (Meeting options > **Who can present**). External participants and guests are ineligible regardless of role.

**Works for one organizer, not another.** The two organizers hold different meeting policies. Re-run Steps 2-3 for the failing user; they are almost certainly on a policy with `AllowBreakoutRooms = $false`.

**Feature vanished mid-rollout.** Confirm the change wasn't overwritten by a **group policy assignment** with higher rank. Review effective assignment:

```powershell
Get-CsUserPolicyAssignment -Identity "organizer@contoso.com" -PolicyType TeamsMeetingPolicy
```

Direct (per-user) assignments win over group assignments; a stray group assignment can still confuse expectations if no direct assignment exists.

**Teams Room / web / mobile organizer.** These endpoints can join breakout rooms but cannot create or manage them. The organizer must manage from a desktop client, or appoint a desktop-based co-organizer/manager.

**Policy shows correct but UI still wrong.** Clear the Teams client cache after confirming the policy, then relaunch. Cached policy is a common cause of a correct backend setting not reflecting in the client.

## Prevention

- Keep `AllowBreakoutRooms = $true` in the **Global** policy unless a business reason requires disabling it, so the default experience is consistent.
- When restricting features, restrict narrowly with a dedicated policy rather than editing the Global policy that most users inherit.
- Standardize on **group-based policy assignment** for meeting policies so new hires inherit the correct settings automatically.
- Document that breakout room **creation/management is desktop-only** in end-user meeting guidance to cut ticket volume.
- Remind organizers to **send invites before** configuring rooms and to appoint co-organizers so meetings aren't dependent on a single host.
- After any meeting-policy change, note the up-to-24-hour propagation window in the ticket to set correct expectations.
